example: The cat was content to nap in the sun.
hook: Content means happy with what you have, like a cat curled up purring in a warm, sunny window.

traps.why: Restless means unable to settle, the opposite of content.
Constant looks like content but means always staying the same.
Thrilled is too strong; content is a calm, quiet kind of happy.

syn1.tip: Think of a cat purring in the sun. Content describes someone who doesn't want anything more.

sc1.stem: Other kids wanted fancy new toys, but Sam was _____ with his old bike and wished for nothing more.

traps.why: A disappointed kid would wish for more, but Sam wished for nothing more.
Sam knows his bike well, but the clue is about being satisfied.
Careless is about how he treats the bike, not how he feels.

sc1.tip: The words "wished for nothing more" tell you Sam was satisfied. The "but" sets him apart from kids who wanted more.

traps.why: Wanting more is the opposite of being content with what you have.
That fits the noun content, as in a book's content, not the adjective.
Giving permission is consent, a lookalike word, not content.

syn2.tip: A content person is pleased and calm. Ask yourself whether the choice shows someone who wants nothing more.

sc2.stem: After a big bowl of soup and a warm bath, Grandpa sat in his favorite chair, smiling quietly, perfectly _____ to spend the evening doing nothing at all.

traps.why: A smiling Grandpa resting in his chair is calm, not restless.
He is smiling about doing nothing, so he is not unwilling.
Nervous has a worried feeling, but the soup, bath, and smile feel peaceful.

sc2.tip: The cozy soup, warm bath, and quiet smile cause Grandpa to feel satisfied, wanting nothing more.

example: We spotted a rare bird in the marsh.
hook: A rare coin or a rare comet is one you might see only once in a lifetime.

traps.why: Ordinary things are everywhere, the opposite of rare.
Rare things are often valuable, but rare means not seen often.
Rear looks like rare but means at the back.

syn1.tip: Rare things are hard to find. Think of a rare bird you might spot only once in your life.

sc1.stem: Halley's Comet is _____, passing close enough to see only once every seventy-six years.

traps.why: Something seen once in seventy-six years is not common.
Comets can be bright, but the clue is about how seldom it appears.
The clue talks about time between visits, not distance.

sc1.tip: "Only once every seventy-six years" tells you the comet is seen very seldom.

traps.why: Plentiful means there is a lot, the opposite of rare.
Rare things can be precious, but rare is about how few there are.
Unknown goes too far; rare things are seen sometimes, just not often.

syn2.tip: Rare and scarce both describe things there are only a few of, like rare stamps.

sc2.stem: Robins visit our backyard every single morning, but a bright red cardinal is so _____ that we cheer whenever one lands on the feeder.

traps.why: The robins are familiar; the but shows the cardinal is different.
Birds at a feeder are hungry, but that wouldn't make us cheer.
Size doesn't explain why we cheer; how seldom it comes does.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts robins that come "every single morning" with the cardinal, so the cardinal must come seldom.

example: Building the fence took hours of labor.
hook: Labor Day honors people who do hard work, from building roads to farming fields.

traps.why: Rest is the break you take after labor, its opposite.
Label looks like labor but means a tag with words on it.
Tools are used during labor, but labor is the work itself.

syn1.tip: You may know Labor Day, a holiday honoring workers. Labor means work, especially hard work.

sc1.stem: Building the stone wall by hand took weeks of hard _____ in the hot sun.

traps.why: Building a wall by hand is the opposite of rest.
Planning comes first, but "by hand" points to physical work.
Hard luck is a phrase, but building needs effort, not luck.

sc1.tip: "By hand" and "hard" over "weeks" in the hot sun tell you the blank is tiring physical work.

traps.why: Time off is a break from work, the opposite of labor.
A sticky tag is a label, a lookalike word, not labor.
A quick chore is too small; labor is hard, tiring work.

syn2.tip: Labor is the kind of work that makes you sweat and ache, like digging or lifting stones.

sc2.stem: Raking every leaf in the yard by hand was exhausting _____, but blowing them into piles with Dad's leaf blower felt almost like play.

traps.why: Exhausting rest makes no sense; raking was the opposite of rest.
The leaf blower is the noisy part, and raking is the tiring part.
Label looks like labor but means a tag, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: The "but" contrasts raking with something that "felt almost like play," so raking must have been hard work.

example: Be honest about who broke the vase.
hook: Abraham Lincoln was nicknamed Honest Abe because people trusted him to tell the truth.

traps.why: Sneaky people hide the truth, the opposite of honest.
Honored looks like honest but means given respect or praise.
Polite is about good manners, not about telling the truth.

syn1.tip: Think of "Honest Abe," the nickname for Abraham Lincoln. An honest person always tells the truth.

sc1.stem: Even though no one saw her break the vase, Mia was _____ and told her mom exactly what had happened.

traps.why: A sneaky girl would hide it, not tell exactly what happened.
Breaking a vase is clumsy, but the clue is about telling the truth.
Mia told her mom everything, so she was not silent.

sc1.tip: "Even though no one saw her," Mia "told her mom exactly what had happened." Telling the truth is being honest.

traps.why: Fake means not real or true, the opposite of honest.
Humble means not bragging, which is a different good quality.
Honest people may say hard things, but rude means not polite.

syn2.tip: Honest describes someone you can trust to tell the truth and mean what they say, the same as sincere.

sc2.stem: The cashier gave Leo five extra dollars by mistake, and because he was _____, he walked right back and returned the money.

traps.why: A greedy boy would keep the money, not return it.
Getting extra money was lucky, but luck doesn't explain returning it.
Selfish people keep extra money; Leo gave it back.

sc2.tip: "Because he was _____" explains why Leo "returned the money." Giving back what isn't yours shows he tells the truth.

example: We saw ancient pottery at the museum.
hook: Ancient Egyptians built the pyramids over four thousand years ago, so ancient means very, very old.

traps.why: Modern means of today, the opposite of ancient.
Some ancient things are famous, but ancient is about age.
Ancient objects can be valuable, but ancient means very old.

syn1.tip: You've heard of ancient Egypt and ancient Rome. They existed thousands of years ago.

sc1.stem: The museum's _____ coins were made more than two thousand years ago, long before anyone invented paper money.

traps.why: Coins from two thousand years ago are not modern.
Coins can be shiny, but the clue is about how old they are.
Recent means made not long ago, the opposite of the clue.

sc1.tip: "More than two thousand years ago" and "long before anyone invented paper money" tell you the coins are very, very old.

traps.why: Brand new is the opposite of ancient.
A little old is too weak; ancient means very, very old.
Far away is about distance in space, not time.

syn2.tip: Ancient things belong to times long, long ago, like dinosaurs, pyramids, and castles.

sc2.stem: Our school was built just last year, but the oak tree beside it is _____, having grown there since long before the town even existed.

traps.why: The school is young; the but shows the tree is the opposite.
A tree older than the town is not recent.
Tiny is about size, and a tree growing that long would be big.

sc2.tip: The "but" contrasts a school built "just last year" with a tree that grew there "long before the town even existed."

example: Their journey across the country took a week.
hook: Journey comes from an old French word for a day's travel; now it means any long trip.

traps.why: A stay means remaining in one place, the opposite of a journey.
Journal looks like journey but means a diary.
You might use a map on a journey, but it isn't the trip.

syn1.tip: Picture packing a suitcase for a long ride. A journey is a long trip from one place to another.

sc1.stem: Each fall, the geese begin their long _____ south, flying thousands of miles to their winter home.

traps.why: Flying thousands of miles is the opposite of a rest.
Geese build nests, but the clue describes traveling, not a home.
Journal looks like journey but means a diary, which geese don't keep.

sc1.tip: "Flying thousands of miles to their winter home" describes a long trip.

traps.why: A short errand is too small; a journey is a long trip.
A diary entry belongs in a journal, a lookalike word.
A ticket helps you travel, but it isn't the trip itself.

syn2.tip: A journey is a long trip, and so is a voyage, which usually crosses water.

sc2.stem: Walking to the corner store takes two minutes, but driving to Grandma's house across three states is a _____ that takes two whole days.

traps.why: An errand is a short trip, too small for two whole days.
A stroll is a short walk, but this trip is a long drive.
A shortcut saves time, but this trip takes two whole days.

sc2.tip: The "but" contrasts a "two minutes" walk with a drive "across three states" taking "two whole days," which is a long trip.

example: She has a talent for drawing animals.
hook: A talent show lets kids share their natural gifts, like singing, juggling, or telling jokes.

traps.why: A weakness is something you are bad at, the opposite of talent.
Talon looks like talent but means a bird's sharp claw.
A hobby is something you enjoy, even if you aren't good at it.

syn1.tip: Think of a talent show, where people show off things they are naturally good at.

sc1.stem: Even as a toddler, Sara showed a natural _____ for drawing, sketching animals that looked almost real.

traps.why: Her lifelike drawings show skill, not a dislike for drawing.
Talon looks like talent but means a claw, which makes no sense here.
Someone afraid of drawing wouldn't sketch animals that look almost real.

sc1.tip: "Natural" and "even as a toddler" plus animals that "looked almost real" show a skill she was born with.

traps.why: A lack of ability is the opposite of a talent.
Talent might win a prize, but the prize isn't the skill.
Practice builds skill, but talent is the skill you're born with.

syn2.tip: A talent is something you are good at naturally, without much training, like having an ear for music.

sc2.stem: Jake practiced the piano for hours and still struggled, but his little sister had such _____ that she played songs perfectly after hearing them once.

traps.why: Jake had trouble; the but shows his sister was the opposite.
Jake is the one who practiced; she played after hearing songs once.
Playing after one listen shows skill, not patience.

sc2.tip: The "but" contrasts Jake's hours of struggling with his sister playing perfectly "after hearing them once," which shows natural skill.

example: The answer was obvious once I read the clue.
hook: When something is obvious, it's right in front of your nose, like an elephant standing in the classroom.

traps.why: Hidden things are hard to see, the opposite of obvious.
Oblivious looks like obvious but means not noticing anything.
Something can be easy to see without being important.

syn1.tip: Obvious things are easy to spot, like a stain on a white shirt. Ask yourself whether everyone could see it.

sc1.stem: With frosting smeared all over his nose, it was _____ to everyone that the dog had eaten the cake.

traps.why: Frosting on his nose made it clear, not unclear.
Frosting everywhere means nothing about it was secret.
Oblivious looks like obvious but means not noticing, which doesn't fit.

sc1.tip: "Frosting smeared all over his nose" is proof anyone could see, so the blank means easy to see.

traps.why: Hard to find is the opposite of obvious.
Obvious is about seeing or understanding, not about doing a task.
Obvious things usually aren't surprising, since everyone can see them.

syn2.tip: If the answer is obvious, you can see it right away without searching.

sc2.stem: Dad thought he had hidden the birthday present well, but the huge, bike-shaped box in the garage made his surprise _____ to the whole family.

traps.why: A huge box in plain view did not keep the surprise secret.
A bike-shaped box gives the surprise away, so it isn't mysterious.
A huge box in the garage is the opposite of invisible.

sc2.tip: The "but" shows Dad's hiding failed. A "huge, bike-shaped box" makes the surprise easy for anyone to see.

example: The cat had a scheme to reach the fish.
hook: A scheme is a sneaky plan, like a cartoon cat plotting step by step to catch a mouse.

traps.why: An accident is unplanned, the opposite of a scheme.
Scream looks a little like scheme but means a loud cry.
A scheme can be tricky like a puzzle, but it is a plan.

syn1.tip: Picture a villain rubbing his hands together and plotting. He is working on a scheme, a secret plan.

sc1.stem: The twins came up with a sneaky _____ to get extra dessert: one would distract Dad while the other grabbed cookies.

traps.why: The twins worked out steps ahead of time, so it wasn't an accident.
Recipes make desserts, but the twins planned to grab cookies, not bake.
An apology says sorry; a sneaky trick has the opposite feeling.

sc1.tip: "Sneaky" plus the steps after the colon, "one would distract Dad while the other grabbed cookies," describe a secret plan.

traps.why: A lucky accident happens without planning, the opposite of a scheme.
That fits color scheme, a different use, not a sneaky plan.
A scheme is often sneaky; an honest promise has the opposite feeling.

syn2.tip: A scheme is a plan someone works out ahead of time, often in secret, like a plot in a story.

sc2.stem: Instead of just knocking over the trash can, the clever raccoon seemed to follow a careful _____, lifting the lid, pulling out one bag, and dragging it under the porch.

traps.why: A careful accident makes no sense; the raccoon acted on purpose.
Raccoons sniff for food, but the steps describe a plan, not a smell.
Scream looks a little like scheme but means a loud cry.

sc2.tip: "Instead of just knocking over" the can, the raccoon did steps in order. A "careful" set of steps is a clever plan.

example: We took a brief break between classes.
hook: A brief speech is over almost before it starts, like a quick thank-you before dinner.

traps.why: Lengthy means long, the opposite of brief.
Brave starts like brief but means not afraid.
A brief talk might be quiet, but brief is about time.

syn1.tip: A brief break between classes lasts only a few minutes. Brief means it doesn't take long.

sc1.stem: The rain shower was _____, lasting only two minutes before the sun came back out over the ballfield.

traps.why: Two minutes of rain is the opposite of endless.
Rain that stopped after two minutes was not constant.
Steady describes how rain falls, not how long it lasts.

sc1.tip: "Lasting only two minutes" tells you the shower did not last long.

traps.why: Endless means it never stops, the opposite of brief.
Sudden means happening without warning, not lasting a short time.
Tiny is about size, but brief is about how long something lasts.

syn2.tip: Brief things end soon, like a quick nap or a short message.

sc2.stem: Mr. Lee usually gives long speeches, but this morning his announcement was so _____ that it ended before we even finished hanging up our coats.

traps.why: His usual speeches are lengthy; the but shows this one was different.
Loudness doesn't explain why it ended so fast.
A boring talk wouldn't end sooner; the clue is about time.

sc2.tip: The "but" contrasts Mr. Lee's usual "long speeches" with one that "ended before we even finished hanging up our coats."

meaning: a large amount of money or riches
example: The pirate dreamed of great wealth.
hook: Picture a dragon asleep on a mountain of gold coins and jewels: that glittering pile is its wealth.

traps.why: Poverty means being poor, the opposite of wealth.
Health rhymes with wealth, but it means how well your body is.
A bank holds money, but wealth is the riches themselves.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "fame and wealth." Wealthy people are rich, so wealth means riches.

sc1.stem: The king's _____ filled ten rooms with gold coins, jewels, and silver crowns.

traps.why: Poverty means being poor, but the rooms are full of gold.
A king wears a crown, but one crown cannot fill ten rooms.
Health sounds like wealth, but health cannot be gold coins and jewels.

sc1.tip: The clue is "filled ten rooms with gold coins, jewels, and silver crowns." That much treasure is a huge amount of riches.

traps.why: A lack means not having enough, the opposite of wealth.
A wallet holds money, but it is not a large amount of riches.
One coin is far too small; wealth means a large amount of money.

syn2.tip: A wealthy person is rich. Look for the choice that means a big pile of money, like winning a fortune.

sc2.stem: Although the old farmer wore patched overalls and drove a rusty truck, he had great _____ hidden away: piles of gold bars in his barn.

traps.why: Patched clothes hint at poverty, but "gold bars" shows he was rich.
Health sounds like wealth, but health cannot be gold bars hidden away.
Rich people may be famous, but fame cannot be hidden in a barn.

sc2.tip: The word "Although" warns you the farmer is not what he looks like. "Piles of gold bars" tells you he had riches.

meaning: extremely large in size or area
example: The vast desert stretched for miles.
hook: Stand on a ship with ocean in every direction and no land in sight: that is a vast sea.

traps.why: Tiny means very small, the opposite of vast.
Fast rhymes with vast, but it is about speed, not size.
Vast places are often empty, but vast is about size, not emptiness.

syn1.tip: Think of "the vast ocean" or "the vast sky." Both stretch on and on, so vast means very big.

sc1.stem: The prairie was _____, a wide-open area spreading flat in every direction for hundreds of miles without a single hill.

traps.why: Narrow means thin, but the prairie is "wide-open."
Hilly is about land shape, but the prairie has no hill at all.
Fast sounds like vast, but land cannot be fast.

sc1.tip: The words after the comma explain the blank: "a wide-open area spreading flat in every direction for hundreds of miles." That means huge.

traps.why: Cramped means squeezed and small, the opposite of vast.
Vague starts like vast, but it means unclear.
Vast lands stretch far, but distant means far away, not huge.

syn2.tip: Picture a vast desert stretching for miles. Pick the word that means extremely big.

sc2.stem: Our classroom fish tank seemed big to us, but compared with the _____ Pacific Ocean, which covers a third of Earth, it was a tiny puddle.

traps.why: The ocean covers a third of Earth, so it is not small.
Frozen is about temperature; the clue is about how big the ocean is.
Vague means unclear, and an ocean is not unclear.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets up a contrast: next to the ocean, the tank is a "tiny puddle." So the ocean must be enormous.

example: The curious child asked a hundred questions.
hook: Curious George, the little monkey who pokes into everything, shows what curious means: always wanting to find out more.

traps.why: Bored means not interested, the opposite of curious.
Furious rhymes with curious, but it means very angry.
Cautious looks similar, but it means careful.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "curious about." If you are curious about bugs, you are interested in them and want to know more.

sc1.stem: The _____ toddler kept opening every drawer and asking "What's this?" about each thing she found inside.

traps.why: A bored toddler would not keep asking "What's this?"
The toddler is opening drawers to learn, not to put things away.
Furious sounds like curious, but nothing shows the toddler is angry.

sc1.tip: The clue is "asking 'What's this?' about each thing." Someone who keeps asking questions wants to learn.

traps.why: Not interested is the opposite of curious.
Curious begins like cure, but it has nothing to do with healing.
Curious people often learn a lot, but curious means wanting to know.

syn2.tip: A curious child asks a hundred questions. Choose the phrase about wanting to know things.

sc2.stem: Because Mia was so _____ about how volcanoes work, she checked out every library book on them and asked her teacher dozens of questions.

traps.why: If Mia were certain, she would not need dozens of questions.
Furious sounds like curious, but being angry would not make her read.
Cautious means careful, which does not explain all her questions.

sc2.tip: The word "Because" points to a cause. Reading "every library book" and asking "dozens of questions" are effects of wanting to know.

example: The puppy looked innocent next to the torn pillow.
hook: A puppy sitting beside a shredded pillow with big sweet eyes is trying hard to look innocent.

traps.why: Guilty means you did the wrong thing, the opposite of innocent.
Babies seem innocent, but innocent does not mean young.
Decent ends like innocent, but it means good enough or proper.

syn1.tip: In a courtroom, a person is found "innocent" or "guilty." Innocent means no one should blame you.

sc1.stem: The video proved that Jack was _____; he had not been anywhere near the window when the baseball broke it.

traps.why: Jack was nowhere near the window, so he could not be guilty.
Careless means not careful, but Jack was not even there.
Decent looks like innocent, but the video proves where he was, not manners.

sc1.tip: The clue is "he had not been anywhere near the window." If he wasn't there, he did not break it.

traps.why: Proven guilty is the opposite of innocent.
Blamed people can feel nervous, but that does not make them innocent.
Someone not caught might still have done it.

syn2.tip: Innocent starts with in-, meaning not. Innocent people did not do the wrong thing.

sc2.stem: Everyone blamed Max for eating the cookies, but he was actually _____; his little sister confessed that she had taken them all.

traps.why: "But" shows a switch: his sister took them, so Max was not guilty.
Hungry is about cookies, but the clue is about who took them.
His sister took the cookies, so nothing shows Max was greedy.

sc2.tip: The word "but" tells you Max is the opposite of what everyone thought. His sister "confessed," so Max did nothing wrong.

example: The legend tells of a giant who lived here.
hook: Robin Hood and King Arthur are legends: famous old stories retold so long that nobody knows how much is true.

traps.why: A fact is surely true; a legend is an old story that may not be.
A map's legend is its key, but here legend means an old story.
Some legends are told in poems, but a legend is the story itself.

syn1.tip: Think of "the legend of King Arthur." A legend is a famous old story, just like a myth.

sc1.stem: According to the town's famous old _____, a giant fish has lived at the bottom of Silver Lake for two hundred years.

traps.why: A map legend is a key, but a key cannot say a fish lives there.
Stories may teach lessons, but "famous old" points to the story itself.
A giant fish living two hundred years sounds like a tale, not a fact.

sc1.tip: Look at "famous old" and the giant fish living "for two hundred years." That sounds like a story people have told for ages.

traps.why: A news report tells true, new events, not old stories.
A star can be called a legend, but the word's main meaning is a story.
History books tell what really happened; legends may be made up.

syn2.tip: Legends are stories like Paul Bunyan or Robin Hood. Pick the phrase that means a story from long ago.

sc2.stem: Grandpa swears the tale of the ghost ship is true history, but Mom says it is only a _____ that sailors made up and retold for centuries.

traps.why: Mom disagrees with Grandpa, so she would not call it a fact.
A map legend is a key, but sailors did not make up a key.
Mom is saying the story isn't true, not that it teaches something.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "true history," and "made up and retold for centuries" describes an old story that may not be true.

example: There was an odd smell coming from the fridge.
hook: If your dog suddenly started meowing like a cat, that would be odd: strange and out of the ordinary.

traps.why: Normal means usual, the opposite of odd.
Old looks a bit like odd, but it is about age.
Odd things can be scary, but odd just means unusual.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "that's odd" when something doesn't make sense. Odd means weird or not usual.

sc1.stem: It was an _____ morning, a little strange but not spooky, because the usually noisy parrot hadn't said one word.

traps.why: The morning was "a little strange," so it was not ordinary.
Eerie means spooky, but the sentence says "not spooky."
Early is about the time, but the clue is about something strange.

sc1.tip: The words after the comma explain the blank: "a little strange but not spooky." Pick the word that means just strange.

traps.why: Typical means just like usual, the opposite of odd.
Terrifying is far too strong; odd just means a little strange.
Even only pairs with odd when talking about numbers.

syn2.tip: Think of "the odd one out," the thing that doesn't match the rest. Odd means not usual.

sc2.stem: Most cats run from water, so it was _____ that my cat Pepper jumped into the bathtub and splashed around happily.

traps.why: Most cats avoid water, so Pepper's splashing was not expected.
Even pairs with odd for numbers, not for strange behavior.
Pepper splashed happily, so nothing terrible happened; it was just surprising.

sc2.tip: The sentence says "Most cats run from water," but Pepper jumped in. Doing the opposite of most cats is strange.

example: I felt nervous before my piano recital.
hook: Butterflies in your stomach before a big test are that nervous feeling, your nerves buzzing with worry.

traps.why: Calm means peaceful, the opposite of nervous.
Terrified is much too strong; nervous is a smaller worry.
Excited is a happy jittery feeling, but nervous is worried.

syn1.tip: Think of "nervous before a test." That uneasy, worried feeling is the same as being anxious.

sc1.stem: Simon's hands shook and his stomach fluttered before his first piano recital; he had never felt so _____ in his life.

traps.why: Shaking hands and a fluttering stomach do not show a calm person.
Cold can make hands shake, but the clue is the recital, not weather.
Proud is a good feeling, but the clues show worry.

sc1.tip: The clues are "hands shook" and "stomach fluttered" right "before his first piano recital." Those are signs of worry.

traps.why: Relaxed means loose and easy, the opposite of nervous.
Having "the nerve" can mean being bold, but nervous means worried.
Nerves can upset your stomach, but nervous is not the same as sick.

syn2.tip: Picture shaky hands before a recital. Nervous means feeling uneasy about what might happen.

sc2.stem: Lena usually chats happily with everyone, but on the morning of the spelling bee she was so _____ that she bit her nails and couldn't eat breakfast.

traps.why: "But" shows she was not her usual happy self that morning.
Bold people don't bite their nails and skip breakfast from worry.
A hungry person would eat, but Lena "couldn't eat breakfast."

sc2.tip: The word "but" means Lena was different from usual. Biting her nails and not eating are what worry makes people do.

example: It looked like an ordinary rock, but it glowed.
hook: An ordinary day follows the usual order: wake up, go to school, do homework, eat dinner, go to bed.

traps.why: Special means set apart from others, the opposite of ordinary.
Ordinary contains order, but it doesn't mean neat or in order.
Ordinary things aren't always boring; ordinary just means usual.

syn1.tip: Superheroes do extraordinary things, which means beyond ordinary. So ordinary means usual and common.

sc1.stem: Nothing special happened that day; it was just an _____ Tuesday of school, homework, and dinner.

traps.why: "Nothing special happened," so the day was not exciting.
Awful means very bad, but the day was just regular.
The day was full of school, homework, and dinner, so not empty.

sc1.tip: The clue is "Nothing special happened that day." A day with "school, homework, and dinner" is a normal one.

traps.why: Unique means one of a kind, the opposite of ordinary.
Ordinary looks like it holds order, but it doesn't mean neat.
Dull is a negative word; ordinary is not good or bad.

syn2.tip: Think of "just an ordinary day." Nothing special happens, so ordinary means normal.

sc2.stem: Everyone expected the magician's hat to be special, but when Jake looked inside, it was just an _____ black hat with no secret pocket at all.

traps.why: "But" shows the hat was not special or amazing at all.
Ordinary contains order, but the clue is about not being special.
Nothing says the hat was bad; it was just plain.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "special," and "just" and "no secret pocket" show the hat was nothing unusual.

example: Can you assist me with these heavy boxes?
hook: In basketball, an assist is the pass that helps a teammate score, and to assist someone is to help them.

traps.why: To block someone is to get in their way, the opposite of assist.
Insist sounds like assist, but it means to demand firmly.
Rescue means save from danger, much stronger than simply helping.

syn1.tip: A teacher's assistant is someone who helps the teacher. To assist means to help.

sc1.stem: On the first day of school, the fifth graders will _____ the kindergartners by helping them find their classrooms.

traps.why: The fifth graders are helping, so they are not ignoring the little kids.
Helping kids find classrooms is kind, not scary.
The fifth graders lead the way, so they are not following.

sc1.tip: The clue is "by helping them find their classrooms." The word "by" explains how, so the blank means to help.

traps.why: Getting in the way is the opposite of assisting.
A boss gives orders; an assistant helps with the work.
A basketball assist is a pass, but assist itself means to help.

syn2.tip: Think of "Can you assist me with these boxes?" That person wants you to help them.

sc2.stem: Grandma could not carry all the grocery bags by herself, so I offered to _____ her by taking the two heaviest ones up the stairs.

traps.why: Carrying her bags is not ignoring Grandma.
You might visit Grandma, but carrying bags is not visiting.
Resist sounds a little like assist, but it means to fight against.

sc2.tip: The word "so" shows cause and effect: Grandma "could not carry all the grocery bags," so you took some to help her.

example: You must obtain a ticket to enter.
hook: To obtain a library card, a ticket, or a prize is to get it, usually by asking or working for it.

traps.why: Lose is the opposite of obtain.
Obey starts like obtain, but it means to follow orders.
Keeping is holding on to something; obtaining is getting it first.

syn1.tip: Think of "obtain a ticket." If you obtain something, you end up with it, so it means to get.

sc1.stem: To _____ a library card, you must fill out a form and show proof of where you live.

traps.why: You don't fill out a form to lose a library card.
Obey looks like obtain, but you can't obey a card.
You read library books, but you don't fill out a form to read a card.

sc1.tip: The clue is "fill out a form and show proof of where you live." Those are the steps to get a card.

traps.why: To give something away is the opposite of obtaining it.
Explain rhymes with obtain, but it means to make clear.
You may want something, but obtaining it means you actually get it.

syn2.tip: Obtain ends like gain and sounds a bit like it. Both mean to get something you didn't have before.

sc2.stem: Tickets for the concert sold out in minutes, so even though Ben waited in line all night, he was unable to _____ a single one.

traps.why: Ben never had a ticket, so losing one makes no sense.
Explain sounds like obtain, but explaining a ticket makes no sense.
Ben waited all night, so he clearly wanted one; he just couldn't get it.

sc2.tip: The clue is "sold out in minutes" and "even though Ben waited in line." The tickets were gone, so he could not get one.

example: Can you recall your first day of school?
hook: To recall is to call a memory back into your mind, the way you might call a dog back home.

traps.why: Forget is the opposite of recall.
Recall looks like "call again," but it means bringing back a memory.
Imagining makes up something new; recalling brings back something that really happened.

syn1.tip: Think of "re" meaning back. When you recall something, you call it back into your mind.

sc1.stem: Grandpa can still _____ the name of every kid in his third-grade class, even sixty years later.

traps.why: "Still" and "sixty years later" praise his memory, so forget is backwards.
He learned the names long ago; now he is bringing them back.
Call is inside recall, but the sentence is about memory, not calling out.

sc1.tip: "Can still" and "even sixty years later" tell you Grandpa hasn't lost the names. The word means to remember.

traps.why: Putting something out of mind is forgetting, the opposite of recall.
Call is inside recall, but recall isn't about shouting.
A reminder helps memory, but recall means the remembering itself.

syn2.tip: Try it in a question: "Can you recall her name?" means "Can you remember her name?"

sc2.stem: My little sister forgot where she hid her candy, but I could easily _____ the exact spot because I watched her put it under the couch.

traps.why: "But" sets you against her forgetting, so you remember instead.
Hiding is what your sister did; you are bringing the spot back to mind.
Guessing means not being sure; watching her means you know for certain.

sc2.tip: "Forgot... but" sets up a contrast, and "because I watched her" shows you know the spot. You need a word meaning remember.

example: The river's rapid current carried the leaf away.
hook: River rapids are the fast, rushing parts of a river where rafts zoom over the rocks.

traps.why: Slow is the opposite of rapid.
Fast rivers are often loud, but rapid is about speed, not sound.
River rapids are rocky, but rapid as a describing word means fast.

syn1.tip: Think of river rapids, where the water rushes along. Rapid describes something that moves or happens fast.

sc1.stem: Bamboo shows _____ growth, shooting up as much as three feet in a single day.

traps.why: Three feet in one day is the opposite of slow.
Bamboo is green, but the clue is about how fast it grows.
Slight means a little; three feet a day is a lot, and fast.

sc1.tip: "Three feet in a single day" is a huge amount of growth in a tiny time. That means very fast.

traps.why: Gradual means little by little, the opposite of rapid.
Early is about when something happens; rapid is about how fast.
Steady means even and constant; it doesn't say anything about being fast.

syn2.tip: You may know "rapid fire" or "rapid breathing." Both mean happening very fast.

sc2.stem: Unlike the slow, creaky elevator in our old building, the new one is so _____ that we reach the tenth floor in just a few seconds.

traps.why: "Unlike the slow" elevator tells you the new one is not slow.
A quiet elevator isn't the reason you reach the tenth floor in seconds.
Shiny is about looks; reaching the top in seconds is about speed.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the slow" tells you the new elevator is the opposite of slow, and "in just a few seconds" confirms it.

example: Water is vital for all living things.
hook: Your vital organs, like your heart and lungs, are the ones you cannot live without.

traps.why: Unneeded is the opposite of vital.
Vital things often keep you healthy, but vital means necessary.
Helpful is too weak; vital means you truly cannot do without it.

syn1.tip: Doctors check your "vital signs," like your heartbeat. Those are signs of things you must have to stay alive.

sc1.stem: Sunlight is _____ for plants; without it, they cannot make food and will not survive.

traps.why: Plants die without sunlight, so sunlight helps them; harmful is backwards.
Sunlight is warm, but the clue says plants can't survive without it.
Pleasant is too mild; plants die without sunlight, so it's needed.

sc1.tip: "Without it, they cannot make food and will not survive" means plants must have sunlight. Look for a word meaning necessary.

traps.why: Not needed at all is the opposite of vital.
A little helpful is much too weak; vital means a must.
Health is a related topic, but vital means very important in general.

syn2.tip: Think of your vital organs, like your heart. You can't live without them, so vital means very important.

sc2.stem: Dad said the snacks were nice to have, but the water bottle was _____ on our long desert hike, since we could not go a mile without a drink.

traps.why: "But" contrasts the water with things that are just nice to have.
Useful is too weak; not going a mile without a drink means necessary.
Visual looks a bit like vital, but it means about seeing.

sc2.tip: "Nice to have, but" sets up a contrast: the water is more than nice. "Could not go a mile without a drink" shows it was necessary.

example: A balloon expands as you blow air into it.
hook: When something expands, it spreads out and gets bigger, like a balloon filling up as you blow air into it.

traps.why: Shrink is the opposite of expand.
Explode is far too strong; expanding is growing bigger, not bursting apart.
Explain starts the same way, but it means to make something clear.

syn1.tip: Picture a balloon you blow up. As it expands, it gets larger and larger.

sc1.stem: When you heat popcorn, each little kernel will _____ to many times its size and burst open.

traps.why: "Many times its size" means getting bigger, the opposite of shrinking.
Heat can melt things, but melting doesn't make anything many times bigger.
Kernels may brown, but darkening doesn't make them many times bigger.

sc1.tip: "To many times its size" tells you the kernel gets much bigger. Choose the word that means grow larger.

traps.why: Getting smaller is the opposite of expanding.
Ex- can mean out, but expand means grow bigger, not go outside.
Balloons fill with air, but expand covers anything that grows larger.

syn2.tip: You might hear that a store will "expand" by adding more space. That means it will grow bigger.

sc2.stem: Our school has so many new students that the principal plans to _____ the library, giving everyone more room to sit and read.

traps.why: Shrinking the library would give everyone less room, not more.
Painting changes how the library looks but doesn't add any room.
Closing the library would give students no room at all.

sc2.tip: "So many new students" is the cause, and "giving everyone more room" is the effect. The library must get bigger.

meaning: bravery when facing danger or fear
example: It took courage to sing on stage alone.
hook: The Cowardly Lion in The Wizard of Oz went searching for courage, the bravery to face his fears.

traps.why: Fear is the opposite of courage.
Rage hides inside courage, but it means wild anger, not bravery.
Strength is about muscles; courage is about facing fear.

syn1.tip: Think of the Cowardly Lion, who wanted courage. He wanted to stop being scared and act brave.

sc1.stem: It took great _____ for Mia to jump off the high dive, even though her knees were shaking with fear.

traps.why: Mia felt fear; what she needed to jump anyway was bravery.
Patience is about waiting; the clue is about being afraid.
Rage is wild anger; Mia was scared, not angry.

sc1.tip: "Even though her knees were shaking with fear" shows Mia was scared but jumped anyway. Doing something while afraid takes bravery.

traps.why: Being afraid is the opposite of courage.
Reckless is a negative word for foolish risks; courage is admired.
You may feel proud after brave acts, but pride isn't bravery.

syn2.tip: Courage is a good, admired quality. Firefighters and heroes have it when they face danger.

sc2.stem: Telling the truth about the broken vase felt scary, but Leo found the _____ to admit it, and his mom said she was proud of how brave he was.

traps.why: Leo already felt fear; he found the opposite to admit it.
His mom felt pride, but Leo needed bravery to speak up.
An excuse avoids blame, but Leo bravely admitted what he did.

sc2.tip: "Felt scary, but" and "how brave he was" tell you Leo faced his fear. The missing word means bravery.

example: We reached the summit by lunchtime.
hook: Picture a flag planted at the summit, the very tip-top of a snowy mountain.

traps.why: The base is the bottom of a mountain, the opposite of the summit.
Summit begins with sum, but it means a mountain top, not a total.
A slope is the side of a mountain, not its top.

syn1.tip: Climbers race to reach the summit. It's the highest point, where there's nowhere higher to go.

sc1.stem: After climbing for six hours, the hikers finally stood on the _____ and could see the whole valley below.

traps.why: After six hours of climbing, they were at the top, not the bottom.
The valley is what they saw below them, not where they stood.
Summary looks like summit, but it means a short retelling, not a place.

sc1.tip: "After climbing for six hours" and "see the whole valley below" tell you they reached the highest spot, the mountain top.

traps.why: The lowest point is the opposite of the summit.
A steep trail leads up a mountain, but the summit is the top.
Summary looks like summit, but it means a short retelling.

syn2.tip: Hikers say "we made it to the summit" when they reach the very top of the mountain.

sc2.stem: While the rest of us stayed at the bottom of the hill, my brother raced all the way up to the _____ and waved down at us from the very top.

traps.why: The base is the bottom, where everyone else stayed.
Middle is only partway; "all the way up" means the top.
A valley is low land between hills, not the top.

sc2.tip: "While the rest of us stayed at the bottom" sets up a contrast, and "from the very top" tells you exactly where he went.

meaning: luck; or a large amount of money
example: We had the good fortune of sunny weather.
hook: A fortune cookie promises good luck, and a fortune can also mean a huge pile of money.

traps.why: Skill comes from practice; luck just happens to you.
Fort is inside fortune, but fortune has nothing to do with castles.
You wish for luck, but a wish isn't luck itself.

syn1.tip: Think of a fortune cookie or "good fortune." Both are about luck coming your way.

sc1.stem: By good _____, we found Mom's lost ring in the sand just before the tide came in.

traps.why: Good manners are polite behavior; they don't help you find a lost ring.
Weather doesn't find rings; the lucky timing points to luck.
Being healthy has nothing to do with finding a ring just in time.

sc1.tip: "Good" plus a lucky find "just before the tide came in" points to luck. You've heard "by good luck" said the same way.

traps.why: A plan is made on purpose; fortune is what happens by chance.
Fortune tellers talk about the future, but fortune itself means luck.
Fourteen sounds a bit like fortune, but it's just a number.

syn2.tip: "By good fortune" means "by lucky chance." Fortune is what happens to you without your planning it.

sc2.stem: Hana had lost every raffle she had ever entered, but this year, with a bit of _____, her ticket was the one pulled from the jar.

traps.why: Practice can't help in a raffle; tickets are pulled by chance.
Sadness fits her past losses, but "but this year" turns things happy.
Trying hard can't change which raffle ticket gets pulled.

sc2.tip: "Lost every raffle... but this year" signals a change, and raffles are won by chance. The missing word means luck.

example: Grandpa told a tale about a magic horse.
hook: Tale sounds like tail, so picture a dog wagging its tail while Grandpa tells a tale.

traps.why: Tail sounds the same, but it's the part an animal wags.
Tile looks like tale, but it's a flat square on a floor.
An author writes stories, but the author isn't the story.

syn1.tip: You may know "fairy tale" or "tall tale." Both are kinds of stories.

sc1.stem: Every night at the campfire, Grandpa told us a _____ about a talking bear who lived in the hills.

traps.why: Tail sounds like tale, but you can't tell someone a tail.
A talking bear isn't real, so it can't be a fact.
Songs are sung, not told, and the clue says Grandpa told it.

sc1.tip: "Told us" plus a talking bear points to a made-up story. Campfires and grandparents are famous for telling these.

traps.why: Tail sounds like tale but means the end of an animal.
A list of facts has no plot; a tale tells events like a story.
The teller tells the tale, but the tale is the story itself.

syn2.tip: Tale and tell go together: you tell a tale. Think of fairy tales read at bedtime.

sc2.stem: My little brother's _____ about the dragon in our garage was so wild and silly that nobody believed a single word of it.

traps.why: Tail sounds like tale, but a tail has no words to believe.
Nobody believed it, so it was not a fact.
A drawing is a picture; "a single word of it" means it was told.

sc2.tip: "Nobody believed a single word of it" tells you he said something with words, and "wild and silly" shows it was a made-up story.

meaning: fully grown or sensible like an adult
example: She was very mature for her age.
hook: Mature fruit is ripe and ready to eat; a mature person acts grown-up and sensible.

traps.why: Childish is the opposite of mature.
Natural looks a lot like mature but means coming from nature.
Elderly is too strong; mature means grown up, not very old.

syn1.tip: When adults say "act mature," they mean act grown-up. Mature describes someone or something that is fully grown.

sc1.stem: Though only ten, Zara was so _____ that she calmly cared for her baby brother, acting just like a sensible grown-up.

traps.why: "Acting just like a sensible grown-up" is the opposite of childish.
She is young, but "though only ten" says she acts older.
Bossy is a negative word; she "calmly cared" for him, which is praise.

sc1.tip: "Acting just like a sensible grown-up" tells you what the word means. "Though only ten" is a contrast: she is young but acts older.

traps.why: Silly is the opposite of mature.
Being tall is about size; mature is about acting grown-up.
Strict is about rules; mature means sensible, not hard on others.

syn2.tip: Mature is a compliment. A mature kid makes good choices and stays calm, the way a sensible adult would.

sc2.stem: The apples on our tree were finally _____, so we picked them, and they tasted sweet and juicy instead of hard and sour.

traps.why: Green apples are not ready and taste hard and sour.
Rotten is past ready; rotten apples aren't sweet and juicy.
Natural looks like mature, but it doesn't explain why they turned sweet.

sc2.tip: "Finally" plus "sweet and juicy instead of hard and sour" tells you the apples were fully grown. The word means grown and ready.

meaning: a ship or boat; or a container
example: The vessel sailed into the harbor.
hook: A vessel carries things: a ship carries people over water, and your blood vessels carry blood around your body.

traps.why: Vessel starts like vest, but a vest is something you wear.
Ships stay in a harbor, but a harbor is a place, not a ship.
An anchor holds a ship in place; it isn't the ship.

syn1.tip: Think of a fishing vessel sailing out to sea. Big vessels carry people and cargo across water.

sc1.stem: The fishing _____ sailed out of the harbor at dawn, its nets piled high on the deck.

traps.why: The nets were on the boat; a net can't sail out of a harbor.
Vest looks like vessel, but a vest can't sail or have a deck.
A pier stays put at the shore; it can't sail out of a harbor.

sc1.tip: "Sailed out of the harbor" and "nets piled high on the deck" describe a boat. Only a ship sails and has a deck.

traps.why: A lid goes on a container; it doesn't hold things itself.
A vessel holds liquid, but it isn't the liquid.
A voyage is a trip; a vessel is what holds or carries.

syn2.tip: Your blood vessels hold and carry blood. That shows vessel can also mean something that holds things.

sc2.stem: Since we had no vase for the wildflowers, Mom said any _____ that could hold water would do, so we used an old glass pickle jar.

traps.why: A lid covers a jar, but it can't hold water for flowers.
A leak lets water out, which is the opposite of holding it.
Vest looks like vessel, but clothing can't hold water for flowers.

sc2.tip: "That could hold water" and "an old glass pickle jar" tell you the blank means a container. Vessel can mean a container as well as a ship.

example: The bold explorer sailed into unknown waters.
hook: A bold kid raises a hand first, walks onstage without shaking, and says hello to the new student.

traps.why: Timid means shy and easily scared, the opposite of bold.
Bald looks like bold but means having no hair.
Bold people may speak up, but bold means brave, not noisy.

syn1.tip: Think of a bold move in a game: you take a brave chance. Daring means willing to take chances too.

sc1.stem: Though most kids were too shy to speak, Ava was _____ enough to walk up and introduce herself to the famous author.

traps.why: Timid fits the shy kids, but "though" shows Ava was different.
Shy kids stay quiet, but Ava did the opposite and spoke up.
Bald looks like bold but means having no hair.

sc1.tip: "Though most kids were too shy" sets up a contrast. Ava walked up and spoke, so she was brave and confident.

traps.why: Shy means afraid to speak up, the opposite of bold.
Bold print is dark and thick, but a bold person is brave.
Boastful means bragging, a negative word; bold is a compliment.

syn2.tip: A bold person acts confidently even when things feel scary. Look for the choice about courage.

sc2.stem: Because the new climbing wall looked so tall and scary, only the most _____ campers volunteered to climb all the way to the very top first.

traps.why: Cautious campers would stay back from a scary wall, not volunteer first.
Timid means easily scared, so timid campers would not go first.
Boastful means bragging; facing a scary wall takes courage, not bragging.

sc2.tip: "Because" the wall was "tall and scary," only campers with courage would go first. You need a word meaning brave.

example: An enormous whale swam past our boat.
hook: Picture a whale so enormous that its tail alone is longer than your school bus.

traps.why: Tiny means very small, the opposite of enormous.
Enormous has "norm" inside, but it does not mean normal.
Big things are often heavy, but enormous is about size.

syn1.tip: Say "an enormous elephant" out loud. The word stretches long, just like something very big.

sc1.stem: Our class pumpkin grew into an _____ one, so heavy that six of us needed a wagon to roll it to the fair.

traps.why: An average pumpkin would not need six kids and a wagon.
Pumpkins are orange, but color does not explain why it was so heavy.
Unusual is too general; the heavy wagon clue points to size.

sc1.tip: Look at "so heavy that six of us needed a wagon." Only a very large pumpkin would need that much help.

traps.why: Little means small, the opposite of enormous.
Tall is only about height; enormous means big in every way.
Large things may be strong, but enormous only tells size.

syn2.tip: Think of a giant. Gigantic has giant inside it, and enormous means giant sized.

sc2.stem: My little brother's hamster is tiny, but the dog next door is _____, so big that it can rest its chin on our kitchen table.

traps.why: Little matches the hamster, but "but" shows the dog is different.
Enormous contains "norm," but a normal dog cannot reach the table.
Dogs can be friendly, but the clue is about size.

sc2.tip: "Tiny, but" signals a contrast, and "so big that" confirms it. The dog must be very large.

example: Helping the lost child was a noble act.
hook: Knights in old stories make noble promises: protect the weak, tell the truth, and keep their word.

traps.why: Shameful means something to be ashamed of, the opposite of noble.
Nobles were rich families, but a noble act means a good one.
Noble heroes may become famous, but noble means good, not well known.

syn1.tip: Think of a noble knight who always does the right thing. Noble describes good character.

sc1.stem: Returning the lost wallet full of cash without asking for any reward was a _____ thing for Diego to do.

traps.why: Sneaky means tricky, but Diego was honest and asked for nothing.
Some might call it foolish, but returning money is praised, not mocked.
Royal describes kings and queens, not an honest act.

sc1.tip: "Returning the lost wallet" and "without asking for any reward" show honesty and goodness. Choose the word for a good, honorable act.

traps.why: Selfish means caring only for yourself, the opposite of noble.
Noble families were often wealthy, but a noble deed means a good one.
Polite is too weak; noble means truly good and honorable.

syn2.tip: A noble act is one people look up to. Pick the word for something people admire.

sc2.stem: The knight could have run away to save himself, but he made the _____ choice to stay and protect the small village from the dragon.

traps.why: Running away would be selfish, but "but" shows he did the opposite.
Protecting a village is praised in the story, not called foolish.
Royal is about kings, but the clue is about a good choice.

sc2.tip: "Could have run away... but" shows a contrast. Staying to protect others is a good, honorable choice.

example: We gathered shells along the shore.
hook: When the coach shouts "Gather round," the whole team huddles together in one tight circle.

traps.why: Scatter means spread apart, the opposite of gather.
Lather looks like gather but means make soap bubbles.
You might count what you gather, but gather means bring together.

syn1.tip: Think of "gather round" or gathering shells at the beach. Both mean bringing things into one place.

sc1.stem: The teacher asked us to _____ around the fish tank so that everyone could see the baby fish.

traps.why: Scattering spreads people apart, but they needed to come close to see.
The fish swim in the tank, but the students do not.
Wandering is moving around loosely, not coming together in one spot.

sc1.tip: "So that everyone could see" tells you the class came close together around the tank.

traps.why: Spreading apart is the opposite of gathering.
Lining up puts things in a row, not into one group.
You may sort what you gather, but gathering is collecting it.

syn2.tip: A family gathering is when everyone comes together. Look for the choice about coming or bringing together.

sc2.stem: Before the storm, the farmer hurried to _____ his chickens into the barn, because the birds had wandered all over the yard.

traps.why: The chickens were already scattered; the farmer wanted them together.
Farmers feed chickens, but the clue is about bringing them in.
Release means let go, but he wanted them safe inside.

sc2.tip: The birds "had wandered all over the yard," and a storm was coming. He had to bring them together into the barn.

example: The donkey carried a heavy burden up the hill.
hook: Picture a backpack stuffed with bricks: that heavy weight pressing on your shoulders is a burden.

traps.why: Relief is when a weight is taken away, the opposite of a burden.
Border looks a bit like burden but means an edge or line.
A basket can hold a load, but it is not the load itself.

syn1.tip: Think of a pack animal carrying a burden up a hill. It is the heavy thing being carried.

sc1.stem: The donkey trudged up the hill under its _____, a load of firewood so heavy that its back sagged.

traps.why: A donkey may wear a saddle, but the sentence says the load was firewood.
Donkeys can carry riders, but the comma explains it was firewood.
Relief means less weight, but its back sagged from heaviness.

sc1.tip: The words after the comma, "a load of firewood so heavy," tell you exactly what fills the blank: a heavy load.

traps.why: A helpful gift makes life easier; a burden makes it harder.
You might carry a burden on a journey, but it means the load.
Small is too weak; a burden is heavy and hard to carry.

syn2.tip: People say something is "a burden on my shoulders." Picture the weight pressing down.

sc2.stem: Carrying the heavy suitcase felt like a _____ at first, but once Dad added wheels to it, pulling it through the airport was easy.

traps.why: A breeze means easy, but "but" shows it only became easy later.
Airports mean journeys, but the clue is about weight.
A prize feels good, but carrying the suitcase felt hard.

sc2.tip: "But once Dad added wheels" it "was easy," so at first it was the opposite: a hard, heavy load.

example: Our generous neighbor shared her tomatoes with everyone.
hook: A generous friend splits her last cookie with you and hands you the bigger half.

traps.why: Stingy means unwilling to share, the opposite of generous.
General looks like generous but means broad or overall.
Rich people can give, but generous means willing to share.

syn1.tip: A "generous helping" of food is a big, kind serving. Generous people give freely.

sc1.stem: Unlike his stingy brother, who never shares a single chip, Leo happily hands out his snacks to the whole bus because he is _____.

traps.why: Greedy describes the brother, but "unlike" shows Leo is the opposite.
Snacks connect to hunger, but a hungry boy would keep them.
Sharing happily is praised here, not called wasteful.

sc1.tip: "Unlike his stingy brother" signals a contrast. Leo "happily hands out his snacks," so he loves to share.

traps.why: Greedy means wanting everything for yourself, the opposite of generous.
Gentle looks a little like generous but means soft and careful.
Wasteful is a negative word for using too much; generous is praise.

syn2.tip: Generous people are happy to give and share. Find the word about giving.

sc2.stem: When the bake sale ran out of money for supplies, a _____ neighbor donated fifty dollars and three dozen cookies without even being asked.

traps.why: A stingy neighbor would never donate money and cookies.
Greedy people keep things; this neighbor gave a lot away.
General looks like generous but means broad, not giving.

sc2.tip: The neighbor "donated fifty dollars and three dozen cookies without even being asked." That example shows someone happy to give.

example: My loyal dog waits for me after school.
hook: A loyal dog waits by the door every afternoon, sticking with you no matter what happens.

traps.why: A false friend turns on you, the opposite of a loyal one.
Royal sounds like loyal but means having to do with kings.
Loyal friends are friendly, but loyal means sticking by someone.

syn1.tip: Think of a loyal pet that always stays by your side. Loyal means you can count on them.

sc1.stem: Even when the team lost every game, Kai stayed a _____ fan, wearing his jersey to every match and never switching teams.

traps.why: A doubtful fan might give up, but Kai never switched teams.
Royal sounds like loyal but means having to do with kings.
Fans can be noisy, but the clue is about never switching teams.

sc1.tip: "Even when the team lost every game" and "never switching teams" show Kai stuck with them. That is faithfulness.

traps.why: Unreliable means you cannot count on someone, the opposite of loyal.
Loyal friends may help, but loyal means staying true to someone.
Stubborn is a negative word for not changing; loyal is praise.

syn2.tip: A loyal fan or friend sticks with you through good times and bad. Pick the word for staying true.

sc2.stem: Some friends drift away when you move to a new school, but Maya stayed _____, writing me a letter every single week for two whole years.

traps.why: Distant fits friends who drift away, but "but" shows Maya was different.
Silent means saying nothing, but Maya wrote every week.
Polite is too weak; weekly letters for years show deep faithfulness.

sc2.tip: "Some friends drift away... but Maya" sets up a contrast. Writing every week for two years means she stayed true.

example: The sandcastle collapsed when the wave hit.
hook: Pull one card from the bottom of a card house and watch the whole thing collapse into a flat pile.

traps.why: Stand means stay upright, the opposite of collapse.
Collide looks like collapse but means crash into something.
Things may shake before falling, but collapse means actually falling.

syn1.tip: Picture a sandcastle when a wave hits: it falls in on itself. Topple also means fall over.

sc1.stem: If you pull out the bottom block, the whole tower will suddenly _____ into a heap on the table.

traps.why: Pulling out the base would never make a tower rise.
Wobble is too weak; the tower ends up in a heap.
Collide looks like collapse but means crash into something else.

sc1.tip: "Pull out the bottom block" causes the tower to end up "into a heap." It must fall down suddenly.

traps.why: Standing firm means staying up, the opposite of collapsing.
Shaking slightly is too weak; collapse means falling all the way.
Sliding moves something over; collapsing makes it fall down.

syn2.tip: A collapsed tent lies flat on the ground. Collapse means fall down suddenly.

sc2.stem: The old wooden bridge looked sturdy from far away, but when the truck rolled onto it, the rotten boards began to _____ beneath its wheels.

traps.why: Hold fits "sturdy," but "but" and "rotten" show the boards gave way.
Rotten boards get weaker under weight, not harder.
Collect looks like collapse but means gather together.

sc2.tip: "Looked sturdy... but" signals a surprise, and the boards were "rotten." Under a heavy truck, they would fall down.

example: The doctor examined my sore throat.
hook: At a checkup, the doctor shines a little light to examine every corner of your ears.

traps.why: Ignore means pay no attention, the opposite of examine.
Explain also starts with ex but means tell how something works.
A glance is a quick look; examine means a long, close look.

syn1.tip: Picture a doctor examining a sore throat with a light. You look closely at every detail.

sc1.stem: Using a magnifying glass, the young scientist bent down to _____ the beetle's tiny legs one by one.

traps.why: Nobody uses a magnifying glass to ignore something.
Bugs sometimes get squashed, but a scientist studies the legs carefully.
Explain looks like examine but means tell about something.

sc1.tip: "Using a magnifying glass" and looking "one by one" show careful, close looking.

traps.why: Turning away means not looking, the opposite of examining.
A quick glance is too weak; examining takes a careful look.
Artists study things to draw them, but examine only means look closely.

syn2.tip: An eye exam or a test checks things carefully. Examine means study with close attention.

sc2.stem: Instead of just glancing at the used bike, Dad wanted to _____ it carefully, checking the brakes, the chain, and every tire for leaks.

traps.why: Ignoring the bike means not checking anything, but Dad checked everything.
Skim means a quick look, which is what "instead of just glancing" rules out.
Explain looks like examine but means tell how something works.

sc2.tip: "Instead of just glancing" means the opposite of a quick look. Checking brakes, chain, and tires means looking closely.

example: Use gentle hands when you hold the hamster.
hook: A gentle breeze barely ruffles the leaves, and gentle hands hold a baby bird without squeezing it.

traps.why: Rough means harsh and hard, the opposite of gentle.
Gentle people may move slowly, but gentle means soft and kind.
Weak is a negative word; gentle is soft by choice and kind.

syn1.tip: Think of "gentle hands" holding a hamster. Gentle means soft, kind, and careful.

sc1.stem: The vet was _____ with the scared kitten, stroking it softly and lifting it with great care.

traps.why: Rough is the opposite of stroking softly and lifting with care.
Strict sounds stern, but the vet was soft and kind.
Vets may work quickly, but "great care" shows softness, not speed.

sc1.tip: "Stroking it softly" and "lifting it with great care" describe the blank. You need a word for soft and careful.

traps.why: Harsh means rough or cruel, the opposite of gentle.
Calm things can seem sleepy, but gentle means soft and kind.
Dull is a negative word meaning boring; gentle is a compliment.

syn2.tip: A gentle soap or a gentle breeze is soft, not strong. Look for the word that means soft and calm.

sc2.stem: My little sister plays roughly with her toys, but she is always _____ with our old cat, petting him slowly so she never hurts him.

traps.why: Careless fits the rough play, but "but" shows she acts differently with the cat.
Forceful means using strength, but she pets him slowly to avoid hurting him.
She does play, but the clue is about being soft and careful.

sc2.tip: "Plays roughly... but" signals a contrast. "Petting him slowly so she never hurts him" means soft and careful.

example: The friends embraced at the airport.
hook: Inside embrace is brace, from an old word for arms, so to embrace someone is to take them in your arms.

traps.why: Pushing moves someone away from you; embracing pulls them close.
Embarrass starts like embrace, but it means to make someone feel awkward.
Waving is a way to greet someone, but it uses no arms around them.

syn1.tip: Picture arms wrapping around a friend. Embrace is what you do when you are very happy to see someone you love.

sc1.stem: When Sofia spotted her grandmother at the airport, she ran to _____ her, wrapping her arms around her tightly.

traps.why: She ran, but chasing does not mean wrapping your arms around someone.
Scolding is angry; wrapping arms around someone tightly is loving.
Avoiding someone means staying away, not running to hold them.

sc1.tip: Look at "wrapping her arms around her tightly." That describes a hug, so the blank must mean hug.

traps.why: Pushing away is the opposite of pulling someone close in a hug.
A handshake is a greeting too, but it is not a hug.
Brace yourself means get ready, but embrace is not about trouble.

syn2.tip: Embrace has the word brace inside, which comes from an old word for arms. Think arms around someone.

sc2.stem: My little brother usually squirms out of everyone's arms, but after his scary dream he ran to _____ Mom and would not let go of her.

traps.why: Escape fits his usual squirming, but the "but" says this time was different.
Teasing is playful or mean, and it does not fit holding on tight.
Embarrass looks like embrace, but it means make someone feel awkward.

sc2.tip: The word "but" tells you he did the opposite of squirming away, and "would not let go of her" shows a hug.

example: The swift rabbit darted into the bushes.
hook: The swift is a bird so fast that it can catch and eat insects while zooming through the air.

traps.why: Slow is the opposite of swift.
Strong animals can be powerful, but swift is about speed, not strength.
Active just means busy moving; it does not say how fast.

syn1.tip: Think of "swift as the wind." Swift describes something that zooms by quickly.

sc1.stem: The cheetah, the fastest runner on land, is so _____ that it can catch up to a speeding jeep in seconds.

traps.why: A lazy animal could never catch a speeding jeep.
Cheetahs are spotted, but spots do not help them catch a jeep.
Cheetahs can be fierce, but the clue is about running fast.

sc1.tip: The sentence says "fastest runner on land" and "catch up to a speeding jeep." Both point to speed.

traps.why: Sluggish means slow and lazy, the opposite of swift.
Graceful is about smooth, pretty movement, not about speed.
Swollen starts like swift, but it means puffed up.

syn2.tip: A swift runner wins races. Ask yourself which choice describes something that moves quickly.

sc2.stem: Grandpa's old turtle takes all morning to cross the yard, but our new puppy is so _____ that she reaches the fence in two seconds.

traps.why: Slow describes the turtle; the "but" says the puppy is different.
Puppies are playful, but that does not explain reaching the fence in two seconds.
A sleepy puppy would not dash across the yard in two seconds.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets the puppy against the slow turtle, and "in two seconds" shows she is very fast.

example: The doctor got an urgent phone call.
hook: An urgent message shouts, "Drop everything and deal with me now," like a fire alarm ringing.

traps.why: Unimportant things can wait; urgent things cannot.
Alarms are loud, but urgent means it must be handled now, not noisy.
Danger can make things urgent, but urgent itself means needing action now.

syn1.tip: You hear urgent in "urgent care," where doctors see you right away. A pressing problem also pushes you to act now.

sc1.stem: The note from the farmer was _____: "Come to the barn right now; the cow is having her calf!"

traps.why: Casual means relaxed, but "right now" shows there is no time to relax.
A calf being born right now is serious news, not a joke.
The note is about a note's message, and this one is short and rushed.

sc1.tip: The farmer says "right now." A note that needs action right away is urgent.

traps.why: Something that can wait is the opposite of urgent.
Urgent things may come with alarms, but urgent is about timing, not noise.
Urgent looks like urge, but it does not mean wanting something badly.

syn2.tip: Think of an urgent phone call from a doctor. It cannot wait until later.

sc2.stem: Because the water from the broken pipe was quickly flooding the kitchen, Dad said fixing it was _____ and called the plumber before finishing his dinner.

traps.why: Optional means it could wait, but he stopped dinner to call.
Fixing pipes may be boring, but that would not make Dad stop eating.
A flooding kitchen is a problem, not something delightful.

sc2.tip: The cause is "quickly flooding the kitchen," and the effect is calling "before finishing his dinner." It could not wait.

example: Maya is keen to join the chess club.
hook: A keen kid's hand shoots up first, eager to answer every single question the teacher asks.

traps.why: Bored is the opposite of keen; a keen person is excited to do something.
Clean rhymes with keen, but it means not dirty.
Nervous is a jumpy feeling too, but it means worried, not eager.

syn1.tip: You might hear "keen to help" or "keen on soccer." Both mean really wanting to do it.

sc1.stem: Ravi has always taken a _____ interest in insects, spending every recess searching under rocks for new beetles.

traps.why: Searching every single recess shows much more than a slight interest.
The sentence says "always," so his interest is not sudden.
Someone who hunts beetles every recess truly cares; the interest is real.

sc1.tip: Ravi spends "every recess searching under rocks." That much effort shows a very eager interest.

traps.why: Not caring is the opposite of being keen.
Slightly curious is too weak; keen means very interested.
Keen sounds like clean, but it has nothing to do with tidiness.

syn2.tip: A keen fan never misses a game. Keen means strong interest, not just a little.

sc2.stem: Most of the class groaned about the long field trip to the museum, but Jamal was _____ to go and had his lunch packed the night before.

traps.why: Unwilling fits the groaning class, but "but" says Jamal felt differently.
Packing lunch early shows excitement, not fear.
Someone unable to go would not pack lunch the night before.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets Jamal against the groaning class, and packing "the night before" shows he could not wait.

example: Use precise measurements when you bake.
hook: A precise cut lands exactly on the line, not a hair to the left or the right.

traps.why: A rough guess is the opposite of a precise answer.
Precious looks like precise, but it means very valuable.
Pre can mean before, but precise has nothing to do with time.

syn1.tip: Think of "precise measurements" in a recipe or science lab. Precise means exactly right.

sc1.stem: The scientist needed a _____ measurement, accurate to a tenth of a millimeter, so she used a special ruler.

traps.why: A rough measurement would never be accurate to a tenth of a millimeter.
Scientists may want speed, but the clue is about accuracy.
Precious looks like precise but means valuable, which does not fit a measurement.

sc1.tip: The sentence says "accurate to a tenth of a millimeter." That is an exact measurement.

traps.why: A rough guess is close at best; precise means exactly right.
Precise work can look neat, but precise means exact, not pretty.
Pre often means before, but precise is not about doing things early.

syn2.tip: A precise answer is not just close. Look for the choice meaning exactly right.

sc2.stem: The directions for the model rocket were so _____ that Leo built it perfectly on the first try without guessing where even one tiny screw belonged.

traps.why: Vague directions would force Leo to guess, but he never had to.
Colorful pictures are nice, but color does not explain a perfect first try.
Crumpled paper says nothing about whether the directions were clear and exact.

sc2.tip: Look at the result: Leo built it "perfectly" and "without guessing." Directions that cause that must be exact.

example: The library is my haven on busy days.
hook: A haven was first a harbor, a calm spot where ships hide safely from storms at sea.

traps.why: Danger is the opposite of a haven, which keeps you safe.
People seek a haven during a storm, but the storm is not the haven.
Raven looks like haven, but it is a black bird.

syn1.tip: You may hear "safe haven." A haven is a place you go to be safe and protected.

sc1.stem: During the storm, the old barn became a _____ for the chickens, keeping them warm, dry, and safe.

traps.why: A trap catches animals; the barn kept the chickens safe.
A prison holds you against your will; this barn was a welcome shelter.
Chickens might play there, but the clue is about staying safe from the storm.

sc1.tip: The sentence says the barn kept the chickens "warm, dry, and safe." A place that keeps you safe is a haven.

traps.why: A dangerous place is the opposite of a haven.
Ships run to a haven to escape a stormy sea.
Haven sounds a bit like heaven, but it just means a safe place.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "safe haven." A haven is where you feel protected.

sc2.stem: The school hallway was loud and crowded, but the quiet art room became Mia's _____, a place where she could breathe and draw in peace.

traps.why: A nightmare is scary, but the art room gave Mia peace.
Drawing may be her hobby, but the blank names a place.
Art rooms have lessons, but a lesson is not a peaceful place.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets the art room against the loud hallway, and it is "a place" of peace. That is a haven.

meaning: a friend who goes along with you
example: My dog is my favorite hiking companion.
hook: Com means with and pan comes from bread, so a companion is someone you share bread with.

traps.why: An enemy is against you; a companion goes along with you as a friend.
Compass starts like companion, but it is a tool for finding direction.
A leader goes in front of a group; a companion simply goes with you.

syn1.tip: Com means with. A companion is someone who is with you, like a buddy on a trip.

sc1.stem: On the long road trip, our dog Biscuit was a faithful _____, riding beside me in the back seat the whole way.

traps.why: Pest is annoying, but faithful shows Biscuit was a welcome friend.
A stranger is someone you don't know, not your faithful dog.
Road trips need a driver, but Biscuit was riding in the back seat.

sc1.tip: Biscuit is "faithful" and rode "beside me" "the whole way." A friend who goes along with you is a companion.

traps.why: An enemy is the opposite of a friend who keeps you company.
Companion comes from words for sharing bread, but it does not mean baker.
Companion looks like company, but it does not mean a business owner.

syn2.tip: Think of a "travel companion." It is a friend who goes along with you.

sc2.stem: Since Grandpa lives alone and gets lonely, our family adopted a gentle cat to be his _____, and now he always has someone to sit with on the porch.

traps.why: An enemy would not fix loneliness; the cat is a friend.
A chore is a job you dislike; the cat makes Grandpa less lonely.
A guard keeps you safe, but the problem here is loneliness, not danger.

sc2.tip: The cause is that Grandpa "gets lonely," and the effect is he "always has someone to sit with." That is a companion.

example: The humble champion thanked her whole team.
hook: A humble hero says, "Thanks, team," instead of "Look at me," even after winning the big game.

traps.why: Proud is the opposite of humble; a humble person does not show off.
Humid looks like humble, but it means damp and sticky air.
Bumbling rhymes with humble, but it means clumsy.

syn1.tip: A humble winner does not brag. Look for the word that means not showing off.

sc1.stem: Even after becoming the most famous scientist in the country, Dr. Lin stayed _____, never acting more important than her helpers.

traps.why: Proud fits fame, but she was "never acting more important."
Famous scientists may be busy, but the clue is about not acting important.
Scientists are curious, but that does not match how she treated her helpers.

sc1.tip: The words "Even after" signal a contrast, and "never acting more important than her helpers" means not proud.

traps.why: Acting important is the opposite of being humble.
Humble is a good quality; it does not mean feeling down.
That describes humid, a word that only looks like humble.

syn2.tip: Humble is a compliment for someone who does great things but never brags.

sc2.stem: When reporters asked about her winning goal, the _____ soccer player just pointed to her teammates and said she could not have done it without them.

traps.why: A boastful player would take all the credit, not give it to teammates.
Thanking teammates is kind, not rude.
An injury would not explain why she gave her team the credit.

sc2.tip: Her actions show who she is: she "pointed to her teammates" instead of taking credit. That is humble.

example: We had a mild winter with little snow.
hook: Mild salsa barely tickles your tongue, while hot salsa makes your eyes water and your nose run.

traps.why: Harsh is the opposite of mild; mild is soft and gentle.
Wild looks and sounds like mild, but it means untamed.
Mild is not an insult; it just means not too strong.

syn1.tip: Think of "mild salsa" or "mild weather." Both are soft and gentle, not harsh.

sc1.stem: This salsa is so _____ that even little kids who hate spicy food can eat it happily.

traps.why: Fiery salsa is very spicy, and kids who hate spice could not eat it.
Salsa can be chunky, but that has nothing to do with spice.
Being famous would not make spicy food easy for kids to eat.

sc1.tip: The sentence says kids "who hate spicy food" can eat it. So the salsa must be gentle, not hot.

traps.why: Very spicy is the opposite of mild.
Too strong a change; mild food still has some flavor, just not much heat.
Mild weather is pleasant, not cold and icy.

syn2.tip: On a menu, mild is the choice that is not hot. It means gentle, not too strong.

sc2.stem: Instead of a bad case of the flu, Tia had only a _____ cold, so she felt well enough to read and play board games in bed.

traps.why: Severe means very bad, but Tia felt well enough to play.
Colds spread, but that does not explain why she felt well enough to play.
Wild looks like mild, but a wild cold makes no sense here.
