sc2.tip: "Instead of a bad case" and "felt well enough" both show the cold was gentle, not strong.

meaning: peaceful agreement; or sounds that blend
example: The neighbors lived in harmony.
hook: In harmony, different voices or people fit together like puzzle pieces into one pleasing whole.

traps.why: Conflict means fighting, the opposite of harmony.
Harmony starts with harm, but it has nothing to do with hurting.
A melody is a tune; harmony is sounds or people blending together.

syn1.tip: People who "live in harmony" get along. Harmony means everyone fits together peacefully.

sc1.stem: The choir sang in perfect _____, their many voices blending together into one beautiful sound.

traps.why: Chaos is a messy jumble, but the voices were blending beautifully.
A choir that sang could not be in silence.
Choirs may wear matching outfits, but the clue is about blending voices.

sc1.tip: The sentence says "voices blending together into one beautiful sound." That is harmony.

traps.why: An argument is the opposite of harmony.
Harmony is about music, but it needs sounds blending, not one note.
Harmony begins with harm, but it means getting along, not hurting.

syn2.tip: In a choir, harmony is when different voices blend together nicely. Look for a choice about mixing well.

sc2.stem: My two cats used to hiss and swat at each other all day, but now they live in _____, sharing a food bowl and napping side by side.

traps.why: Danger fits the old fighting, but "but now" says things changed.
Cats napping side by side are relaxed, not afraid.
Harmony can be about music, but these cats are getting along, not singing.

sc2.tip: The words "but now" show a change from fighting. "Sharing a food bowl" means they get along peacefully.

example: I had a sudden urge to eat ice cream.
hook: An urge is that tug inside you, like an invisible hand pulling you toward the cookie jar.

traps.why: Reluctance means not wanting to do something, the opposite of an urge.
To urge someone is to advise strongly, but the noun urge is your own desire.
A habit is something you do often, not a sudden strong wish.

syn1.tip: Think of the verb urge, to push someone. An urge is a push from inside you to do something right now.

sc1.stem: Walking past the bakery, I felt a sudden _____ to buy a warm cinnamon roll right that minute.

traps.why: Reluctance means not wanting to buy, but the sentence shows wanting.
A habit is not sudden, and the sentence says sudden.
A suggestion comes from someone else, but this feeling comes from inside you.

sc1.tip: The words "sudden" and "right that minute" show a strong want that pops up fast. That is an urge.

traps.why: A lack of interest is the opposite of a strong wish.
An urge is strong, so a small wish is too weak.
Fear can come suddenly too, but an urge is wanting, not fearing.

syn2.tip: An urge pulls you toward something, like the urge to scratch an itch. That is a strong desire.

sc2.stem: Although Marcus had promised to save his allowance, he fought a powerful _____ to spend it all on the new video game at the store.

traps.why: He would not need to fight an unwillingness to spend; that matches his promise.
A duty is something you must do, not something you crave.
Permission comes from someone else, and nobody fights against permission.

sc2.tip: "Although he had promised to save" sets up a fight inside him. He had to fight a strong want to spend.

meaning: a friend or partner who helps you
example: My best friend is my ally in every game.
hook: An ally is the teammate who has your back, like Robin standing beside Batman in every fight.

traps.why: An enemy works against you, the opposite of an ally.
Alley looks like ally, but it means a narrow street.
A leader guides a group, but an ally stands beside you as a helper.

syn1.tip: Countries that join together in a war are called allies. Think of someone who is on your side.

sc1.stem: When the older kids tried to take over the swings, Rosa found an _____ in Tom, who stood beside her and helped.

traps.why: Tom helped Rosa, so he was not her enemy.
An umpire judges fairly and does not take one side.
An audience only watches, but Tom stood beside her and helped.

sc1.tip: Tom "stood beside her and helped." Someone who takes your side and helps is an ally.

traps.why: A bitter rival competes against you, the opposite of an ally.
A narrow street is an alley, a word that only looks like ally.
A neighbor lives near you but does not have to help you.

syn2.tip: An ally is on your team. When someone sides with you and helps, that person is your ally.

sc2.stem: Because Jada had helped him study for every spelling test, Leo considered her his strongest _____ in the whole class.

traps.why: A rival competes against you, but Jada helped Leo.
A critic points out faults, but Jada was kind and helpful.
Everyone in the class is a classmate, so it misses the helping.

sc2.tip: "Because Jada had helped him" is the cause. Someone who helps you is on your side, your ally.

example: He was anxious about the big spelling test.
hook: Anxious ends in -ous, full of: anxious means full of anxiety, like butterflies before a big test.

traps.why: Calm means peaceful and relaxed, the opposite of anxious.
Angry is a different upset feeling; anxious is about worry.
Terrified means extremely scared, much stronger than anxious.

syn1.tip: Anxious ends in -ous, full of. It means full of anxiety, that nervous worry before something big.

sc1.stem: Waiting all afternoon for the doctor to call with her test results, Hana felt _____ and worried the whole time.

traps.why: Long waits can be boring, but the sentence says she was worried.
Cheerful does not go with worried the whole time.
Waiting all afternoon might make you sleepy, but the clue is worry.

sc1.tip: The sentence says she was "worried the whole time" while waiting. The blank goes with worried, so anxious fits.

traps.why: Relaxed means at ease, the opposite of anxious.
Cautious ends like anxious, but it means careful.
Ashamed is feeling bad about something you did, not worry about what's coming.

syn2.tip: Picture the jittery feeling before a test or a doctor visit. Anxious and nervous both describe that feeling.

sc2.stem: Ben usually felt calm on the soccer field, but before the championship game his stomach churned and he felt more _____ than ever.

traps.why: The word but shows a change away from calm, so not relaxed.
A churning stomach shows nerves, not confidence.
A churning stomach might seem like hunger, but here it shows nerves.

sc2.tip: "Usually felt calm, but" signals a change to the opposite of calm. A churning stomach before a big game means nervous.

meaning: an old story about gods or heroes
example: We read a Greek myth about Zeus.
hook: Myths are ancient stories, like Zeus hurling lightning bolts or Hercules battling a many-headed monster.

traps.why: A fact is something true, while a myth is an old made-up story.
Moth looks like myth, but it is an insect.
A riddle is a puzzling question, not an old story about gods.

syn1.tip: Think of Greek myths about Zeus and Athena. A myth is an old story passed down for ages, like a legend.

sc1.stem: In the ancient Greek _____, the god Apollo drove a golden chariot that pulled the sun across the sky.

traps.why: Greeks worshiped gods in temples, but a temple is a building, not a story.
A newspaper reports real events, not a god pulling the sun.
Greek is a language, but a language does not tell about Apollo's chariot.

sc1.tip: A god driving "a golden chariot that pulled the sun" could only happen in a story. An old story about gods is a myth.

traps.why: A true report tells real facts, unlike a myth.
Jokes are told aloud too, but a myth is an old tale of gods.
Myths explained nature, like the sun, but they are not science.

syn2.tip: Myths are very old tales about gods and heroes, often explaining things like thunder. Look for the choice meaning an old story.

sc2.stem: Grandpa explained that the tale of a giant who dug the Grand Canyon is only a _____, since scientists know a river carved it.

traps.why: Scientists say a river carved it, so the giant tale is not a fact.
A theory is a science idea, but the giant tale is a story.
Scientists take measurements, but a giant tale is not one.

sc2.tip: "Only a" plus "since scientists know a river carved it" tells you the giant tale is not true. It is an old made-up story.

example: She felt grief when her goldfish died.
hook: Grief is the heavy heart you feel when you lose someone you love, like a beloved pet.

traps.why: Joy is great happiness, the opposite of grief.
Anger is a different strong feeling; grief is sadness.
Disappointment is a mild letdown, much weaker than grief.

syn1.tip: Grief has a heavy, sad feeling. You hear it in grieving, which is what people do after someone they love dies.

sc1.stem: When their beloved old horse died, the whole family was filled with _____ and cried for days.

traps.why: Relief is a good feeling, but crying for days shows sadness.
Worry is about what might happen; the horse had already died.
Annoyance is too weak to make a family cry for days.

sc1.tip: The horse was "beloved" and the family "cried for days." That shows deep sadness, which is grief.

traps.why: Great happiness is the opposite of grief.
Mild annoyance is far too weak, and it is not sadness.
Fear is a different feeling; grief is sadness over a loss.

syn2.tip: Grief is what people feel after losing someone they love. It is not a small sadness but a deep one.

sc2.stem: Mia's house had always been full of laughter, but after her grandmother passed away, a quiet _____ settled over the family for months.

traps.why: The word but shows a change from laughter, so not joy.
A quiet house might seem boring, but losing a grandmother brings sadness.
Confusion is not knowing what is happening, not sadness over a loss.

sc2.tip: "Always been full of laughter, but after her grandmother passed away" signals a change to deep sadness. That is grief.

example: The cat gave the new puppy a hostile stare.
hook: A hostile cat arches its back, hisses, and dares anyone to come one step closer.

traps.why: Welcoming means warm and friendly, the opposite of hostile.
Shy people may seem distant, but they are not against you.
Annoyed is only a little bothered, weaker than hostile.

syn1.tip: Picture a hostile crowd booing the other team. Hostile describes someone who acts against you, like an enemy.

sc1.stem: Instead of welcoming the new goat, the older goats were _____, snorting angrily and butting it away from the hay.

traps.why: Instead of welcoming tells you they were not friendly.
They were near the hay, but snorting angrily shows unfriendliness, not hunger.
Butting can be play, but angrily shows a bad feeling.

sc1.tip: "Instead of welcoming" tells you the goats did the opposite of being friendly, and "snorting angrily" confirms it. They were hostile.

traps.why: Acting like a friend is the opposite of hostile.
Shyness is quiet and nervous, not angry and against you.
A bit grumpy is too mild; hostile means ready to fight.

syn2.tip: You may hear about hostile armies facing each other. A hostile person treats you like an enemy.

sc2.stem: After the new kid knocked over his Lego castle on purpose, Jamal gave him a _____ glare and refused to share his blocks for the rest of the day.

traps.why: Nobody is grateful when their castle is knocked over on purpose.
Curious means wanting to know, but refusing to share shows anger.
Playful is a happy feeling, but Jamal was upset.

sc2.tip: The castle was knocked over "on purpose," so Jamal "refused to share." That cause and effect points to an unfriendly, hostile glare.

example: The tailor will alter the dress to fit.
hook: A tailor can alter your jeans, shortening the legs so they fit you just right.

traps.why: To keep something the same is the opposite of altering it.
Destroy means wreck completely, much stronger than alter.
Tailors measure before they alter, but measuring changes nothing.

syn1.tip: Think of a tailor who alters clothes to fit. To alter something is to make it different in some way.

sc1.stem: When the rain started, we had to _____ our picnic plans and move the whole party into the garage.

traps.why: They moved the party, so they did not keep the plan the same.
Plans can be written, but moving indoors means the plan changed.
Sharing a plan does not explain moving the party into the garage.

sc1.tip: "Move the whole party into the garage" shows the plan became different because of rain. To make a plan different is to alter it.

traps.why: Leaving something the same is the opposite of altering it.
A copy is the same as the original, not different.
Throwing something away is much more than changing it.

syn2.tip: When you alter a plan, you don't throw it out. You just make it different.

sc2.stem: Grandma's famous cookie recipe is perfect just the way it is, so she warned us never to _____ even one ingredient.

traps.why: Measuring keeps a recipe right, so Grandma would not warn against it.
You must mix ingredients to make cookies, so that warning makes no sense.
Cookies need their ingredients, so she would not forbid including them.

sc2.tip: The recipe is "perfect just the way it is," so the warning must be about not making it different. That means alter.

example: The judge declared Lily the winner.
hook: In the Declaration of Independence, America declared to the whole world that it was free.

traps.why: To hide something is to keep it secret, the opposite of declaring.
Whispering is quiet and soft, much weaker than a firm declaration.
Decide starts like declare, but it means make up your mind.

syn1.tip: Think of the Declaration of Independence, where the colonies announced their freedom. To declare is to say something out loud, firmly.

sc1.stem: On the morning announcements, the principal will officially _____ a snow day for the whole school district.

traps.why: Kids enjoy snow days, but the principal is making an announcement.
Imagining happens in your head, not on the morning announcements.
Doubt means feeling unsure, the opposite of saying something officially.

sc1.tip: "Officially" and "on the morning announcements" tell you the principal is formally saying something to everyone. That is declare.

traps.why: Keeping something secret is the opposite of declaring it.
Asking is a question; declaring is a firm statement.
A quiet guess is far weaker than a firm, official statement.

syn2.tip: A referee declares a winner and a judge declares a verdict. Declare is formal and firm, so look for official saying.

sc2.stem: Instead of quietly hinting that he wanted the last slice of pizza, Diego stood up to _____ to the whole table that it was his.

traps.why: Instead of quietly means he was not quiet, so not whisper.
Mumbling is unclear and soft, far weaker than standing up and saying it.
Pretending is acting, but Diego stood up to say it plainly.

sc2.tip: "Instead of quietly hinting" tells you Diego did the opposite: he said it boldly and clearly. That is declare.

example: Dogs can detect smells we cannot.
hook: A detective detects clues, noticing tiny things like a muddy footprint that everyone else missed.

traps.why: To overlook something is to miss it, the opposite of detect.
Protect ends like detect, but it means keep safe.
Detectives solve cases, but detect only means notice or find.

syn1.tip: Detect is inside detective. A detective notices clues others miss, so detect means to notice or discover.

sc1.stem: Our smoke alarm can _____ even a tiny amount of smoke and will beep loudly to warn us.

traps.why: An alarm that misses smoke would not beep to warn us.
A smoke alarm does not make smoke; it senses it.
Protect looks like detect, but nobody protects smoke.

sc1.tip: The alarm will "beep loudly to warn us," so first it must sense the smoke. Sensing or noticing is detect.

traps.why: To ignore something is to pay no attention, the opposite of detect.
Reject sounds like detect, but it means refuse.
Inventing creates something new; detecting finds something already there.

syn2.tip: Smoke detectors and metal detectors find things you can't see. To detect is to discover something that is there.

sc2.stem: Although the sugar was mixed so well into the lemonade that you could not see it, your tongue could easily _____ the sweet taste.

traps.why: Although sets up a contrast, so your tongue did not miss it.
The sugar was hidden from your eyes, but your tongue found it.
A tongue cannot take sugar out of lemonade.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast: you "could not see" the sugar, but your tongue could still notice it. To notice is to detect.

meaning: wanting very much to do something
example: The eager students raised their hands at once.
hook: An eager puppy wags its whole body and races to the door the moment it hears the leash jingle.

traps.why: Unwilling means not wanting to, the opposite of eager.
Nervous is also a feeling before an event, but it is worry.
Desperate is much stronger and comes from a bad situation.

syn1.tip: Picture an eager student waving a hand to answer first. Eager means wanting very much to do something, and so does keen.

sc1.stem: Lena was so _____ for the aquarium field trip that she packed her lunch three nights early and could barely sleep.

traps.why: The sentence mentions sleep, but she could barely sleep, so not sleepy.
She packed three nights early, so she was not unprepared.
Packing three nights early is the opposite of being late.

sc1.tip: She "packed her lunch three nights early" and "could barely sleep." Those actions show she wanted to go very much, so she was eager.

traps.why: Bored and slow is the opposite of eager.
Worry is a different feeling before an event, not happy wanting.
Pushy and greedy are negative; eager is a positive kind of wanting.

syn2.tip: Eager has a happy feeling, like an eager beaver or kids rushing to recess. Look for the choice that means excited and ready.

sc2.stem: Most of the class groaned when Mr. Park mentioned the science fair, but Priya was _____ to start, sketching ideas for her volcano that very afternoon.

traps.why: The word but shows Priya felt differently from the groaning class.
Someone afraid to start would not sketch ideas that very afternoon.
Starting that very afternoon is quick, not slow.

sc2.tip: "Most of the class groaned, but Priya" signals she felt the opposite of the class. Sketching ideas that very afternoon shows she was eager.

example: He was modest about winning the prize.
hook: A modest winner just smiles and says thanks instead of shouting that they are the best.

traps.why: Boastful means bragging, the opposite of modest.
Honest rhymes with modest, but it means telling the truth.
Winners may become famous, but modest is about not bragging.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "modest about winning." A modest person keeps quiet about their success, just like a humble person.

sc1.stem: Jamal was _____ about his science-fair win, saying only that he had been lucky and his partner deserved the credit.

traps.why: A boastful winner would brag, not give his partner the credit.
Jealousy fits contests, but Jamal won and shared the praise.
A greedy person keeps the credit, but Jamal gave it away.

sc1.tip: Jamal said "only that he had been lucky" and that "his partner deserved the credit." Someone who won't brag is modest.

traps.why: Showing off is what a modest person does not do.
Modest people can be skilled, but modest is about how they talk.
This is about manners too, but it is negative and modest is positive.

syn2.tip: Modest is a kind, positive word for someone who does not brag about what they can do.

sc2.stem: Although she scored all three goals in the championship game, Maya stayed _____ and told everyone the whole team deserved the win.

traps.why: A boastful player would take the credit, not give it to the team.
Players get tired, but that does not explain sharing the credit.
Games can make you nervous, but the clue is about sharing credit.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a surprise: she scored every goal, yet she "told everyone the whole team deserved the win." She did not brag.

example: The rain ceased just before the game.
hook: A cease-fire is when both sides in a fight agree to stop shooting.

traps.why: Begin means start, the opposite of cease.
Seize sounds like cease, but it means grab.
Slowing down is too weak; cease means stop completely.

syn1.tip: Think of a cease-fire, when the shooting stops. To cease is to stop.

sc1.stem: The coach blew her whistle and told the players to _____ running and gather around her.

traps.why: Players can't keep running and gather around the coach at once.
Practice fits sports, but the whistle tells them to stop.
Enjoying running does not fit a whistle that calls players in.

sc1.tip: The coach "blew her whistle" so they would "gather around her." To gather, the players must stop running.

traps.why: Keeping on going is the opposite of ceasing.
That means seize, which only sounds like cease.
Slowing down is too weak; ceasing means stopping fully.

syn2.tip: When the rain ceased before the game, it came to an end. Cease means something stops completely.

sc2.stem: Instead of letting the music keep blaring all night, the neighbors agreed to _____ their party at ten o'clock so everyone could sleep.

traps.why: Continuing the party would keep everyone awake.
Parties are planned, but this one had to stop so people could sleep.
Seize sounds like cease but means grab.

sc2.tip: "Instead of letting the music keep blaring" points to the opposite of keep going. They stopped "so everyone could sleep."

example: The crew had to abandon the sinking ship.
hook: Picture sailors rowing away from a sinking ship they will never see again: they abandon it.

traps.why: Keeping something is the opposite of abandoning it.
Wandering is roaming around, not leaving something behind for good.
Bandage looks like abandon but means to wrap a wound.

syn1.tip: Think of "abandon ship," when sailors leave a ship forever. To desert something means the same.

sc1.stem: Once the chicks learn to fly, the robins will _____ their nest for good and never come back to it.

traps.why: Robins build nests, but the clue says they never come back.
Defending means staying to protect it, not leaving forever.
Sharing a nest does not match never coming back to it.

sc1.tip: The words "for good and never come back to it" tell you the robins leave the nest forever.

traps.why: Holding on is the opposite of abandoning.
A break is short; abandoning is leaving for good.
You might pack before leaving, but packing is not leaving forever.

syn2.tip: When you abandon something, you go away and leave it behind, never coming back for it.

sc2.stem: Even when the storm knocked down half of their tent, the campers refused to _____ the trip and kept hiking toward the lake.

traps.why: They kept hiking, so they refused to quit, not refused to continue.
Enjoying fits a trip, but the clue is about not giving up.
The trip was already happening, so planning does not fit.

sc2.tip: "Refused to" and "kept hiking" are opposites of the blank. Since they kept going, the blank means give up and leave.

example: The wicked witch cast a spell on the prince.
hook: Think of the Wicked Witch of the West, cackling as she plots nasty tricks against Dorothy.

traps.why: Kind is the opposite of wicked.
Naughty is too weak; wicked means truly evil.
Wicked witches are magical, but wicked is about being evil.

syn1.tip: Picture the Wicked Witch in fairy tales. Wicked describes someone truly bad, like a villain.

sc1.stem: In the fairy tale, the _____ stepmother made Cinderella scrub the floors while she planned cruel tricks.

traps.why: A gentle stepmother would not plan cruel tricks.
Loving people don't plan cruel tricks.
Naughty is too mild for someone planning cruel tricks.

sc1.tip: She "planned cruel tricks" and made Cinderella scrub floors. That shows a truly evil character.

traps.why: Kind and gentle is the opposite of wicked.
Some people use wicked as slang for awesome, but the test means evil.
Silly is far too mild for wicked.

syn2.tip: Wicked has a dark, negative feeling. Think of the villains in stories.

sc2.stem: Unlike the kind old wizard who helped the village, the _____ sorcerer cast spells to ruin the farmers' crops and frighten their children.

traps.why: A helpful sorcerer would not ruin crops.
Both wizards are magical, so this does not show the contrast.
Wise is a positive word, but this sorcerer is cruel.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the kind old wizard" tells you the sorcerer is the opposite of kind. He wants to "ruin" and "frighten."

example: Mom was furious when the dog chewed her shoes.
hook: Furious is fury plus -ous, so full of fury you turn red and stamp your feet.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of furious.
Annoyed is too weak; furious means extremely angry.
Curious sounds like furious, but it means wanting to know.

syn1.tip: Furious contains fury, a wild anger. Enraged contains rage. Both mean extremely angry.

sc1.stem: Mr. Park was not just a little annoyed; he was _____, red-faced and stamping his feet, when the puppy chewed his new shoes.

traps.why: Grumpy is only a little upset, but he was more than that.
Cheerful people don't stamp their feet over chewed shoes.
Puzzled is a feeling, but red faces and stamping show anger.

sc1.tip: "Not just a little annoyed" means he was much angrier than annoyed. "Red-faced and stamping his feet" backs that up.

traps.why: Perfectly calm is the opposite of furious.
A bit grumpy is much too weak for furious.
Curious only rhymes with furious.

syn2.tip: Look for fury inside furious. The -ous ending means full of, so furious is full of fury.

sc2.stem: When her little brother spilled grape juice all over her finished art project, Lena was so _____ that she shouted and slammed her bedroom door.

traps.why: Nobody is pleased when their art project gets ruined.
Bothered is too weak for shouting and slamming doors.
Worry is a feeling, but shouting and slamming show anger.

sc2.tip: The spill caused her to have "shouted and slammed her bedroom door." That reaction shows extreme anger.

example: We got lost in the dense fog.
hook: Dense fog is so thick and packed that you can barely see your own hand.

traps.why: Thin is the opposite of dense.
Tense rhymes with dense, but it means stiff or nervous.
Dense forests can be dark, but dense means closely packed.

syn1.tip: Think of "dense fog" or a "dense forest," where everything is packed so thick you can hardly see through.

sc1.stem: The forest was so _____, with trees packed tightly together, that sunlight barely reached the ground.

traps.why: An open forest would let sunlight in.
Forests can be quiet, but quiet does not block sunlight.
Tense sounds like dense but describes a feeling, not trees.

sc1.tip: "With trees packed tightly together" explains the blank. Tightly packed trees block the sun.

traps.why: Spread far apart is the opposite of dense.
Dense forests may have tall trees, but dense means packed tightly.
Slightly crowded is too weak; dense means very tightly packed.

syn2.tip: Picture a dense crowd squeezed shoulder to shoulder. Dense means lots of things packed into a small space.

sc2.stem: Our backyard grass is thin and patchy, but the grass at the park is so _____ that you can't see any dirt between the blades.

traps.why: Bare grass would show lots of dirt.
Short grass can still have dirt showing between the blades.
Soft grass feels nice, but softness doesn't hide the dirt.

sc2.tip: "But" sets up a contrast with "thin and patchy." Grass with no dirt showing is thick and packed.

example: Beavers construct dams out of sticks.
hook: Construct holds the root struct, meaning build, just like structure and construction site.

traps.why: Destroy is the opposite of construct.
Instruct looks like construct, but it means teach.
Designing is planning; constructing is actually building.

syn1.tip: Look for struct, meaning build. You see it in construction site, where workers build things.

sc1.stem: For the science fair, our team will _____ a bridge out of popsicle sticks and glue that can hold a brick.

traps.why: You can't destroy a bridge so that it can hold a brick.
You cross bridges, but you can't cross one made of popsicle sticks.
Instruct looks like construct but means teach.

sc1.tip: The bridge is made "out of popsicle sticks and glue." Making something from materials means building it.

traps.why: Knocking down is the opposite of constructing.
Drawing plans comes before building, but it is not building.
Fixing repairs something that already exists; constructing makes something new.

syn2.tip: Think of a construction crew putting together a new building piece by piece.

sc2.stem: Instead of buying a birdhouse at the store, Grandpa decided to _____ one himself from old boards, nails, and a can of paint.

traps.why: Ordering is still buying, which Grandpa chose not to do.
You can't destroy a birdhouse you don't have yet.
Borrowing doesn't use boards and nails to make something.

sc2.tip: "Instead of buying" shows he did the opposite, and "boards, nails, and a can of paint" are building materials.

example: Ice on the steps is a hazard.
hook: A car's hazard lights blink to warn other drivers that there is danger ahead.

traps.why: Safety is the opposite of a hazard.
A hazard can cause an accident, but the hazard is the danger itself.
Haze looks like hazard, but it means light fog.

syn1.tip: Think of hazard lights or a hazard sign. They warn you about danger.

sc1.stem: Mom taped down the loose cord, since it was a tripping _____ for anyone walking through the hall.

traps.why: A loose cord is not safe, which is why Mom taped it.
A sign gives a warning; the cord itself is the danger.
The hall may be a path, but a loose cord is no shortcut.

sc1.tip: Mom "taped down the loose cord" because someone could trip. Something that could make people fall is a danger.

traps.why: Protection keeps you safe, the opposite of a hazard.
A sign warns you about a hazard, but the hazard is the danger.
A hazard might cause an injury, but it is the risk, not the hurt.

syn2.tip: A hazard is something that could hurt you, like ice on steps. It is a risk before anything happens.

sc2.stem: The pool was usually safe, but the broken glass near the diving board was a real _____, so the lifeguard closed the area until it was cleaned.

traps.why: Broken glass is not a comfort; it could cut people.
A treat is something nice, but broken glass is bad.
Nothing here is a puzzle; the glass is closed off because it's dangerous.

sc2.tip: "Usually safe, but" tells you the blank means the opposite of safe. The lifeguard "closed the area" to protect swimmers.

meaning: to hold tightly, or to understand
example: Grasp the rope with both hands.
hook: When you grasp a monkey bar, your fingers wrap tight; when you grasp an idea, your mind holds it.

traps.why: Release means let go, the opposite of grasp.
Gasp looks like grasp, but it means to breathe in sharply.
Touching is too light; grasping means holding tightly.

syn1.tip: Picture grasping a rope with both hands. Your fingers close tight around it, just like a grip.

sc1.stem: The toddler reached up to _____ her dad's finger, holding on tightly as she took her first wobbly steps.

traps.why: She was holding on tightly, not letting go.
A tap is too light for holding on tightly.
Grasp can mean understand, but you hold a finger, not understand it.

sc1.tip: "Holding on tightly" restates the blank. The toddler wraps her hand around the finger.

traps.why: Forgetting is the opposite of grasping an idea.
You explain to others, but grasping is understanding it yourself.
A guess is not sure; grasping an idea means really getting it.

syn2.tip: Grasp also means to understand, as in "I finally grasp how fractions work." Your mind gets hold of the idea.

sc2.stem: The math lesson moved so fast that at first Tara couldn't _____ how fractions worked, but after her teacher drew pizza slices, it finally made sense.

traps.why: Fractions were new to her, so there was nothing to forget.
The teacher teaches; Tara is the one trying to learn.
Ignoring doesn't fit someone who finally understood the lesson.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "couldn't" with "it finally made sense." So the blank means understand.

example: I admire my sister's hard work.
hook: When you admire someone, you look up to them, like a fan cheering for a favorite athlete.

traps.why: Dislike is the opposite of admire.
Admit looks like admire, but it means to confess.
Envy means wanting what someone has, which is a negative feeling.

syn1.tip: Think of someone you look up to, like a hero. You admire them because you think highly of them.

sc1.stem: I _____ my soccer coach because she works so hard and always treats every player fairly.

traps.why: You wouldn't dislike a coach for working hard and being fair.
Envy is a negative feeling, but these reasons are all good.
Admit looks like admire but means to confess something.

sc1.tip: "Because she works so hard and always treats every player fairly" gives good reasons, so the feeling must be positive.

traps.why: Looking down on someone is the opposite of admiring them.
Staring is just looking, not thinking highly of someone.
Fear is a feeling about someone, but admiring is warm and positive.

syn2.tip: Admire is a warm, positive word. You admire people whose work or kindness makes you think highly of them.

sc2.stem: Some kids laughed at Omar's homemade costume, but I _____ how he built a whole robot suit from cardboard boxes all by himself.

traps.why: Mocking is what the other kids did, but "but" shows you didn't.
He clearly built it, so there is nothing to doubt.
Forgetting doesn't contrast with laughing at his costume.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts you with the kids who "laughed." Building a robot suit "all by himself" is something to think highly of.

example: Use caution when you light the candles.
hook: Yellow CAUTION tape around a wet floor or a deep hole tells you to slow down and take care.

traps.why: Recklessness means ignoring danger, the opposite of caution.
Caption looks similar but means the words under a picture.
Caution is about avoiding danger, not the danger itself.

syn1.tip: Think of yellow caution signs on a wet floor. They ask you to take care.

sc1.stem: The sign by the frozen pond warned skaters to use _____ because the ice near the middle was thin.

traps.why: Thin ice calls for care, not ignoring the danger.
Courage is about facing danger, but a warning sign asks for care.
Speed is part of skating, but thin ice is a reason to be careful.

sc1.tip: Look at "warned" and "because the ice near the middle was thin." A warning about danger asks for care.

traps.why: Carelessness means not paying attention, the opposite of caution.
Fear is much stronger; caution is calm care, not being scared.
Caution can lead to safety, but caution is the care you take.

syn2.tip: A cautious driver keeps a careful watch on the road. Caution means watching out for danger.

sc2.stem: Max rushed across the busy street without looking, but his little sister crossed with _____, checking both ways twice before stepping off the curb.

traps.why: Haste means hurrying, which is what Max did, not his sister.
Boldness means daring; checking both ways twice shows careful worry about danger.
Excitement is a feeling, but checking twice shows care, not thrill.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets the sister against Max's rushing, and "checking both ways twice" shows great care.

example: Winning the spelling bee was a triumph.
hook: Picture a runner crossing the finish line first, arms raised in triumph as the crowd roars.

traps.why: Defeat means losing, the opposite of triumph.
Trumpet sounds a bit like triumph but is a musical instrument.
You might win a trophy for a triumph, but a trophy is a prize.

syn1.tip: Triumph has a winning feeling. Picture arms raised at the finish line.

sc1.stem: Beating the undefeated champions was a huge _____ for our small-town team, and the whole town celebrated.

traps.why: A disaster would not make the whole town celebrate.
Embarrassment is a bad feeling, but the town was celebrating.
Trumpet sounds like triumph but is an instrument, not a win.

sc1.tip: Look at "Beating the undefeated champions" and "the whole town celebrated." Both point to a great win.

traps.why: A crushing loss is the opposite of a great win.
A small step is too weak; a triumph is a big win.
People cheer after a triumph, but the cheer is not the win.

syn2.tip: People say someone returned "in triumph" after winning big. It names a great success.

sc2.stem: Last year our robot fell apart in the first round, so this year finishing in first place felt like a real _____ for the whole science club.

traps.why: Failure fits last year, but first place this year is a win.
A chore is boring work; winning first place feels great.
Winners may get a trophy, but the blank names the success itself.

sc2.tip: The change from "fell apart in the first round" to "finishing in first place" shows a great win after a loss.

example: She wore an elegant blue gown.
hook: Picture a swan gliding across a lake or a dancer in a flowing gown: smooth, graceful, and stylish.

traps.why: Clumsy means awkward and stumbling, the opposite of elegant.
Elephant starts like elegant but is an animal.
Elegant things may cost a lot, but elegant is about grace, not price.

syn1.tip: Think of an elegant swan gliding smoothly. Elegant means moving or looking with grace.

sc1.stem: The ice skater looked _____ in her simple black dress, gliding across the rink with grace and style.

traps.why: Awkward is the opposite of gliding with grace and style.
The dress was simple, but "grace and style" calls for more than plain.
Nervous is an uneasy feeling; gliding with grace shows calm beauty.

sc1.tip: The sentence tells you the answer: "with grace and style." Pick the word that means graceful and stylish.

traps.why: Sloppy means messy, the opposite of elegant.
Showy is a negative word for trying too hard; elegant is a compliment.
Elegant people may be rich, but elegant describes style, not money.

syn2.tip: An elegant dinner or an elegant dress is neat, graceful, and tasteful. It is a compliment about style.

sc2.stem: Instead of his usual muddy jeans and torn sneakers, Leo arrived at the wedding in a neat suit and shiny shoes, looking surprisingly _____.

traps.why: Sloppy fits his usual muddy jeans, not the neat suit.
Comfort is about clothes, but a neat suit shows style, not comfort.
Grumpy is a bad mood; the sentence is about how fine he looked.

sc2.tip: "Instead of" sets the muddy jeans against "a neat suit and shiny shoes." The blank describes the stylish new look.

example: We had a feast on Thanksgiving.
hook: Think of Thanksgiving: a table so loaded with turkey, potatoes, and pies that everyone needs a nap afterward.

traps.why: A snack is a tiny bite, the opposite of a huge meal.
Fast looks like feast but means going without food.
A recipe tells how to cook a dish; it is not the meal.

syn1.tip: Picture a holiday table piled with food. A feast is a big, special meal, like a banquet.

sc1.stem: For Grandpa's eightieth birthday, we cooked a huge _____ of ten special dishes for forty relatives.

traps.why: A snack is small, not ten dishes for forty people.
A salad is just one dish, too narrow for ten dishes.
Recipes help you cook, but you serve forty people a meal.

sc1.tip: Look at "huge," "ten special dishes," and "forty relatives." That much food for a birthday is a large, special meal.

traps.why: A tiny quick snack is the opposite of a feast.
A feast is served on a table, but it is the food itself.
An ordinary dinner is too plain; a feast is big and special.

syn2.tip: People say "a feast for the eyes" about something wonderful and plentiful. A feast is a huge, special meal.

sc2.stem: After eating only crackers during the long hike, the campers were thrilled to sit down that night to a _____ of roast chicken, corn, potatoes, and pie.

traps.why: Crackers were the snack; dinner was much bigger than that.
A nibble is far too small for chicken, corn, potatoes, and pie.
Fast looks like feast but means eating nothing at all.

sc2.tip: The contrast with "only crackers" and the word "thrilled" tell you the campers got a big, special meal.

example: The movie was so dull that I fell asleep.
hook: A dull knife won't cut and a dull class won't keep you awake; both are missing their edge.

traps.why: Exciting is the opposite of dull.
Full looks like dull but means holding as much as possible.
Dull things can make you sleepy, but sleepy describes you, not them.

syn1.tip: People say "never a dull moment" when things are exciting. So dull means boring.

sc1.stem: Although the movie was short, it was _____, with no action, no jokes, and nothing interesting at all.

traps.why: Thrilling cannot describe a movie with no action and no jokes.
"Although the movie was short" rules out lengthy.
Full looks like dull, but the movie had nothing in it.

sc1.tip: Look at "no action, no jokes, and nothing interesting at all." That describes a boring movie.

traps.why: Full of action is the opposite of dull.
Easy work can feel boring, but easy means not hard.
Length is a different thing; short things can still be dull.

syn2.tip: Dull has a flat, tired feeling. A dull speech makes you yawn because nothing in it grabs you.

sc2.stem: My brother thinks fishing is _____ because you sit in a boat for hours and wait, but Grandpa says the quiet is the best part.

traps.why: Sitting and waiting for hours is not exciting to the brother.
Peaceful is Grandpa's happy view, but the blank is the brother's complaint.
Sitting and waiting is not hard work; the brother finds it boring.

sc2.tip: The reason follows "because": "you sit in a boat for hours and wait." The word "but" shows Grandpa disagrees with the brother.

example: A fierce wind blew the leaves off the trees.
hook: Picture a mother bear roaring to protect her cubs; that wild, powerful energy is fierce.

sc1.stem: The lion let out a _____ roar, so wild and powerful that every zebra on the plain looked up.

traps.why: A soft roar would not be wild and powerful.
Fearful looks like fierce but means scared; this roar was powerful.
Lions get hungry, but the clue describes the roar as wild and powerful.

sc1.tip: The words "so wild and powerful" describe the roar. Pick the word that means wild and strong.

traps.why: Calm and mild is the opposite of fierce.
A bit rough is too weak; fierce means very strong.
Fierce things can be big, but fierce is about force, not size.

syn2.tip: A fierce wind or fierce game is strong and intense. Think of the most powerful version.

sc2.stem: Our kitten is sweet and cuddly with us, but when the neighbor's dog comes near, she arches her back and becomes a _____ little fighter.

traps.why: Gentle fits her with us, but "but" signals a change near the dog.
Kittens are furry, but the clue is about how she fights.
A kitten arching her back to fight is wide awake.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "sweet and cuddly" with how she acts near the dog. "Arches her back" and "fighter" point to wild and strong.

example: It is polite to say thank you.
hook: Please, thank you, and excuse me are the three magic words every polite person uses.

traps.why: Rude is the opposite of polite.
Political looks like polite but is about government.
Polite people can be quiet, but polite means having good manners.

syn1.tip: Saying please and thank you is polite. It means treating others with good manners and respect.

sc1.stem: It is not _____ to talk with your mouth full or to interrupt someone, so Mom reminds us to use our manners.

traps.why: If you miss "not," rude seems to fit, but Mom wants manners.
Talking with your mouth full is easy to do; the issue is manners.
Political looks like polite but is about government.

sc1.tip: Notice the word "not" and the phrase "use our manners." Talking with your mouth full is not good manners.

traps.why: Bad manners is the opposite of polite.
Shy people may be quiet, but shyness is not about manners.
Acting proud has a bragging feeling; polite is kind and respectful.

syn2.tip: The word impolite means rude. So polite means the opposite: having good manners.

sc2.stem: Even when the waiter brought the wrong soup, Dad stayed _____, smiling and saying, 'Excuse me, could we please have the tomato soup instead?'

traps.why: Dad smiled and said please, the opposite of rude.
The wrong soup might upset someone, but Dad was smiling.
Dad spoke up, so he did not stay quiet.

sc2.tip: Dad's words "Excuse me" and "please" show good manners. "Even when" tells you he stayed nice despite the mistake.

example: After the storm, debris covered the yard.
hook: Say it duh-BREE: the scraps a storm leaves behind, like branches, glass, and shingles scattered everywhere.

traps.why: Storms cause debris, but debris is the broken pieces left after.
Treasure is valuable; debris is worthless broken junk.
Debt looks like debris but means money you owe.

syn1.tip: Picture a yard after a storm, covered with broken branches and shingles. Those scattered pieces are debris.

sc1.stem: After the windstorm, _____ was scattered all over the yard: broken branches, shingles, and pieces of the fence.

traps.why: Sun may follow a storm, but sunlight is not broken branches.
Treasure is valuable; broken shingles and fence pieces are junk.
Debt looks like debris but means money owed.

sc1.tip: After the colon comes the list: "broken branches, shingles, and pieces of the fence." Those are scattered broken pieces.

traps.why: Whole objects are unbroken, the opposite of debris.
Strong winds can make debris, but they are not the pieces.
One crumb is too narrow; debris is many scattered pieces.

syn2.tip: News reports say crews cleared "debris" after storms or crashes. It means the broken bits left lying around.

sc2.stem: Because the tornado had smashed houses all along Maple Street, workers spent weeks clearing _____ from the roads before cars could drive through.

traps.why: Smashed houses leave junk, not valuable treasure.
Debt looks like debris but means money owed.
The tornado caused the mess, but workers cleared the pieces it left.

sc2.tip: "Because the tornado had smashed houses" tells you the cause. Smashing leaves broken pieces that must be cleared.

example: She glanced at the clock during the test.
hook: A glance is just a flick of your eyes, like checking the clock without turning your head.

traps.why: Stare means look for a long time, the opposite of glance.
Dance rhymes with glance but means moving to music.
Listening uses your ears; glance is about your eyes.

syn1.tip: People say "at first glance" for a first quick look. A glance is quick, like a peek.

sc1.stem: During the test, Ella would _____ at the clock for only a split second before returning to her work.

traps.why: Staring lasts long, but she looked for only a split second.
Gazing is long and steady, not a split second.
Dance rhymes with glance, but you can't dance at a clock.

sc1.tip: The words "only a split second" tell you the look was very quick.

traps.why: Gazing for hours is the opposite of a quick look.
Glow looks like glance but means give off light.
Nodding is quick too, but it uses your head, not your eyes.

syn2.tip: Think of "at a glance," meaning in one quick look. To glance is to look fast.

sc2.stem: Instead of studying the map carefully, Jake only had time to _____ at it before the bus pulled away, so he got lost later.

traps.why: He had no time for a long look, so stare is wrong.
Peering means looking closely, but he only had a moment.
Dance rhymes with glance but has nothing to do with looking.

sc2.tip: "Instead of studying the map carefully" and "only had time" both show the look was quick and short.

example: Plants pull moisture from the soil.
hook: Breathe on a cold mirror and watch the fog appear; that tiny bit of water is moisture.

traps.why: Dryness is the opposite of moisture.
Mixture looks like moisture but means things stirred together.
Heat often comes up with weather, but moisture is about water.

syn1.tip: Moisture is inside the word moist, which means slightly wet. Think of a damp sponge.

sc1.stem: A cactus stores _____ inside its thick stems, so it can survive for months in the dry desert.

traps.why: A cactus fights the dryness; it stores water to survive.
Deserts have sand, but a cactus doesn't store sand to survive.
Mixture looks like moisture but means things stirred together.

sc1.tip: Look at "so it can survive" in the "dry desert." To live where it's dry, a cactus must store water.

traps.why: A drought is a long dry time, the opposite of moisture.
A flood is far too much water; moisture is a small amount.
Soil can hold moisture, but soil is dirt, not water.

syn2.tip: Moist means a little wet, and moisture is the noun. Lotion adds moisture to dry skin.

sc2.stem: After the rainstorm, the towels on the line were still heavy with _____, so Mom brought them inside to finish drying in the dryer.

traps.why: Towels that need to finish drying are wet, not dry.
Towels outside can get dusty, but a dryer removes water, not dust.
Sunlight dries towels, but it cannot make them heavy.

sc2.tip: The effect tells you the cause: Mom put them in the dryer "to finish drying," so the towels held rainwater.

example: It was foolish to leave my lunch at home.
hook: A fool does foolish things, like wearing flip-flops to build a snowman.

traps.why: Wise is the opposite of foolish.
Playful is a happy, harmless word; foolish means making an unwise choice.
Clumsy is about bumping into things, not about bad thinking.

syn1.tip: You can see the word fool inside foolish. A fool acts without thinking, so foolish means silly or not wise.

sc1.stem: It was _____ of Tim to leave his ice cream in the hot car, and of course it melted all over the seat.

traps.why: Sensible means wise, but leaving ice cream in a hot car was not.
Generous is about giving to others, not about a choice that melted ice cream.
Funny is a cheerful word, but a melted mess shows a bad choice.

sc1.tip: Look at "and of course it melted all over the seat." The choice caused a mess, so it was not wise.

traps.why: Very smart is the opposite of foolish.
To fool someone is to trick them, but foolish means acting unwisely.
Rude and foolish are both bad behavior, but foolish is about poor thinking.

syn2.tip: Think of the saying "Don't be foolish." People say it when someone is about to make a choice that isn't wise.

sc2.stem: My little brother thought jumping off the shed with an umbrella was a great idea, but Mom said it was _____ and could get him badly hurt.

traps.why: Brilliant is what the brother thought, but "but" shows Mom disagreed.
Mom's worry is about getting hurt, not about being dull.
Lazy means not wanting to work, and jumping off a shed is not lazy.

sc2.tip: The word "but" means Mom thought the opposite of "a great idea." The words "could get him badly hurt" show it was unwise.

example: A butterfly emerged from its cocoon.
hook: When a chick emerges from its egg, it pokes out into the world for the first time.

traps.why: Vanish is the opposite of emerge.
Merge looks similar but means to join together.
A butterfly grows before it emerges, but emerge means to come out.

syn1.tip: The e at the start means out, like in exit. To emerge is to come out where people can see you.

sc1.stem: After sleeping all winter, groundhogs _____ from their burrows in early spring and blink in the sunlight.

traps.why: The groundhogs blink in sunlight, so they come out, not vanish.
Merge means to join together, which doesn't fit leaving a burrow.
Hibernate means sleep all winter, which they had already finished.

sc1.tip: The clue is "from their burrows" and "blink in the sunlight." The groundhogs come out into view.

traps.why: Going back in is the opposite of emerging.
Blend together is what merge means; emerge means come out.
Animals may wake up first, but emerge means come out into view.

syn2.tip: Think of a butterfly that emerges from its cocoon. It comes out into the open.

sc2.stem: The moon hid behind thick clouds for most of the night, but around midnight it began to _____, and suddenly the whole backyard was bright.

traps.why: If the moon faded, the backyard would get darker, not bright.
A setting moon goes down and away, so the yard would not turn bright.
Merge means to join together, not to come out from behind clouds.

sc2.tip: "Hid" and "but" show a change. Then "suddenly the whole backyard was bright" tells you the moon came out into view.

example: The immense castle had over a hundred rooms.
hook: Immense comes from Latin for "not measured": something so huge you could never measure it.

traps.why: Tiny is the opposite of immense.
Intense looks similar but means very strong, not very big.
Big things can be heavy, but immense is about size.

syn1.tip: Picture "an immense castle with a hundred rooms." Immense is a big word for something extremely large.

sc1.stem: Finishing her first marathon at age seventy gave Grandma an _____ sense of pride, bigger than anything she had ever felt.

traps.why: Ordinary pride would not be bigger than anything she had felt.
Uneasy is a worried feeling, but Grandma felt proud.
Grandma is seventy, but the blank describes her pride, not her age.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "bigger than anything she had ever felt." You need a word meaning extremely large.

traps.why: Little is the opposite of immense.
Tall is only about height; immense means huge in every way.
Big things may matter, but immense is about size, not importance.

syn2.tip: The "im" means not, and "mense" is like measure. Something immense is too huge to measure.

sc2.stem: From the beach the ship looked like a tiny toy, but up close it was _____, taller than our school and longer than three football fields.

traps.why: Miniature means tiny, which is how it looked before the word "but."
A ship can be crowded, but the clue is about its size.
Intense means very strong, not very big.

sc2.tip: "Tiny toy" plus "but" means the answer is the opposite of tiny. "Taller than our school" proves it.

meaning: to eat, drink, or use up
example: Pandas consume a lot of bamboo each day.
hook: A hungry campfire consumes every log you toss in, burning it all up.

traps.why: Produce means make, the opposite of consume.
Assume sounds like consume but means to suppose something is true.
Cooking is about food too, but consume means eat or use up.

syn1.tip: A consumer is a person who uses things up. "Pandas consume bamboo" means they eat it.

sc1.stem: Our old van seems to _____ a whole tank of gas every week, using it up faster than any other car.

traps.why: Saving gas is the opposite of "using it up."
Hold tells how big the tank is, not that the van uses gas up.
Assume sounds like consume but means to suppose, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank: "using it up faster than any other car." You need a word meaning to use up.

traps.why: Saving up is the opposite of using up.
Shoppers pay for things, but consume means to use them up.
Throwing something away is wasting it, not using it up.

syn2.tip: Think of how a car consumes gas. When you consume something, you use it until it's gone.

sc2.stem: My sister nibbles a single cracker for a snack, but our hungry dog can _____ a whole bowl of food in about ten seconds.

traps.why: A hungry dog wouldn't refuse food, and "but" shows it acts unlike the sister.
Sniffing a bowl wouldn't take ten seconds to finish it; the dog gobbles it.
Spilling is messy, but "hungry" shows the dog is eating the food.

sc2.tip: "Nibbles a single cracker" is set against "but our hungry dog." The dog does the opposite of nibbling and eats it all.

example: His directions were too vague to follow.
hook: A vague answer is like a foggy window: you can tell something is there, but nothing is clear.

traps.why: Exact is the opposite of vague.
Vain looks similar but means too proud of your looks.
Vague directions may be correct, just not clear or exact.

syn1.tip: Think of "vague directions" like "go that way somewhere." They are fuzzy and unclear.

sc1.stem: Lily's directions were so _____, just "go somewhere near a big tree," that we wandered around lost for an hour.

traps.why: Precise directions would not have left everyone lost for an hour.
Helpful is positive, but these directions got everyone lost.
The word "just" shows the directions were short, not lengthy.

sc1.tip: The example "go somewhere near a big tree" gives no exact place, and "we wandered around lost" shows the directions were unclear.

traps.why: Very detailed is the opposite of vague.
Something vague can still be true; it just isn't exact.
Long directions can be very clear; vague means not exact.

syn2.tip: When a friend says "I'll be there sometime," that answer is vague. It leaves out the exact details.

sc2.stem: Mr. Diaz gave us very exact instructions for the science project, but his notes about the field trip were _____, so nobody knew when the bus would leave.

traps.why: Clear notes would tell everyone when the bus would leave.
Neat is about how notes look, not whether they explain things.
Cheerful is a happy feeling, but the problem was nobody knew the time.

sc2.tip: "Very exact" is followed by "but," so the field trip notes were not exact. "Nobody knew when" confirms it.

example: Handle the fragile glass ornament carefully.
hook: Boxes that hold glass are often stamped FRAGILE, warning everyone that what's inside breaks easily.

traps.why: Sturdy is the opposite of fragile.
Fragrant looks similar but means sweet smelling.
Fragile things may be worth a lot, but fragile is about breaking easily.

syn1.tip: Picture a box marked "Fragile: handle with care." The thing inside is delicate and could break.

sc1.stem: Pack the antique teacups in bubble wrap, because they are so _____ that even a small bump could break them.

traps.why: Sturdy teacups would not break from a small bump.
Antique teacups may be pretty, but that's not why a bump breaks them.
Fragrant means sweet smelling, which has nothing to do with breaking.

sc1.tip: The clue is "even a small bump could break them." You need a word meaning easily broken.

traps.why: Hard to break is the opposite of fragile.
Fragile things could break easily, but they aren't broken yet.
Fragile things can cost a lot, but fragile is about breaking.

syn2.tip: Fragile sounds a bit like fragment, a broken piece. Fragile things break into fragments easily.

sc2.stem: Our plastic picnic plates can be dropped again and again without a scratch, but Mom's glass dish is _____ and must stay safely on the high shelf.

traps.why: Tough describes the plastic plates, and "but" shows the dish is different.
Glass can be shiny, but shine isn't why it must stay safe.
Heavy things aren't kept on high shelves for safety; breakable ones are.

sc2.tip: "Dropped again and again without a scratch" is set against "but Mom's glass dish." The dish must be the opposite: easily broken.

example: The lively music made everyone dance.
hook: A lively party is full of energy: music playing, people dancing, and nobody sitting still.

traps.why: Sluggish is the opposite of lively.
Lovely looks similar but means beautiful.
Lively places can be noisy, but lively means full of energy.

syn1.tip: Lively has the word live inside it. Something lively is bursting with life and energy.

sc1.stem: The puppies were so _____ that they tumbled, chased, and wrestled all afternoon without ever slowing down.

traps.why: Sleepy puppies would slow down, not play all afternoon.
Lonely looks similar, but the puppies were playing together.
Puppies may be fluffy, but that doesn't explain playing nonstop.

sc1.tip: The examples "tumbled, chased, and wrestled all afternoon without ever slowing down" show the puppies were full of energy.

traps.why: Low on energy is the opposite of lively.
Lively has live inside, but it means energetic, not just alive.
Lively things may be loud, but lively is about energy.

syn2.tip: Think of "lively music" that makes everyone jump up and dance. Lively means full of energy.

sc2.stem: At the start of the hike my little sister was tired and grumpy, but after a snack she became _____, skipping and singing all the way up the trail.

traps.why: Drowsy matches "tired," but "but" shows she changed.
She just ate a snack, and hunger doesn't explain the skipping.
Lonely looks similar but means sad from being alone.

sc2.tip: "Tired and grumpy" changes after "but." Then "skipping and singing" shows she was full of energy.

example: Thanks for your prompt reply to my letter.
hook: A prompt student is in her seat the second the bell rings, never a minute late.

traps.why: Delayed is the opposite of prompt.
A reply can be polite, but prompt is about speed.
Proper looks a bit like prompt but means correct or fitting.

syn1.tip: Think of "a prompt reply": an answer that comes back right away. Prompt means quick.

sc1.stem: The bike shop sent a _____ reply to my email, answering my question within five minutes.

traps.why: Answering within five minutes is fast, not delayed.
Rude is negative, but nothing in the sentence shows a bad reply.
The clue is about how fast they answered, not how long the reply was.

sc1.tip: The example "answering my question within five minutes" shows the reply came quickly.

traps.why: Running late is the opposite of prompt.
Good manners are nice, but prompt is about timing.
Prompt means right on time, not far too early.

syn2.tip: Teachers praise students who are prompt, meaning they arrive right when they should. Prompt means on time.

sc2.stem: Jake is usually ten minutes late to soccer practice, but today he was _____ and stood on the field ready to play before anyone else arrived.

traps.why: Tardy means late, which is his usual habit before the word "but."
Tired doesn't explain arriving before everyone else.
Absent means not there at all, but Jake was on the field.

sc2.tip: "Usually ten minutes late" plus "but" means today was different. "Before anyone else arrived" shows he was on time.

example: After the long hike, fatigue set in.
hook: After a full day at the amusement park, fatigue hits so hard you fall asleep in the car.

traps.why: Energy is the opposite of fatigue.
Fatigue starts with fat, but it has nothing to do with weight.
Bored people may yawn, but fatigue means being very tired.

syn1.tip: You may have heard of "muscle fatigue" after hard exercise. It means great tiredness.

sc1.stem: After running the marathon, Dad felt such _____ that he slept for twelve hours straight.

traps.why: Someone full of energy wouldn't sleep twelve hours straight.
Dad may be proud, but pride doesn't make you sleep twelve hours.
Hunger would send him to eat, not to sleep for twelve hours.

sc1.tip: Look at the result: "he slept for twelve hours straight." Only great tiredness would cause that.

traps.why: Great energy is the opposite of fatigue.
After hard work you may be hungry too, but fatigue means tiredness.
Mild sleepiness is too weak; fatigue is deep tiredness.

syn2.tip: Fatigue is what you feel after a long hike or a big game. It is a strong, heavy tiredness.

sc2.stem: Even though Maya had stayed up late finishing her book, she showed no sign of _____ at the swim meet, racing hard and winning three events.

traps.why: She raced hard and won, so she clearly showed energy.
Winning three events shows plenty of talent, so "no sign" doesn't fit.
Winning races takes speed, so she did show it.

sc2.tip: "Even though" she stayed up late, which usually makes you tired, she raced hard. So she showed no sign of tiredness.

meaning: a natural feeling of what to do
example: Birds fly south by instinct.
hook: No one teaches a spider to spin a web; it knows how by instinct from the day it hatches.

traps.why: Training is learned, the opposite of an instinct you are born with.
Instant looks similar but means a very short moment.
A habit is learned by doing something often; an instinct is natural.

syn1.tip: Think of "Birds fly south by instinct." Nobody teaches them; it's a natural inner sense, like a gut feeling.

sc1.stem: Baby sea turtles crawl toward the ocean by _____; no one ever has to teach them the way.

traps.why: Instruction means teaching, but "no one ever has to teach them."
By accident sounds natural, but all baby turtles do it every time.
Heading to the ocean is the right move, not a mistake.

sc1.tip: After the semicolon, "no one ever has to teach them the way" explains the blank. It's something they know naturally.

traps.why: A learned lesson is taught, the opposite of an instinct.
Animals use smell, but instinct is an inner feeling of what to do.
Instant looks like instinct and means a quick moment.

syn2.tip: People say "trust your instincts," meaning follow the feeling you're born with, not something you were taught.

sc2.stem: Because a cat's _____ tells it to hunt, even a well-fed house cat will still chase a moth across the room.

traps.why: The cat is "well-fed," so hunger is not the reason.
Owners don't tell cats to hunt moths; cats do it naturally.
Instant looks similar but means a moment, which can't tell a cat anything.

sc2.tip: "Even a well-fed" cat chases the moth, so it isn't hungry. Something inside it, a natural feeling, causes the hunting.

example: She gave a sincere apology to her friend.
hook: You sign letters "Sincerely" to show every word is truly meant, straight from the heart.

traps.why: Fake is the opposite of sincere.
Polite words can still be fake; sincere means truly meant.
Severe looks like sincere, but it means harsh or very serious.

syn1.tip: Sincere is in "sincerely," the word at the end of a letter that means you truly mean what you wrote.

sc1.stem: Her thank-you note to the bus driver was _____, written from her heart and not just because her parents told her to.

traps.why: The note was not just because her parents told her, so not forced.
Her parents asked, but "from her heart" shows more than a requirement.
Nothing in the sentence tells you how long the note was.

sc1.tip: The words "from her heart" tell you the note was honest and truly meant.

traps.why: Pretending is the opposite of being sincere.
Nice words can be empty; sincere is about meaning them.
Sincere people may be serious, but sincere means honest.

syn2.tip: Think of a sincere apology: the person is not just saying sorry, they really mean it.

sc2.stem: Mia could tell the apology was not _____ because her brother rolled his eyes and smirked while he mumbled that he was sorry.

traps.why: Eye rolling shows the apology was fake, so "not fake" is wrong.
Smirking is rude, so saying it was "not rude" makes no sense.
He acted careless, so "not careless" goes against the clue.

sc2.tip: Eye rolling and smirking cause Mia to doubt him. The apology was not honest or truly meant.

meaning: to put up with something hard
example: Camels can endure long days without water.
hook: Endure shares a Latin root with durable: something that endures lasts through hard times without breaking.

traps.why: Avoiding something hard is the opposite of enduring it.
You endure hard things; enjoy is far too happy a feeling.
Ensure looks like endure, but it means to make certain.

syn1.tip: Endure is related to "durable," meaning long lasting. To endure something hard is to last through it.

sc1.stem: To reach the warm cabin, the hikers had to _____ three hours of freezing rain without any shelter.

traps.why: With no shelter, the hikers could not avoid the rain.
Freezing rain with no shelter is not something to enjoy.
Predicting the weather is not the same as getting through it.

sc1.tip: "Freezing rain without any shelter" shows the hikers had to put up with something hard.

traps.why: Giving up is the opposite of enduring.
People may complain about hard things, but enduring means getting through them.
Endure is about hard things, not happy ones you wait for.

syn2.tip: Picture camels enduring long days without water. They do not like it, but they put up with it.

sc2.stem: The new puppy was cute, but our family had to _____ weeks of chewed shoes and late-night barking before he finally learned good manners.

traps.why: "Had to" and "before he finally learned" show they could not skip it.
Chewed shoes and barking are not things to celebrate.
Ensure looks like endure, but no one wants to make chewed shoes certain.

sc2.tip: "Cute, but" signals a contrast: the puppy was sweet, yet the family had to put up with hard weeks.

example: Honey is a remedy for a sore throat.
hook: Remedy and medicine both come from a Latin word meaning to heal; a remedy fixes what is wrong.

traps.why: A disease is the problem; a remedy is what cures it.
A doctor may give a remedy, but a remedy is the cure itself.
Reminder starts like remedy, but it helps you remember something.

syn1.tip: Remedy and medicine come from the same Latin root. Honey is a remedy for a sore throat: it helps fix it.

sc1.stem: Grandma's favorite _____ for hiccups is to drink a glass of water while holding your breath.

traps.why: Drinking water while holding your breath stops hiccups; it does not cause them.
A symptom is a sign of sickness, not a way to stop it.
Drinking water is not why hiccups happen; it is how to stop them.

sc1.tip: Drinking water "while holding your breath" is a way to stop hiccups, so it is a fix.

traps.why: A problem is what needs a remedy, not the remedy.
A symptom is a sign of sickness, not what cures it.
A remedy may be mixed like a recipe, but its job is to cure.

syn2.tip: A remedy solves a problem, whether it is a cold, hiccups, or a broken plan.

sc2.stem: The scraped knee was stinging badly, so the school nurse reached for her best _____, a cool cloth and a bandage that soon made it feel better.

traps.why: The cloth and bandage solved the problem; they were not the problem.
The scraped knee was the injury; the cloth and bandage fixed it.
Reminder looks like remedy, but a bandage does not help you remember.

sc2.tip: "Soon made it feel better" shows the cloth and bandage worked as a cure for the scrape.

example: Sam was reluctant to jump into the cold pool.
hook: Picture a reluctant cat being lowered into a bath, legs stiff, pulling back the whole way.

traps.why: Eager means wanting to do something, the opposite of reluctant.
Relevant looks like reluctant, but it means connected to the topic.
Fear can make you reluctant, but reluctant just means not wanting to.

syn1.tip: Picture someone dragging their feet. "I was reluctant to go" means I did not want to go.

sc1.stem: Although Ben was _____ to taste the spicy soup, he finally took one tiny sip after his aunt begged him.

traps.why: If Ben were eager, his aunt would not need to beg.
Being allowed is about permission, but begging shows he did not want to.
A hungry boy would not need begging to take a sip.

sc1.tip: "Although" and "finally" signal a change, and his aunt "begged" him, so at first Ben did not want to taste it.

traps.why: Being excited to try is the opposite of reluctant.
A reluctant person can do it; they just do not want to.
Reluctant people hold back, but they often do it in the end.

syn2.tip: Reluctant people hang back and drag their feet, but they may still do it in the end.

sc2.stem: Tasha was _____ to lend her new markers to her little brother because the last time she did, he left all the caps off and they dried out.

traps.why: Dried out markers would not make her happy to lend more.
Nothing about dried markers would make her proud to lend them.
The reason given is about ruined markers, not about permission.

sc2.tip: The word "because" gives the cause: last time the markers "dried out," so now she does not want to lend them.

example: Animals flee when they smell smoke.
hook: Flee rhymes with free: when you flee a danger, you run until you are free of it.

traps.why: Remaining means staying put, the opposite of fleeing.
A chase involves running, but chasing goes toward something, not away.
Free looks like flee, but it means to let someone go.

syn1.tip: You hear it in "fled the scene." Animals flee a fire: they run away to get safe.

sc1.stem: When the thunderstorm rolled in, the frightened deer turned to _____ into the forest as fast as they could.

traps.why: Strolling is too slow for frightened deer going "as fast as they could."
Tiptoeing is quiet and slow, not "as fast as they could."
Parading is showing off, not what frightened animals do.

sc1.tip: "Frightened" and "as fast as they could" tell you the deer were running away from danger.

traps.why: Standing firm means staying and facing danger, the opposite of fleeing.
Hiding is another way to stay safe, but fleeing means running away.
Strolling is too slow and calm; fleeing is fast and urgent.

syn2.tip: Flee is about danger and speed. Think of animals running from smoke or a storm.

sc2.stem: Most animals _____ a wildfire, but firefighters rush toward the flames to put them out and keep everyone safe.

traps.why: "But" shows animals do the opposite of rushing toward the fire.
Fighting fire is what the firefighters do, not the animals.
Free looks like flee, but animals do not free a wildfire.

sc2.tip: "But" shows contrast: firefighters "rush toward" the flames, so most animals do the opposite and run away.

example: We sat in the only vacant seats on the bus.
hook: Vacant shares a Latin root with vacuum and vacation: a vacuum is empty space, and a vacant room holds no one.

traps.why: Crowded means full of people, the opposite of vacant.
Vacant places may be run down, but vacant means empty.
Vague looks like vacant, but it means unclear.

syn1.tip: Vacant shares a root with "vacuum," a space with nothing in it. A vacant seat has no one in it.

sc1.stem: The apartment upstairs has been _____ since the Garcias moved out, and no one has lived there for months.

traps.why: "No one has lived there" means it cannot be crowded.
With no one living there, the apartment would not be noisy.
Cozy is a warm, lived-in feeling, but no one lives there.

sc1.tip: "No one has lived there for months" tells you the apartment is empty.

traps.why: Full of people is the opposite of vacant.
An old building may fall apart, but vacant only means empty.
Vacant places can be anywhere; vacant is about being empty.

syn2.tip: Look for "VACANCY" signs at motels: they mean some rooms are empty and no one is using them.

sc2.stem: On Saturday the park was packed with families, but by Monday morning the playground was _____, with no children on the swings at all.

traps.why: "But" shows a change from packed, so it was not crowded.
Cheerful gives a happy feeling, but the clue is about no children.
Nothing says the swings broke; they just had no children on them.

sc2.tip: "Packed with families, but" signals a contrast, and "no children on the swings" shows the playground was empty.

example: The dog seized the ball and ran off.
hook: "Seize the day" means grab your chance; picture an eagle seizing a fish in one swoop.

traps.why: Release means let go, the opposite of seize.
Cease sounds like seize, but it means to stop.
Touching is too gentle; seizing is a sudden, strong grab.

syn1.tip: Think of "seize the day," meaning grab your chance before it slips away.

sc1.stem: The hungry eagle swooped down to _____ the fish in its claws in one quick, sudden grab.

traps.why: A hungry eagle grabs fish; it does not release them.
The eagle may spot the fish, but "grab" says it caught it.
Brushing is too light to hold a fish in its claws.

sc1.tip: "One quick, sudden grab" tells you the eagle grabbed the fish fast and held it.

traps.why: Dropping is letting go, the opposite of seizing.
You might chase something first, but seizing is the grabbing.
A tap is a light touch, far weaker than seizing.

syn2.tip: The dog seized the ball and ran off: it grabbed it quickly and held on tight.

sc2.stem: The moment the referee tossed the ball into the air, Jamal leaped to _____ it before the other team's player could even reach for it.

traps.why: You cannot drop a ball you do not have yet.
Leaping before the other player could reach means he grabbed it.
Jamal leaped toward the ball to beat the other player, not to avoid it.

sc2.tip: He leaped "before the other team's player could even reach for it," so he grabbed it first.

meaning: careful to avoid danger or mistakes
example: Be cautious when you cross a busy street.
hook: Cautious means full of caution, like a driver who slows down at every yellow CAUTION sign.

traps.why: Reckless means not caring about danger, the opposite of cautious.
Curious looks like cautious, but it means wanting to know things.
Terrified is much too strong; cautious people are careful, not panicked.

syn1.tip: Cautious is "caution" plus -ous, meaning full of. Yellow CAUTION signs warn you to be careful.

sc1.stem: Unlike her daring cousin, who leaps off the dock without looking, Priya checks the water's depth first because she is _____.

traps.why: Bold describes the daring cousin, and "unlike" means Priya is different.
Reckless fits leaping "without looking," not Priya, who checks first.
Checking the depth first is careful work, not laziness.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her daring cousin" signals contrast. Priya does the opposite of leaping "without looking," so she is careful.

traps.why: Being ready for risks is the opposite of being cautious.
Cautious people avoid danger by being careful, not by running.
That is too strong; cautious people are careful, not scared of everything.

syn2.tip: Hear the word "caution" inside it. A cautious person looks both ways and thinks before acting.

sc2.stem: After slipping on the icy sidewalk last winter, Leo became much more _____, taking small steps and holding the railing whenever the ground looked slick.

traps.why: Small steps and holding the railing are not careless.
Slipping is about balance, but small steps show care, not grace.
Curious looks like cautious, but nothing here is about wanting to know.

sc2.tip: "After slipping" gives the cause, and "small steps" and "holding the railing" show the effect: Leo became careful.

example: Don't hesitate to ask for help.
hook: When you hesitate, your finger hovers over the button for a moment before you finally press it.

traps.why: Rushing means acting fast, the opposite of hesitating.
Refusing is too strong; hesitating is only a short pause.
Imitate sounds like hesitate, but it means to copy.

syn1.tip: You hear it in "don't hesitate to ask," meaning don't wait or hold back before asking.

sc1.stem: If you know the answer, don't _____ or pause; raise your hand right away before someone else does.

traps.why: The sentence wants you to act "right away," so not hurrying is wrong.
Shouting is about answering, but "or pause" tells you the meaning.
Imitate sounds like hesitate, but copying has nothing to do with pausing.

sc1.tip: "Or pause" restates the blank, and "right away" shows the opposite, so the word means to pause before acting.

traps.why: Acting right away is the opposite of hesitating.
Giving up is too strong; hesitating is just a short wait.
You might think while hesitating, but hesitate means pausing.

syn2.tip: Picture someone at the edge of a pool, waiting a second before jumping. That short pause is hesitating.

sc2.stem: Usually Ana dives right in, but at the top of the tall slide she began to _____, gripping the rails while the kids behind her waited.

traps.why: Kids waiting behind her show she was not zooming down.
Gripping the rails shows worry, not a happy cheer.
"But" shows she did not dive right in, so she did not rush.
