sc2.tip: "But" shows a contrast with farmers who "struggled to pay their bills." When crops grew tall, the farmers did well and had money.

example: The barn was a refuge from the rain.
hook: Refuge shares a root with refugee, a person who flees danger to find a safe place.

traps.why: Danger is the opposite of a safe place.
Refund looks similar but means money given back.
People take refuge from a storm, but the storm is not the safe place.

syn1.tip: Think of "take refuge," which means find a safe place. People take refuge from storms, danger, or noise.

sc1.stem: When the rain began to pour, the hikers took _____ under a rocky ledge until the storm passed.

traps.why: Taking chances means risking danger, but the hikers were staying safe.
Refund looks like refuge but means money back, which makes no sense here.
To take flight means to run off, but the hikers stayed under the ledge.

sc1.tip: "When the rain began to pour" and "until the storm passed" show the hikers needed protection. Taking it "under a rocky ledge" means finding shelter.

traps.why: A place of danger is the opposite of a refuge.
That is refuse, a lookalike word; refuge means a safe place.
You seek refuge from stormy weather, but refuge is the shelter.

syn2.tip: A refuge is where you go to get away from trouble. Picture a cozy library as a refuge from a noisy, crowded house.

sc2.stem: The noisy cafeteria gave Mia a headache, so the quiet school library became her _____, a peaceful spot where she could read and escape the crowd.

traps.why: A prison is a place you cannot escape, not a peaceful spot.
The cafeteria gave her a headache; the library is where she escaped it.
A chore is a task, not a peaceful spot to escape the crowd.

sc2.tip: The phrase after the comma restates the blank: "a peaceful spot where she could read and escape the crowd." That describes a safe place.

example: This blunt knife can't cut the bread.
hook: A blunt pencil needs sharpening, and a blunt friend tells you straight out that your shirt is on backward.

traps.why: Sharp is the opposite of blunt.
Blurry looks similar but means hard to see clearly.
A blunt knife still works a little; broken means it does not work.

syn1.tip: Blunt describes an edge or point that is not sharp. Think of a "blunt pencil" that needs sharpening before you can write neatly.

sc1.stem: Kindergarten safety scissors have _____, rounded tips instead of sharp points, so no one can get poked.

traps.why: Pointed is the opposite of the rounded tips the sentence describes.
Kids' scissors are often colorful, but the clue is about the tips' shape.
Blurry looks like blunt but means hard to see, not rounded.

sc1.tip: "Instead of sharp points" tells you the blank is the opposite of sharp. "Rounded tips" also points to an edge that is not sharp.

traps.why: Gentle words soften the truth, the opposite of blunt words.
Cruel is too strong; a blunt person is honest, not trying to hurt.
Blunt words are often short, but blunt means direct, not brief.

syn2.tip: Blunt also describes how people talk. A blunt person says exactly what they think without softening it, like "That drawing is messy."

sc2.stem: Grandpa is always _____; when I asked how my cookies tasted, he said plainly that they were burned and too salty.

traps.why: A gentle grandpa would soften the news about burned cookies.
Dull matches blunt's knife meaning, but here Grandpa speaks plainly.
The sentence is about cookies, but it shows how Grandpa talks, not eats.

sc2.tip: "He said plainly that they were burned and too salty" shows Grandpa speaks directly without softening the truth.

example: The persistent woodpecker kept tapping.
hook: Persistent comes from persist, meaning to keep going, so a persistent puppy keeps nudging your hand until you pet it.

traps.why: Lazy people give up easily; persistent people keep going.
Personal starts the same way but means private or about one person.
Persistence can annoy people, but persistent mostly praises steady effort.

syn1.tip: Persistent contains persist, which means to keep going. A persistent person does not give up, even when things get hard.

sc1.stem: Even after her robot failed nine times, the _____ inventor kept fixing it until it finally worked on the tenth try.

traps.why: A lazy inventor would not keep fixing the robot ten times.
A hopeless inventor would stop, but this one kept fixing the robot.
Personal looks like persistent but does not describe someone who keeps trying.

sc1.tip: "Kept fixing it until it finally worked on the tenth try" shows an inventor who would not give up after failing.

traps.why: Quick to quit is the opposite of persistent.
Being on time is a good habit, but persistent means not giving up.
Pushy is a negative word; persistent is mostly a compliment.

syn2.tip: Think of a "persistent cough" that will not go away. Persistent people and things keep on going and do not stop.

sc2.stem: Most of the kids gave up on the tricky jigsaw puzzle after ten minutes, but _____ Jamal kept working on it all afternoon until every piece fit.

traps.why: Impatient kids gave up quickly, but Jamal stayed with it all afternoon.
A bored kid would quit, but Jamal kept working until the end.
Lazy describes quitting, but "but" shows Jamal was different.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Jamal with the kids who "gave up." He "kept working on it all afternoon," so he refused to quit.

example: The stern librarian asked us to whisper.
hook: Picture a stern judge peering over her glasses: no smile, no jokes, just strict rules and a serious face.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite of stern; a stern person is firm, not soft.
The stern is the back of a boat, but a stern person is strict.
Furious is far too strong; a stern person is serious, not raging.

syn1.tip: Think of a stern teacher's look when the class gets noisy. It feels serious and firm, like someone enforcing rules.

sc1.stem: With a _____ look and a serious, strict voice, the coach told the team that nobody would skip practice again.

traps.why: A friendly look clashes with the serious, strict voice.
Worried is a feeling on a face, but the clue says strict.
Bored describes a face, but nothing in the sentence shows boredom.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "a serious, strict voice." The look should match that voice.

traps.why: Playful is the opposite of stern, which means serious and strict.
Cruel goes too far; stern people are strict but not meant to hurt.
A stern voice may be loud, but stern is about being serious.

syn2.tip: Stern goes with words like warning and look. Ask yourself what face fits a stern warning: a serious one.

sc2.stem: Our new principal seemed friendly in the hallway, but in assemblies she was _____, never smiling and insisting that every rule be followed.

traps.why: Relaxed fits the hallway, but "but" tells you assemblies were different.
Playful people smile, and she was "never smiling."
Nervous is a feeling, but nothing says she was afraid or uneasy.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets up a contrast with "friendly." Then "never smiling" and "every rule be followed" describe a strict, serious person.

example: The prince was heir to the throne.
hook: Heir sounds just like air because the h is silent; an heir is next in line to inherit the crown.

traps.why: An ancestor came before you; an heir comes after.
Air sounds the same as heir but means what you breathe.
An heir may rule someday, but is not the ruler yet.

syn1.tip: Heir is inside the word inherit. An heir is the one who takes over next, so think of who comes after.

sc1.stem: As the king's only child, the young prince was the _____ to the throne and would one day rule.

traps.why: Air sounds like heir, but you cannot be the air to a throne.
A servant works near the throne but would not one day rule.
An ancestor came before the king, not after him.

sc1.tip: The clues are "the king's only child" and "would one day rule." The blank names the person who will take over the throne.

traps.why: That describes an ancestor, the opposite of an heir.
An heir will rule later; someone else rules now.
Heir looks a bit like hire, but heirs inherit, they are not hired.

syn2.tip: Look inside inherit and you will find heir. An heir is the person who will receive something from someone else.

sc2.stem: Because Grandpa wanted his old stamp collection to stay in the family, he named me his _____, so the albums will be mine someday.

traps.why: Grandpa is the ancestor here; you are the one coming after.
A customer buys things, but the albums will be given, not sold.
A neighbor lives nearby, which does not keep the stamps in the family.

sc2.tip: Follow the cause and effect: Grandpa wants it "to stay in the family," so "the albums will be mine someday." The blank names who receives them.

meaning: to check that something is true
example: Verify your answers before you turn it in.
hook: Verify starts like very, which once meant true; to verify is to make sure something is true.

traps.why: Disprove means show something is false, the opposite of verify.
Vary looks like verify but means to change.
Guessing is about facts too, but verify means checking for sure.

syn1.tip: The ending -ify means to make. Verify starts like very, an old word for true, so verify means make sure it is true.

sc1.stem: Before adding the fact to her report, Ava checked an encyclopedia to _____ that it was actually true.

traps.why: Deny means say it is not true, but Ava wanted to use the fact.
Imagining does not need an encyclopedia and does not check facts.
Hoping a fact is true is not the same as checking it.

sc1.tip: The clue is "checked an encyclopedia" to see "that it was actually true." The blank means to check that something is true.

traps.why: Telling a lie spreads falsehood; verifying finds the truth.
Guessing is not checking; verify means you make sure.
Writing something down does not prove it is true.

syn2.tip: You might hear "verify your password" on a computer. The computer is checking that it is really true and correct.

sc2.stem: Instead of just believing the rumor that school was canceled, Marcus called the office to _____ it, and learned classes were still on.

traps.why: People spread rumors, but Marcus called to check, not to tell others.
Calling the office is the opposite of ignoring the rumor.
Marcus did not make up the rumor; he checked it.

sc2.tip: "Instead of just believing" sets up a contrast. Marcus did not just believe it; he called to check whether it was true.

example: We were optimistic about winning.
hook: Optimistic comes from the Latin word optimus, meaning best; optimistic people expect the best and see the glass half full.

traps.why: Gloomy people expect bad things, the opposite of optimistic.
Optical starts the same way but means having to do with eyes.
Certain is too strong; optimistic people hope, they are not sure.

syn1.tip: Optimistic starts like optimum, the best. An optimistic person has a bright, positive feeling about what is coming.

sc1.stem: Even after losing three games in a row, Zoe stayed _____, sure that her team would win the next one.

traps.why: Discouraged fits the losses, but Zoe is "sure that her team would win."
Worried people expect trouble, but Zoe expects a win.
Losing might tire her, but the clue is about her expectations.

sc1.tip: "Even after losing" signals a contrast. Despite the losses, she was "sure that her team would win," so she expected good things.

traps.why: Expecting the worst is pessimistic, the opposite of optimistic.
Optim means best, but optimistic is about expecting, not choosing.
Hard work may help, but optimistic describes a hopeful attitude.

syn2.tip: Think of a glass half full. An optimistic person looks ahead and expects good things to happen.

sc2.stem: The weather report showed sunshine all week, so Dad felt _____ that our camping trip would be dry and fun.

traps.why: Sunshine all week gives no reason to doubt a dry trip.
A sunny report would cheer Dad up, not make him gloomy.
Uneasy means worried, but the good forecast removes any worry.

sc2.tip: Look at cause and effect: "sunshine all week, so" Dad expected the trip "would be dry and fun." Good news leads to a hopeful feeling.

meaning: strong enough to survive hard conditions
example: Hardy plants survive the cold winter.
hook: Hardy plants are survivors: a cactus in scorching desert heat and a pine on a frozen mountain are both hardy.

traps.why: Delicate things break easily, the opposite of hardy.
Tardy rhymes with hardy but means late.
Hardy contains hard, but it means strong, not difficult.

syn1.tip: Gardeners call plants hardy when they survive frost. Think of something that can handle tough conditions without dying.

sc1.stem: Only _____ pine trees could survive the freezing winds and thin soil high on the rocky mountaintop.

traps.why: Weak trees could not survive freezing winds and thin soil.
Decorative is about looks, not about surviving harsh weather.
Potted trees do not grow in mountaintop soil and wind.

sc1.tip: The clue is "could survive the freezing winds and thin soil." Only strong trees could do that.

traps.why: Fragile things break easily; hardy things hold up.
Big things are not always tough; hardy is about surviving.
Harsh describes the conditions; hardy describes what survives them.

syn2.tip: Picture a hardy weed growing through a crack in the sidewalk. It is strong and survives where other plants cannot.

sc2.stem: Most of Grandma's flowers wilted during the dry, scorching summer, but her _____ cactus kept growing as if nothing had happened.

traps.why: A delicate plant would wilt like the others, but "but" shows contrast.
Thirsty fits a dry summer, but the cactus kept growing fine.
Tardy means late, which says nothing about surviving heat.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the cactus with the flowers that "wilted." It "kept growing as if nothing had happened," so it was strong.

meaning: not well known; or hard to see
example: He collects songs by obscure bands.
hook: An obscure band is one hardly anyone has heard of, and an obscure path is half hidden in shadow.

traps.why: Famous means known by many, the opposite of obscure.
Secure rhymes with obscure but means safe.
Obscure things may seem strange, but obscure means little known.

syn1.tip: Think of "an obscure fact" in a trivia game: one hardly anyone knows. The word feels hidden or out of sight.

sc1.stem: Mia loves an _____ band so little known that none of her friends has ever heard of it.

traps.why: Obvious means easy to notice, the opposite of little known.
An international band is known around the world, not little known.
An overplayed band is heard everywhere, so her friends would know it.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "so little known that none of her friends has ever heard of it."

traps.why: Easy to spot is the opposite of obscure.
Kept safe means secure, which only sounds like obscure.
Old things can be forgotten, but obscure does not mean old.

syn2.tip: Obscure has two meanings: little known, or hidden from view. Fog can obscure a road, making it hard to see.

sc2.stem: Everyone knew the famous facts about George Washington, but the fact Ben shared was so _____ that even our teacher had never heard it.

traps.why: A familiar fact is one people know, but the teacher never heard it.
Popular facts are widely known, which does not fit "never heard it."
Being important would not explain why the teacher never heard it.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Ben's fact with the "famous facts." The result, "even our teacher had never heard it," shows the fact was little known.

example: Can you clarify the directions?
hook: Clarify shares its start with clear: to clarify is to make things clear, like wiping fog off a window.

traps.why: Confuse means make less clear, the opposite of clarify.
Classify looks similar but means sort into groups.
Repeating something does not make it any clearer.

syn1.tip: Clarify starts like clear, and -ify means to make. So clarify means to make clear.

sc1.stem: Because the game's directions were confusing, Mr. Park took a moment to _____ them so everyone understood.

traps.why: Complicating confusing directions would not help everyone understand.
Skipping the directions would not make everyone understand them.
Classify looks like clarify but means sort, which does not help here.

sc1.tip: The directions "were confusing," and afterward "everyone understood." The blank is what turns confusing into clear.

traps.why: Making something cloudy is the opposite of making it clear.
Louder does not mean easier to understand.
That means classify, which only looks like clarify.

syn2.tip: Look for clar, as in clear, plus -ify, meaning to make. Put them together and you get make clear.

sc2.stem: At first nobody understood Ms. Lee's riddle, but after she drew a picture on the board to _____ it, the whole class finally got the joke.

traps.why: Making the riddle harder would not help the class finally get it.
Decorating a riddle would not help anyone understand it.
Hiding the riddle would stop the class from getting the joke.

sc2.tip: "At first nobody understood," "but" after the picture, "the whole class finally got the joke." The picture made the riddle clear.

example: Her smile conveyed how happy she was.
hook: A conveyor belt carries groceries to the cashier; to convey means to carry something, even a feeling or a message.

traps.why: Hide means keep something secret, the opposite of convey.
Convince looks similar but means persuade someone to agree.
Survey ends the same way but means look over or question.

syn1.tip: Think of a conveyor belt that carries things along. When you convey a message, you carry it to someone else.

sc1.stem: Without saying a single word, the actor used only his face to _____ how sad his character felt.

traps.why: The actor was "without saying a single word," so he could not shout.
You cannot measure sadness with your face.
Using his face to forget sadness makes no sense in a performance.

sc1.tip: "Without saying a single word" and "used only his face" tell you he showed the feeling to the audience.

traps.why: Drop means let fall, the opposite of carrying something along.
Lifting raises something, but convey means move it somewhere.
Storing keeps things in place; conveying moves them.

syn2.tip: Convey can mean carry as well as communicate. A conveyor belt at the store carries your groceries.

sc2.stem: The pipes in our school are so old that they can no longer _____ water to the fountains, so we have to bring water bottles.

traps.why: Pipes cannot drink water; they move it.
Freezing water to the fountains makes no sense.
Wasting water would not explain why fountains have no water.

sc2.tip: Follow the cause and effect: the old pipes fail, "so we have to bring water bottles." The pipes no longer carry water.

example: That was a deliberate push, not an accident.
hook: A deliberate foul is no accident: the player planned it and meant to do it.

traps.why: Accidental means by mistake, the opposite of deliberate.
Delicate starts the same way but means easily broken.
A deliberate act can be calm; deliberate means planned.

syn1.tip: You often hear "a deliberate mistake" or "that was deliberate" when someone did something on purpose.

sc1.stem: It was no accident: Leo's choice to skip the hard question was _____, since he planned to come back to it later.

traps.why: The sentence says "it was no accident."
Leo had a plan, so his choice was not careless.
Delicate looks similar but means fragile, which does not describe a choice.

sc1.tip: "It was no accident" and "he planned to come back to it" both tell you the choice was made on purpose.

traps.why: Done by mistake is the opposite of deliberate.
Set free means liberate, which only looks like part of deliberate.
Deliberate acts are planned, not necessarily angry.

syn2.tip: Ask: was it an accident or a plan? A deliberate act is one the person meant to do.

sc2.stem: Maya had spent all week practicing the trick, so when she dropped the ball behind her back, the move was _____, meant to fool her opponent.

traps.why: "Dropped" sounds clumsy, but she practiced it and meant to fool someone.
Luck is not planned, and she practiced all week.
The move was "meant to fool her opponent," so not an accident.

sc2.tip: She "spent all week practicing," so the drop was part of the plan. "Meant to fool her opponent" confirms it was on purpose.

example: Reckless biking can cause accidents.
hook: Reck is an old word for care, so reckless means without care, like riding a bike downhill with no brakes.

traps.why: Cautious people watch for danger, the opposite of reckless.
Restless looks similar but means unable to sit still.
Brave sounds admiring; reckless is negative, ignoring danger foolishly.

syn1.tip: The ending -less means without. Reckless means without care, the way a reckless driver ignores danger.

sc1.stem: Racing his bike downhill with no helmet and no brakes, Jake was _____, paying no attention to the danger.

traps.why: No helmet and no brakes is the opposite of cautious.
Racing downhill might tire him, but the clue is about danger.
Nothing says Jake did not know where he was.

sc1.tip: "No helmet and no brakes" and "paying no attention to the danger" describe someone who ignores danger.

traps.why: Very careful is the opposite of reckless.
Courage is praised; reckless is a criticism of foolish risk.
That describes restless, which only looks like reckless.

syn2.tip: You may hear "reckless driving" in news stories. It describes someone who acts without caring about danger.

sc2.stem: Mom calls my older sister a careful driver who always checks her mirrors, but she says my cousin is _____ because he texts while driving.

traps.why: Cautious fits the sister, but "but" shows the cousin is different.
Skillful is praise, and texting while driving deserves none.
Patience is not the issue; texting while driving is dangerous.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the cousin with the "careful driver." "Because he texts while driving" shows he ignores danger.

example: I persuaded Dad to get pancakes.
hook: Picture a kid persuading Mom with a long list of reasons why the family needs a puppy.

traps.why: Discourage is the opposite: it talks someone out of doing something.
Pursue looks like persuade, but it means to chase.
Forcing gives no choice; persuading wins someone over with words.

syn1.tip: When you persuade someone, you talk them into it, the way you might convince a friend to play your favorite game.

sc1.stem: With a strong speech full of facts, Liam managed to _____ the class to vote for a museum field trip.

traps.why: Forbid means to not allow, the opposite of getting them to vote.
A classmate can't order the class; a speech full of facts wins them over.
Allowing is giving permission, but Liam is changing minds, not giving permission.

sc1.tip: Look at "a strong speech full of facts." Facts and speeches are used to win people over, so Liam talked the class into it.

traps.why: Talking someone out of something is the opposite of persuading.
You may argue to persuade, but arguing with someone doesn't mean they agree.
Chase after means pursue, a word that only looks like persuade.

syn2.tip: Think of a salesperson trying to persuade you to buy something. They are trying to talk you into it.

sc2.stem: No matter how many reasons I gave, I could not _____ my little brother to try the spinach, so he pushed his plate away.

traps.why: You give reasons to get someone to try something, not to forbid it.
Allowing is giving permission, but reasons are for changing his mind.
Reminding only brings something to mind; reasons are meant to change his mind.

sc2.tip: The clue is "no matter how many reasons I gave" and "pushed his plate away." You tried to talk him into it and failed.

meaning: a sign or symbol of something
example: He gave her a flower as a token of thanks.
hook: A token of friendship, like a bead bracelet, is a small thing that stands for a big feeling.

traps.why: An arcade token is a coin, but here token means a sign of something.
A prize is won; a token stands for a feeling.
A token shows a feeling openly; a secret stays hidden.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "a token of thanks." The gift isn't the thanks itself; it stands for the thanks, like a symbol.

sc1.stem: As a _____ of their thanks, the class gave their teacher a handmade card signed by every student.

traps.why: A lack of thanks would mean no thanks, but they made a card.
Tokens can be used like tickets, but a card isn't a ticket.
You may owe someone thanks, but the card shows thanks rather than owing it.

sc1.tip: The phrase is "as a _____ of their thanks." The card is something that shows their thanks, so it is a sign or symbol.

traps.why: Ride tokens work like tickets, but this token means a sign of something.
You can say thanks in a speech, but a token is a thing that shows it.
A token of thanks doesn't pay someone back; it just shows how you feel.

syn2.tip: A token stands for something else, the way a heart stands for love. That makes it a sign.

sc2.stem: The small shell bracelet was a _____ of their friendship; it was not worth much money, but it stood for everything the two girls shared.

traps.why: The sentence says it was not worth much money, so it isn't about price.
A lack of friendship would mean no friendship, but they shared everything.
Some tokens are coins, but a bracelet isn't a coin.

sc2.tip: The second half explains the blank: "it stood for everything the two girls shared." Something that stands for a feeling is a token.

example: The cheap glue was inferior to the brand name.
hook: Inferior sits below: a knockoff sneaker that falls apart in a week is inferior to the real thing.

traps.why: Superior means better, the opposite of inferior.
Interior looks like inferior, but it means inside.
Inferior is about being worse in quality, not smaller in size.

syn1.tip: Inferior and superior are a pair. Superior is above and better; inferior is below and not as good.

sc1.stem: Our homemade kite was _____ to the store-bought one, which flew higher, looked nicer, and lasted much longer.

traps.why: The store kite flew higher and looked nicer, so the homemade one wasn't better.
The kites weren't equal; the store kite did everything better.
No one would prefer the kite that flew lower and broke sooner.

sc1.tip: The clue is "which flew higher, looked nicer, and lasted much longer." That describes the store kite, so the homemade one was worse.

traps.why: Higher in quality means superior, the opposite of inferior.
That describes interior, a word that only looks like inferior.
Inferior things are just not as good; they aren't completely useless.

syn2.tip: When something is inferior to something else, it is not as good. Think "below" in quality or rank.

sc2.stem: Although the copycat cereal cost less, its flakes turned soggy in seconds, so most kids agreed it was _____ to the famous brand.

traps.why: Soggy flakes make the copycat cereal worse, not better.
The cereals weren't the same; one went soggy in seconds.
Kids can be loyal to a brand, but this is about the cereal's quality.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast: it was cheaper, but "turned soggy in seconds." That makes it worse than the famous brand.

meaning: to use up completely; or to tire out
example: The long hike exhausted our water supply.
hook: Ex- means out: to exhaust a water bottle is to draw out every last drop until nothing is left.

traps.why: Refresh means to give new energy, the opposite of exhaust.
Exhale looks like exhaust, but it means to breathe out.
Car exhaust is smoke, but the verb exhaust means to use up.

syn1.tip: Think of being "exhausted" after a long day: all your energy has been used up, or drained out of you.

sc1.stem: Running laps in the hot sun for an hour seemed to _____ the players, who flopped onto the grass, completely worn out.

traps.why: The players flopped down worn out, so they weren't given energy.
Entertaining is fun; the players ended up worn out, not amused.
The laps might annoy them, but the clue says they were worn out.

sc1.tip: Look at what happened: the players "flopped onto the grass, completely worn out." The laps tired them out.

traps.why: Saving up keeps things, the opposite of using them all.
Warming up comes before exercise; exhausting is what tires you out.
Slowing down is milder; exhausting means nothing at all is left.

syn2.tip: When you exhaust a supply of snacks, there are none left. You have used them all up.

sc2.stem: We had to be careful not to _____ our supply of firewood on the first night, or there would be nothing left to burn by Saturday.

traps.why: Gathering adds wood, so it wouldn't leave you with nothing.
Stacking wood doesn't make it disappear by Saturday.
Hidden wood would still be there to burn later.

sc2.tip: The effect is "nothing left to burn." The blank must mean using all the firewood up too early.

example: My aunt will accompany us to the zoo.
hook: Accompany has the word company inside it: when you accompany someone, you keep them company along the way.

traps.why: Abandon means to leave someone behind, the opposite of going with them.
Accomplish looks like accompany, but it means to finish a goal.
Visiting means stopping by, not traveling along with someone.

syn1.tip: Find the word company inside accompany. When you accompany people, you keep them company as they go.

sc1.stem: Mom will _____ the class on the field trip, riding the bus with the students and staying by their side all day.

traps.why: Mom stays by their side all day, so she isn't leaving them.
Accomplish looks similar, but you can't finish a class like a task.
Mom rides the bus with them, so she doesn't need to call.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank: "riding the bus with the students and staying by their side all day." Mom is going along with them.

traps.why: Leaving someone behind is the opposite of going with them.
Get done means accomplish, a word that only looks like accompany.
Accompany contains company, but it has nothing to do with businesses.

syn2.tip: A piano player who accompanies a singer plays along with them. To accompany is to go along with someone.

sc2.stem: My little sister was too scared to walk into her new school alone, so Dad offered to _____ her all the way to her classroom door.

traps.why: Sending her would leave her alone, which is what scared her.
Dragging is rough; Dad is being kind by going along.
Chasing her wouldn't help a scared kid feel less alone.

sc2.tip: The cause is "too scared to walk... alone." So Dad helps by going along with her.

example: I caught a glimpse of a deer.
hook: A glimpse is gone in a blink, like spotting a shooting star from a car window before it disappears.

traps.why: A stare is a long look, the opposite of a quick glimpse.
Glimmer looks like glimpse, but it means a faint flicker of light.
A photo shows what you saw, but a glimpse is the look itself.

syn1.tip: People say they "caught a glimpse" of something that went by fast. A glimpse is a quick look, just like a glance.

sc1.stem: We caught only a quick _____ of the deer before it darted back into the woods.

traps.why: The deer ran off fast, so there was no time for a stare.
Glimmer looks like glimpse but means a flicker of light.
"A quick bite" is about food, not seeing the deer.

sc1.tip: The words "only a quick" and "darted back into the woods" tell you the look was very short.

traps.why: A long stare is the opposite of a glimpse.
Faint light means glimmer, which only looks like glimpse.
Eyesight is your ability to see, not one quick look.

syn2.tip: If you only got a glimpse of a famous person, you saw them for just a second. That's a quick look.

sc2.stem: Unlike the long, close look we got at the zoo's lions, we got only a _____ of the cheetah as it raced past.

traps.why: A study is a long, careful look, which the word "unlike" rules out.
A portrait is a picture, not a look at a racing cheetah.
A sniff uses your nose; the sentence is about looking.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the long, close look" sets up a contrast. The cheetah "raced past," so you saw it only for a moment.

example: Is there a park in the vicinity?
hook: Vicinity comes from the Latin word for neighbor, so the vicinity is the neighborhood all around you.

traps.why: Distance is far away; vicinity is close by.
Vicinity ends in city, but it means the nearby area, not a city.
Victory starts like vicinity, but it means a win.

syn1.tip: People ask, "Is there a store in the vicinity?" They mean close by, in the neighborhood.

sc1.stem: Is there a library in the _____ of our school, or do we have to drive all the way across town?

traps.why: The question is about something close, not far, since the other choice is across town.
Victory looks a bit like vicinity but means a win.
A schedule is about time; the sentence is about a place nearby.

sc1.tip: The contrast is with "drive all the way across town." The blank must mean the area close to the school.

traps.why: A faraway place is the opposite of the vicinity.
The ending city is a trick; vicinity means the area near you.
An address is one exact spot; vicinity is the whole area around it.

syn2.tip: Vicinity comes from the Latin word for neighbor. Your neighbors live in the nearby area.

sc2.stem: When our dog ran off, we searched the whole _____ of our house, checking every yard and street within a few blocks.

traps.why: The interior is inside the house, but you checked yards and streets.
The roof is too small an area; you searched several blocks.
A house's value is its price, not the streets around it.

sc2.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "every yard and street within a few blocks." That is the area near your house.

example: We modified the recipe to use less sugar.
hook: Gamers talk about a mod: that's short for modification, a small change someone makes to a game.

traps.why: Preserve means to keep something the same, the opposite of changing it.
Model looks a bit like modify, but it means to show or pose.
Destroying is far too strong; modifying is only a small change.

syn1.tip: A modified bike has had a few parts changed. To modify is to alter something a little.

sc1.stem: Instead of building a brand-new treehouse, the kids decided to _____ the old one a little by adding a rope ladder.

traps.why: "Instead of building a brand-new treehouse" means they did not replace it.
Demolishing knocks it down; they only changed it "a little."
You can't paint something "by adding a rope ladder."

sc1.tip: The signal words are "instead of building a brand-new" and "a little." They changed the old treehouse slightly.

traps.why: Keeping it the same is the opposite of modifying it.
Modifying is a small change, not wrecking the whole thing.
An exact copy has no changes at all.

syn2.tip: Think of a "mod" in a video game. It changes a game slightly without building a new one.

sc2.stem: Because the lemonade tasted too sour at yesterday's stand, Maya chose to _____ her recipe by adding one more spoonful of sugar.

traps.why: Repeating the recipe would keep it sour; she wanted it different.
Memorizing a recipe doesn't change how the lemonade tastes.
Throwing it out is too much; she only added one spoonful.

sc2.tip: The cause is "too sour," and the fix is "adding one more spoonful." That's a small change to the recipe.

example: The naive puppy chased a skunk.
hook: A naive kid believes a classmate who says the cafeteria will serve free ice cream every day forever.

traps.why: Experienced is the opposite; naive people haven't seen much yet.
Native looks like naive, but it means born in a place.
Stupid is a harsh insult; naive just means lacking experience.

syn1.tip: A naive person trusts too easily because they haven't learned better yet, like a young child. Think innocent.

sc1.stem: Having never camped before, Ella was _____ about the woods and packed no bug spray, no flashlight, and no rain jacket.

traps.why: She had "never camped before," so she was not experienced.
Stubborn means refusing to change; the clue is that she lacked experience.
Nothing in the sentence shows a bad mood, only a lack of know-how.

sc1.tip: The cause is "having never camped before," and the proof is everything she forgot. She didn't know what the woods require.

traps.why: Hard to trick is the opposite of naive.
That's the meaning of native, which only looks like naive.
Naive people lack experience, not the ability to learn.

syn2.tip: Someone naive believes things too quickly, so they are easy to trick. Picture a newcomer falling for an April Fools joke.

sc2.stem: My older brother laughed at how _____ I was to believe that the tooth fairy really left me a gold coin, but I was only five.

traps.why: He laughed at you for believing it, so you weren't being clever.
Native looks like naive but means born in a place.
Believing a story isn't brave, and he was laughing at you.

sc2.tip: The clues are "laughed at," "to believe," and "only five." A young child believes stories too easily.

example: This is a potent cleaner, so wear gloves.
hook: Potent shares its root with potential: both are about power, and a potent hot sauce packs huge power into one drop.

traps.why: Weak is the opposite of potent.
Patient looks a bit like potent, but it means calm while waiting.
Potent things are strong, but they can be tiny, like one drop.

syn1.tip: Potent and potential share a root about power. A potent medicine or smell is very powerful.

sc1.stem: The garlic was so _____ that a single clove made the whole pot of soup taste strong and powerful.

traps.why: Mild garlic couldn't flavor a whole pot with one clove.
A single clove is small already; the point is how strong it was.
Patient looks like potent but describes people who can wait.

sc1.tip: Look at the effect: "a single clove made the whole pot of soup taste strong." A tiny bit with a big effect means very strong.

traps.why: Something potent is hard to miss, not barely noticeable.
That's closer to potential; potent means strong right now.
Strong things may cost more, but potent is about strength, not price.

syn2.tip: A potent cleaner is so strong you need gloves. Potent means very strong.

sc2.stem: The medicine looked like plain water, but it was so _____ that the doctor said I should take only one tiny drop each morning.

traps.why: A weak medicine wouldn't need to be limited to one tiny drop.
Good taste wouldn't make a doctor limit you to one drop.
"But" sets up a contrast with looking like water, so clear doesn't fit.

sc2.tip: "Looked like plain water, but" signals a surprise. It only looks harmless, and "only one tiny drop" shows it is very strong.

example: We enjoyed the garden's bounty of tomatoes.
hook: Picture a harvest table piled so high with corn, apples, and pies that it can barely hold more: that's a bounty.

sc1.stem: After a sunny summer, the farmers celebrated the rich _____ of their harvest, with more apples than they could count.

traps.why: A shortage is too little, but they had more apples than they could count.
Farmers sell their harvest, but the sentence is about how much they grew.
Boundary looks like bounty but means an edge, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: The words "rich" and "more apples than they could count" tell you the blank means a large amount.

sc2.stem: Last year the apple tree gave us only a few sour apples, but this fall its _____ filled six baskets to the brim.

traps.why: Scarcity fits last year, but "but" tells you this fall was different.
A trunk is part of the tree, but it cannot fill baskets.
Bounce looks a bit like bounty but has nothing to do with fruit.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets this fall against "only a few sour apples." Six full baskets means a large amount.

meaning: to expect or look forward to
example: We anticipate a big crowd at the fair.
hook: To anticipate is to see it coming, like a goalie who dives the right way before the ball is kicked.

traps.why: To ignore is to pay no attention, the opposite of thinking ahead.
Participate sounds like anticipate but means to take part.
Anti often means against, but anticipate is about looking ahead, not opposing.

syn1.tip: Anticipate is about the future. Think of waiting for your birthday and knowing it is coming.

sc1.stem: Expecting a busy day, the librarian tried to _____ every question visitors might ask and prepared answers ahead of time.

traps.why: She prepared answers, so she did not ignore the questions.
Remember looks back, but these questions have not been asked yet.
Preparing answers ahead of time is the opposite of avoiding questions.

sc1.tip: "Expecting a busy day" and "prepared answers ahead of time" show she thought about the questions before they came.

sc2.stem: Because Maria had found the balloons hidden in the closet, she began to _____ a surprise party and practiced acting shocked.

traps.why: Finding the balloons made her think of the party, not forget it.
The hidden balloons were proof, so she had no reason to doubt.
Practicing acting shocked means the party was for her, so she wasn't planning it.

sc2.tip: "Because" she found the balloons, she knew a party was coming. "Practiced acting shocked" shows she was expecting it.

example: Ferns thrive in shady, damp places.
hook: Picture a plant on a sunny windowsill growing taller and greener every single day: it thrives.

traps.why: Wither means to dry up and weaken, the opposite of thrive.
Strive looks like thrive but means to try hard.
Surviving is just staying alive; thriving is growing strong. Survive is too weak.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "plants thrive in sunlight." Pick the word that means growing well.

sc1.stem: Some kids _____ on challenges, growing stronger and happier every time they face a hard new problem.

traps.why: These kids grow stronger, so they are not stumbling.
Frown on means dislike, but these kids grow happier from challenges.
Survive is too weak; these kids grow stronger and happier.

sc1.tip: The phrase "growing stronger and happier every time" tells you challenges help these kids do very well.

traps.why: Fading away is getting weaker, the opposite of thriving.
Barely getting by is too weak; thriving means doing really well.
Food helps things grow, but thrive means growing strong, not eating.

syn2.tip: Thrive has a happy, healthy feeling. Look for the choice that means doing well and growing.

sc2.stem: The cactus drooped in our damp basement, but once we moved it to the hot, sunny window, it began to _____ and even grew a pink flower.

traps.why: Wilting fits the basement, but "but" shows things got better.
Strive looks like thrive but means try hard, which plants don't do.
A plant that grows a new flower is not fading.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the droopy basement with the sunny window, and "even grew a pink flower" shows the cactus did well.

example: Chocolate or vanilla was a real dilemma.
hook: Dilemma starts with di, meaning two: you're stuck between two choices, like two parties on the same Saturday.

traps.why: A solution ends a problem; a dilemma is being stuck in one.
Diploma looks a bit like dilemma but is a certificate from school.
People may argue about choices, but a dilemma is the hard choice itself.

syn1.tip: A dilemma feels like being stuck. Look for the word that means a difficult situation.

sc1.stem: Jo faced a _____: should she go to her best friend's party or her brother's big game, both on Saturday?

traps.why: Jo is still asking which to pick, so she has no solution yet.
A party is a celebration, but Jo is stuck choosing.
Triumph is a happy win, but Jo is facing a tough decision.

sc1.tip: The question after the colon, "should she go to... or...," shows two options she must pick between.

traps.why: An easy answer is the opposite of a hard choice.
Di means two, but a dilemma is two hard options, not two wins.
A dilemma might put you in a bad mood, but it is a choice.

syn2.tip: The di in dilemma means two. Think of being torn between two options you can't both have.

sc2.stem: Choosing a pizza topping is usually easy for Sam, but deciding which of his two best friends to sit with at lunch was a real _____.

traps.why: A breeze is something easy, but "but" shows this choice was hard.
A treat is pleasant, but choosing between two best friends is hard.
Lunch is a meal, but the sentence is about a hard choice.

sc2.tip: "Usually easy" is set against the lunch choice with "but," so the blank means a hard decision between "two best friends."

example: Cheating brought disgrace to the player.
hook: Grace means honor and favor; dis- takes it away, so disgrace is losing people's respect.

traps.why: Honor is respect, the opposite of disgrace.
Disguise looks like disgrace but means a costume to hide who you are.
Grace can mean smooth movement, but disgrace is about losing respect.

syn1.tip: Dis- means not, and grace here means honor. Without honor, you feel the opposite: think of "a disgrace to the team."

sc1.stem: Getting caught cheating on the test brought _____ to Tim, and he felt ashamed in front of the whole class.

traps.why: Tim felt ashamed, which is the opposite of pride.
Relief is a good feeling, but Tim felt ashamed.
Disguise looks like disgrace but means a costume, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: The words "felt ashamed in front of the whole class" tell you what cheating brought Tim.

traps.why: Gaining honor is the opposite of losing respect.
Grace can mean smooth movement, but disgrace is not about tripping.
Someone in disgrace may be upset, but disgrace means losing respect.

syn2.tip: Break it apart: dis- (not) plus grace (honor or favor). Pick the choice about losing people's good opinion.

sc2.stem: Fans once cheered the star pitcher, but after he was caught cheating, he left the team in _____.

traps.why: Triumph is a proud win, but he was caught cheating.
Leaving in style sounds cool, but cheating made him leave badly.
Glory fits the cheering fans, but "but" shows things changed.

sc2.tip: "Once cheered" is set against "caught cheating" with "but," so he left having lost everyone's respect.

example: Icy roads are hazardous for drivers.
hook: A hazard is a danger and -ous means full of, so hazardous means full of danger, like an icy sidewalk.

traps.why: Safe is the opposite of hazardous.
Hazy looks like hazardous but means foggy or unclear.
Careless people can cause danger, but hazardous describes the danger itself.

syn1.tip: Inside hazardous is hazard, like a "road hazard" sign. Add -ous, full of, and it means full of danger.

sc1.stem: Bleach is _____ to breathe or swallow, so Mom keeps it on a high shelf with a bright danger label.

traps.why: Harmless things don't need a danger label.
Refreshing sounds pleasant, but bleach has a danger label.
Bleach helps clean, but breathing or swallowing it is not helpful.

sc1.tip: The "bright danger label" and keeping it "on a high shelf" tell you bleach can hurt you.

traps.why: Secure means safe, the opposite of hazardous.
Hazards can cause accidents, but accidental means not done on purpose.
Unpleasant is too weak; hazardous means it could actually hurt you.

syn2.tip: Think of a "hazardous waste" sign. Pick the word that means something could get hurt.

sc2.stem: The lake looks calm and inviting in winter, but its thin ice is truly _____, so no one should ever skate on it.

traps.why: If the ice were safe, people could skate on it.
Beautiful fits "inviting," but "but" and "thin ice" point to danger.
Ice is frozen, but that would not explain why no one should skate.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the inviting look with the "thin ice," and "so no one should ever skate" shows the ice is dangerous.

example: We had a spontaneous dance party.
hook: A spontaneous dance party starts the moment a great song comes on, with no plan at all.

traps.why: Rehearsed means practiced ahead, the opposite of spontaneous.
Spongy starts like spontaneous but means soft and squishy.
Spontaneous parties can be loud, but spontaneous means unplanned.

syn1.tip: Think of a "spontaneous dance party" that just happens. Look for the word meaning not planned ahead.

sc1.stem: Without any planning at all, the family took a _____ trip to the beach when the sun suddenly came out.

traps.why: A scheduled trip is planned, but they had no planning at all.
Organized means planned out, but the sentence says no planning.
Simultaneous sounds like spontaneous but means at the same time.

sc1.tip: "Without any planning at all" and "suddenly" tell you the trip was not planned.

traps.why: Careful planning is the opposite of spontaneous.
That is simultaneous, which sounds like spontaneous but means at the same time.
Spontaneous is about not planning, not about speed.

syn2.tip: Spontaneous things happen suddenly, on the spot. Pick the choice that means no plan.

sc2.stem: Ms. Lee's field trips are usually planned weeks ahead, but today's _____ walk to the park happened only because the sunshine was too nice to waste.

traps.why: Scheduled fits "planned weeks ahead," but "but" shows today was different.
Weather matters here, but the sentence says it was sunny.
Monthly means regular, but this walk happened just because of the sunshine.

sc2.tip: "Usually planned weeks ahead" is set against today with "but," so this walk was not planned.

example: These durable boots lasted three winters.
hook: Durable shares a root with endure and during: durable things last, like a lunchbox that survives years of drops.

traps.why: Flimsy means weak and easy to break, the opposite of durable.
Strong things are often heavy, but durable means long-lasting.
Adorable looks like durable but means cute.

syn1.tip: Durable sounds like during and endure. Durable things last a long time, so pick the word meaning strong.

sc1.stem: The _____ backpack lasted all through elementary school, still without a single rip after six years of heavy use.

traps.why: A flimsy backpack would rip quickly, not last six years.
The sentence says "without a single rip."
Disposable things get thrown away fast, but this lasted six years.

sc1.tip: "Lasted all through elementary school" and "without a single rip after six years" show the backpack was strong.

traps.why: Easy to break is the opposite of durable.
Durable things may cost more, but durable means long-lasting.
Strong things can be heavy, but durable is about lasting.

syn2.tip: Think of "durable boots" that last for years. Pick the choice about lasting a long time.

sc2.stem: My cheap plastic sandals snapped after one week, so this summer Mom bought a _____ pair made of thick leather that should last for years.

traps.why: Flimsy describes the old sandals that snapped, not the new pair.
The old pair was plastic, but the new pair is thick leather.
Temporary means for a short time, but these should last for years.

sc2.tip: The old sandals "snapped after one week," so Mom chose the opposite: "thick leather that should last for years."

example: I was skeptical of the talking-dog story.
hook: A skeptical person raises one eyebrow and says, "Prove it," when a friend claims to have seen a unicorn.

traps.why: Trusting means believing easily, the opposite of skeptical.
Skeletal starts like skeptical but means like a skeleton.
A skeptical person may frown, but skeptical is about doubt, not anger.

syn1.tip: Picture a raised eyebrow and the words "I'm not so sure." Skeptical means not believing easily.

sc1.stem: Doubting the ad's claim that a cream could make hair grow overnight, Dad was _____ and did not buy it.

traps.why: Dad doubted the claim, so he was not convinced.
Gullible means easily fooled, but Dad did not buy it.
Eager is excited, but Dad doubted the ad and didn't buy it.

sc1.tip: "Doubting the ad's claim" and "did not buy it" show Dad did not believe the cream would work.

traps.why: Believing quickly is the opposite of being skeptical.
Skeptical is about believing claims, not how fast you learn.
Too strong; a skeptical person doubts but could still be convinced.

syn2.tip: A skeptical person wants proof first. Pick the choice that means needing convincing.

sc2.stem: Most of my friends believed Ben really saw a ghost in the attic, but Mia stayed _____ and asked him for a photo as proof.

traps.why: Convinced fits the other friends, but "but" shows Mia was different.
A trusting person would not ask for proof.
Amazed fits believers, but Mia asked for proof instead.

sc2.tip: "Most of my friends believed" is set against Mia with "but," and she "asked him for a photo as proof."

example: The class vote was unanimous.
hook: Unanimous comes from Latin for "one mind": when every hand in class goes up, everyone is of one mind.

traps.why: Divided means people disagree, the opposite of unanimous.
Anonymous looks like unanimous but means without a name.
Un- here does not mean not; the uni part means one.

syn1.tip: The uni in unanimous means one, like unicycle. Everyone acting as one means they all agree.

sc1.stem: Every single student in the class voted yes, so the decision to adopt a class hamster was _____.

traps.why: Every student voted yes, so the class was not divided.
Anonymous looks like unanimous but means without a name.
Unpopular gives a bad feeling, but every student liked the idea.

sc1.tip: "Every single student in the class voted yes" tells you everyone agreed on the decision.

traps.why: Only a few agreeing is the opposite of everyone agreeing.
Uni means one, but unanimous means one shared mind, not one person.
Votes may be counted by hand, but unanimous means everyone agrees.

syn2.tip: Think of "a unanimous vote," where every hand goes up. Pick the choice meaning everyone agrees.

sc2.stem: Last week the club argued for an hour about the snack, but today the choice of pizza was _____, since not one member wanted anything else.

traps.why: Divided fits last week's argument, but "but" shows today was different.
No one wanted anything else, so there was nothing to debate.
Pizza may be delicious, but a choice is not something you taste.

sc2.tip: "Argued for an hour" is set against today with "but," and "not one member wanted anything else" means all agreed.

example: Steel bars reinforce the bridge.
hook: Picture builders sliding steel bars inside concrete so a bridge can hold heavy trucks; those bars reinforce it.

traps.why: Weaken is the opposite of reinforce.
The re- start makes you think of again, but reinforce means make stronger.
Repair fixes something broken; reinforce makes something stronger, broken or not.

syn1.tip: Think of reinforcements arriving to help an army. They make the side stronger, so reinforce means strengthen.

sc1.stem: Workers added steel beams to _____ the old bridge so it could safely hold heavier trucks.

traps.why: Weakening the bridge would make it less safe for heavier trucks.
Steel beams are for strength here, not for looks.
Inspecting only checks the bridge; it would not let it hold heavier trucks.

sc1.tip: The beams were added "so it could safely hold heavier trucks." That result means the bridge was made stronger.

traps.why: Make weaker is the opposite of reinforce.
Re- often means again, but reinforce is about strength, not repeating.
That is what enforce means, a word that only looks like reinforce.

syn2.tip: Inside reinforce is force, which suggests power. Adding force to something makes it stronger.

sc2.stem: The cardboard fort was flimsy at first, but after we taped extra boxes inside to _____ the walls, it stood firm even when my brother leaned on it.

traps.why: Weak walls would not stand firm when someone leaned on them.
Decorating makes walls pretty, not firm.
Testing walls does not change them from flimsy to firm.

sc2.tip: Look at the contrast: "flimsy at first, but" then "stood firm." The blank is what changed flimsy walls into strong ones.

meaning: to bring back to life or strength
example: Water revived the drooping flowers.
hook: Re means back and viv means life, as in vivid; revive means bring back to life, like water perking up a wilted plant.

traps.why: Exhaust means wear out, the opposite of revive.
Review looks similar but means look over again.
Survive means stay alive; revive means bring back to life.

syn1.tip: Re- means back. Revive brings something back to life or strength, just as restore brings something back to how it was.

sc1.stem: A little water seemed to _____ the drooping sunflower, and within an hour it was standing tall again.

traps.why: A weakened sunflower would not be standing tall again.
Review looks like revive but means look over; water cannot do that.
Water does not shade a plant, and shade would not make it stand tall.

sc1.tip: The flower was "drooping" and then was "standing tall again." Water brought it back to strength.

traps.why: Letting something fade away is the opposite of reviving it.
Revive looks like re plus view, but viv means life, not seeing.
Staying alive is surviving; reviving brings back something that was fading.

syn2.tip: The viv in revive is the same as in vivid and vitamin, words about life. Re- means back.

sc2.stem: After the long, boring assembly, everyone in the gym was half asleep, but the coach's lively music seemed to _____ the tired crowd, and kids began clapping and cheering.

traps.why: Bored kids would not start clapping and cheering.
Survive means stay alive; music does not survive a crowd.
Revise looks like revive but means change or edit.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets up a change: "half asleep" becomes "clapping and cheering." The music brought the crowd back to life.

example: Quitting the team was a rash decision.
hook: A rash decision pops up as fast as an itchy rash, before you have time to think it over.

traps.why: Cautious means careful, the opposite of rash.
That fits a skin rash, not a rash decision.
Brave is a good feeling; rash means foolishly unthinking.

syn1.tip: Think of "a rash decision," one made too fast without thinking. Reckless means the same careless hurry.

sc1.stem: Quitting the team after a single bad practice was a _____ decision that Nina made without any careful thought.

traps.why: A wise decision needs careful thought, which Nina skipped.
Mature choices are thought through; this one had no careful thought.
Luck is about how things turn out; the clue is about not thinking.

sc1.tip: The sentence tells you the answer: "made without any careful thought." Find the word that means exactly that.

traps.why: Carefully planned is the opposite of rash.
That describes the skin rash, a different meaning of the word.
Anger can cause rash acts, but rash means without thought, not angry.

syn2.tip: A rash choice skips the thinking part. Picture someone jumping in before looking.

sc2.stem: Instead of making a _____ choice, Leo spent a whole week comparing bikes, reading reviews, and asking his sister before he spent his birthday money.

traps.why: Leo did make a careful choice; "instead of" means the blank is the opposite.
Leo was sensible, so the word after "instead of" must be unthinking.
Money is mentioned, but the clue is about how much Leo thought.

sc2.tip: "Instead of" means Leo did the reverse of the blank. He thought for a whole week, so the blank means not thinking.

example: The smell of cookies lured us inside.
hook: A fishing lure is a shiny fake bait that wiggles to lure fish toward the hook.

traps.why: Repel means push away, the opposite of lure.
Lurk looks similar but means hide and wait.
Luring comes before catching; lure means draw in, not grab.

syn1.tip: Fishermen use a lure, a shiny bait that tempts fish to come closer.

sc1.stem: Fishermen drop shiny, wiggly bait into the lake to _____ hungry fish toward their waiting hooks.

traps.why: Scared fish would swim away from the hooks, not toward them.
Bait does not warn fish; it draws them to the hooks.
Fishermen release fish later, but bait is for drawing fish in.

sc1.tip: The clue is "shiny, wiggly bait" and "toward their waiting hooks." Bait draws fish closer.

traps.why: Discourage pushes someone away from something, the opposite of lure.
Bait looks like food, but lure means draw closer, not feed.
Force is too strong; a lure tempts gently instead of making you.

syn2.tip: A lure pulls you in like a magnet, using something you want. Attract means the same.

sc2.stem: The ice cream truck's cheerful song was enough to _____ every kid on the block away from their video games and out onto the sunny sidewalk.

traps.why: Bored kids would stay inside, not run out to the sidewalk.
Annoy has the wrong feeling; the song is cheerful and kids want to come.
The song is about sound, but deafening would not pull kids outside.

sc2.tip: Look at the effect: the song pulled kids "away from their video games and out." Something that draws you toward a treat tempts you.

example: Don't worry about such a trivial mistake.
hook: Trivia night is full of fun little facts that rarely matter in real life; trivial things are small and unimportant.

traps.why: Major means big and important, the opposite of trivial.
Small matters can be dull, but trivial means unimportant, not boring.
Tri- often means three, but trivial has nothing to do with three.

syn1.tip: Think of trivia, little facts that are fun but do not really matter. Trivial things are not important.

sc1.stem: Arguing over who got the blue cup was _____, a matter far too small and unimportant to ruin our picnic.

traps.why: The sentence says the matter was too small, not serious.
Urgent things need attention now; this was too small to matter.
Arguing can be loud, but the clue is about how small the matter was.

sc1.tip: After the comma the sentence explains the blank: "a matter far too small and unimportant."

traps.why: Crucial means extremely important, the opposite of trivial.
Trivia games use facts, but trivial means unimportant, not true.
A trivial mistake is small, not necessarily careless or messy.

syn2.tip: "A trivial problem" is a small one you can ignore. Look for the word that means small in importance.

sc2.stem: My little brother cried as if losing his sticker were a huge disaster, but to the rest of us the loss seemed _____ and was forgotten by dinner.

traps.why: That is how the brother felt; "but" shows the others felt the opposite.
Something serious would not be forgotten by dinner.
Fairness is not the point; the clue is that the loss hardly mattered.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the brother's "huge disaster" with how others saw it. They "forgot by dinner," so it was small.

meaning: able to do many different things
example: A versatile player can play any position.
hook: A versatile pocketknife hides scissors, a screwdriver, and a bottle opener; one tool, many jobs.

traps.why: Limited means able to do only a few things, the opposite.
Vers looks like verse, as in poems, but versatile means many skills.
Stubborn people refuse to change, the opposite of adaptable.

syn1.tip: A versatile player can play any position. Think of someone who can switch easily to whatever is needed.

sc1.stem: Our _____ puppy can fetch, swim, herd ducks, and do tricks; there seems to be nothing she cannot learn.

traps.why: A lazy puppy would not fetch, swim, herd, and do tricks.
A clumsy puppy would struggle; this one can learn anything.
Fluffy describes fur, but the clue lists many skills.

sc1.tip: The sentence lists many skills and says "there seems to be nothing she cannot learn." The blank means able to do many things.

traps.why: Being good at only one thing is the opposite of versatile.
Energetic people do a lot, but versatile means many different skills.
That means famous; versatile is about having many skills.

syn2.tip: Versatile goes with variety. A versatile tool or person can handle many different jobs.

sc2.stem: Most kitchen tools do only one job, but a good pocketknife is _____, since it can cut string, open cans, tighten screws, and even file your nails.

traps.why: Limited fits the one-job tools, but "but" shows the pocketknife is different.
Knives can be dangerous, but the clue lists many uses.
Being sharp does not explain tightening screws or opening cans.

sc2.tip: "Only one job, but" sets up a contrast. The pocketknife does many jobs, so look for the word meaning able to do many things.

example: He made an earnest promise to help.
hook: When you make an earnest promise, you look someone in the eye and truly mean every word.

traps.why: Joking is the opposite of earnest.
Earned looks similar but means gained by working.
Grumpy is serious in a bad mood; earnest is serious and sincere.

syn1.tip: Think of "in earnest," which means for real, not joking. Earnest people are serious and mean what they say.

sc1.stem: With a serious, sincere look, Ravi made an _____ promise to take good care of the class rabbit all summer.

traps.why: An empty promise is not meant, but Ravi looked serious and sincere.
Insincere is the opposite of the sincere look described.
A serious look is not angry; the clue says sincere.

sc1.tip: The sentence starts with the clue: "With a serious, sincere look." The promise matches that look.

traps.why: Fake is the opposite of sincere and earnest.
Earn is inside earnest, but the word has nothing to do with money.
Strict is serious in a bossy way; earnest is serious and heartfelt.

syn2.tip: An earnest apology comes from the heart. Look for the word that means truly meaning it.

sc2.stem: Unlike the class clown, who giggled through the whole apology, Sam gave an _____ apology, looking Mrs. Lee in the eye and meaning every word.

traps.why: That fits the giggling clown; "unlike" means Sam was the opposite.
Apologies can feel awkward, but the clue says Sam meant every word.
Sam meant every word, so he cared.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the class clown" tells you Sam was not joking. "Meaning every word" shows he was sincere.

meaning: to save from being lost or ruined
example: We salvaged some toys from the flooded basement.
hook: Divers salvage treasure from sunken ships, saving what the sea almost swallowed forever.

traps.why: Ruin is the opposite of salvage.
Salute looks similar but means greet with a raised hand.
Salvaged things are sometimes sold, but salvage means save.

syn1.tip: Salvage sounds a bit like save, and that is what it means: save something from being lost or ruined.

sc1.stem: Although the cake had burned on top, Dad managed to _____ the bottom half, so the party still had dessert.

traps.why: If Dad tossed the bottom half, there would be no dessert.
Ruining the cake would leave the party without dessert.
Tasting the cake would not make sure the party still had dessert.

sc1.tip: "Although the cake had burned," Dad saved part of it, "so the party still had dessert." The blank means save.

traps.why: Throwing something away is the opposite of saving it.
Sal looks like salt, but salvage has nothing to do with salt.
Too strong: salvaging often saves only part, not making it like new.

syn2.tip: Think of a salvage yard, where people save useful parts from wrecked cars.

sc2.stem: When the rain soaked our campsite, we hurried to _____ the sleeping bags and snacks before the rising stream could carry everything away.

traps.why: Abandoning things would let the stream carry them off.
Unpacking spreads things out; it does not save them from the stream.
The rain already soaked things; you would not hurry to soak them more.

sc2.tip: The danger is the stream that "could carry everything away." You hurry to save things before they are lost.

example: His excuse sounded plausible.
hook: A plausible excuse makes your teacher nod and think, that could really have happened.

traps.why: Unlikely is the opposite of plausible.
Too strong: plausible means it could be true, not that it surely is.
Playful starts like plausible but means full of fun.

syn1.tip: A plausible story makes sense and could be true. Ask yourself whether you would believe it.

sc1.stem: Since the dog was covered in mud, Ella's story that he had been digging in the garden seemed _____ to Mom.

traps.why: The mud supports the story, so it would not seem ridiculous.
The muddy dog makes the story more likely, not less.
The dog is messy, but the blank describes the story.

sc1.tip: "Since the dog was covered in mud" gives proof for Ella's story. With proof, the story sounds true.

traps.why: Hard to believe is the opposite of plausible.
Plaus looks like applause, but plausible means believable today.
Too strong: plausible things only seem true; they are not proven.

syn2.tip: Plausible goes with excuses, stories, and explanations. It describes one that sounds like it could really be true.

sc2.stem: Jake claimed a giant eagle had carried off his homework, but the teacher did not find that excuse _____ and asked him to redo the assignment.

traps.why: The teacher did find it ridiculous; "did not" needs the opposite.
An eagle story does seem impossible, so "did not find it impossible" makes no sense.
The story was clear; the problem was that nobody would believe it.

sc2.tip: A giant eagle stealing homework is hard to believe, and the teacher "did not" accept it. The blank means believable.

example: Please refrain from talking during the movie.
hook: Re means back, so to refrain is to hold yourself back, like a rider pulling the reins.

traps.why: Going ahead is the opposite of holding back.
That fits refrain as a noun, the repeated part of a song.
Re plus rain is a trick of spelling; refrain is not about weather.

syn1.tip: Signs say "Please refrain from talking." They are asking you to hold back from doing it.

sc1.stem: The library sign asked everyone to _____ from talking loudly so that other readers could concentrate.

traps.why: Talking loudly would not help readers concentrate.
Learning from talking loudly has nothing to do with letting others concentrate.
A sign would not ask people to suffer from talking loudly.

sc1.tip: The reason is "so that other readers could concentrate." The sign wants people to hold back from talking.

traps.why: Continue means keep going, the opposite of refrain.
Retrain looks similar but means train again.
A song's refrain repeats, but the verb means hold back.

syn2.tip: Refrain is almost always followed by from, as in "refrain from eating." It means keep yourself from doing it.

sc2.stem: Grandpa's doctor told him to _____ from eating salty snacks, so now he chooses apples instead of potato chips at the movies.

traps.why: Doctors help people recover, but Grandpa stopped eating chips, not healed from them.
Grandpa gave up the chips, so he was not gaining from eating them.
The effect shows Grandpa stopped eating chips, not that he learned something.

sc2.tip: Look at the result: "now he chooses apples instead of potato chips." The doctor told him to hold back from salty snacks.

example: She asserted that she was right.
hook: When you assert something, you say it firmly, like planting a flag and standing right beside it.

traps.why: Deny means to say something is not true, the opposite of firmly stating it.
Assist starts like assert, but it means to help.
Suggest is too gentle; assert means to state something firmly.

syn1.tip: Think of being assertive: speaking up with confidence. To assert is to state something firmly.

sc1.stem: Shy at first, Nora learned to _____ herself in group projects, speaking up firmly so her ideas were heard.

traps.why: Hiding herself is the opposite of speaking up firmly.
Assure looks similar but means to promise or calm someone's worries.
To excuse herself means to leave politely, not to speak up.

sc1.tip: The clue is 'speaking up firmly so her ideas were heard.' To assert yourself is to speak up with confidence.

traps.why: Taking back your words is the opposite of standing firmly behind them.
Hinting quietly is much too weak; asserting is firm and clear.
Asking is a kind of speaking, but asserting is stating, not asking.

syn2.tip: You assert a point when you say it with confidence and do not back down.

sc2.stem: Even though everyone else in the class said the answer was ten, Leo did not back down; he chose to _____ that it was twelve and proved it on the board.

traps.why: Leo proved it was twelve, so he would not deny it.
Guessing is too unsure for someone who did not back down.
Hoping is too weak; Leo proved his answer on the board.

sc2.tip: Look at 'did not back down' and 'proved it.' Leo stated his answer firmly, so the word means to state firmly.

example: The lace had an exquisite pattern.
hook: An exquisite snowflake is so delicate and beautiful that you almost hold your breath while looking at it.

traps.why: Ugly is the opposite of exquisite.
Exquisite things can cost a lot, but exquisite is about beauty.
Exciting starts like exquisite, but it means thrilling, not beautiful.

syn1.tip: Picture an exquisite necklace in a museum case. The word praises something very beautiful and finely made.

sc1.stem: The tiny glass hummingbird was an _____ treasure, with wings so delicate and beautiful that Grandma kept it safe under a dome.

traps.why: Ugly is the opposite of 'delicate and beautiful.'
Unbreakable is about strength, but the wings are described as delicate.
Exciting looks similar, but the clue is about beauty, not thrills.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank: 'so delicate and beautiful.' Pick the word that means delicate and beautiful.

traps.why: Rough and clumsy is the opposite of delicate and lovely.
Pleasant enough is far too weak; exquisite means extremely beautiful.
That describes inquisitive, which looks a bit like exquisite.

syn2.tip: Exquisite is high praise for something finely made, like lace or a tiny carving.

sc2.stem: Most of the cupcakes at the bake sale were plain and lumpy, but Mia's were _____, each topped with tiny sugar flowers that looked almost real.

traps.why: Messy matches the lumpy cupcakes, not Mia's careful ones.
Simple is like plain, but 'but' tells you Mia's were different.
Cupcakes can be delicious, but the clue describes how they looked.

sc2.tip: 'But' sets Mia's cupcakes against 'plain and lumpy.' Tiny sugar flowers that look real show they were delicate and beautiful.

example: The drought caused a famine long ago.
hook: A famine is when a whole land goes hungry, like Ireland's famine when the potato crops failed.

traps.why: Plenty means more than enough, the opposite of famine.
A drought can cause famine, but drought means a lack of rain.
Fame looks like famine, but it means being well known.

syn1.tip: Famine is a cousin of 'famished,' which means very hungry. A famine is a time when people lack food.

sc1.stem: When the rains failed for three years in a row, a _____ spread across the land and families had too little food.

traps.why: A harvest brings food, but families had too little.
A flood comes from too much rain, but the rains failed.
A celebration is happy, but this sentence is about hunger.

sc1.tip: Follow the cause and effect: the rains 'failed for three years,' so 'families had too little food.' That is a famine.

traps.why: Plenty of food is the opposite of a famine.
Lack of rain is a drought, which can cause famine.
That means fame, a word that only looks like famine.

syn2.tip: Think of famished, meaning very hungry. A famine leaves whole regions without enough to eat.

sc2.stem: Unlike the years of plenty, when barns overflowed with grain, the year of the _____ left the shelves of every home empty.

traps.why: A harvest would fill the shelves, not leave them empty.
A feast means lots of food, but the shelves were empty.
A festival is a happy time, but this year brought empty shelves.

sc2.tip: 'Unlike' sets this year against 'years of plenty.' Empty shelves mean no food, so the word means a severe lack of food.

example: The town grew prosperous after the railroad came.
hook: A prosperous town has busy shops, new houses, and people doing well, like a garden in full bloom.

traps.why: Poor is the opposite of prosperous.
Proper starts like prosperous, but it means correct or polite.
Wealthy people may be generous, but prosperous means doing well with money.

syn1.tip: Think of 'prosper,' which means to do well. A prosperous person or place is successful and has plenty of money.

sc1.stem: After the new train station opened, the sleepy town became a _____ place, where shop owners grew successful and wealthy.

traps.why: Poor is the opposite of 'successful and wealthy.'
Dangerous is a bad feeling, but the town became successful.
Proper looks similar but means correct or polite, not wealthy.

sc1.tip: The sentence defines the blank: 'successful and wealthy.' Pick the word that means doing well and rich.

traps.why: Struggling is the opposite of doing well.
Greedy is negative; prosperous is a good thing.
Successful people can become famous, but prosperous is about doing well.

syn2.tip: You may know the phrase 'a prosperous new year.' It wishes someone success and good fortune.

sc2.stem: Grandpa's family was poor when they first arrived, but after years of hard work running their bakery, they became _____ enough to buy a big house.

traps.why: Needy families cannot afford a big house.
Hard work can make you tired, but that cannot buy a house.
Proper looks like prosperous but means polite or correct.

sc2.tip: 'But' shows a change from 'poor.' Being able to 'buy a big house' means the family became wealthy.

example: The king held a banquet for his guests.
hook: Picture a king's long table piled with roast turkey, fruit, and pies: that grand formal meal is a banquet.

traps.why: A snack is a tiny bite, the opposite of a big meal.
Bouquet looks like banquet, but it is a bunch of flowers.
Banquets are cooked in kitchens, but a banquet is the meal itself.

syn1.tip: Think of a banquet hall at a wedding or awards night. A banquet is a big, fancy meal for many guests.

sc1.stem: The awards _____ was held in a grand hall, with fancy tablecloths, speeches, and a formal three-course dinner.

traps.why: A picnic is a meal, but it is casual, not formal.
A snack is tiny, but this was a three-course dinner.
Bouquet looks like banquet but means flowers, not a meal.

sc1.tip: The clues are 'grand hall,' 'fancy tablecloths,' and 'formal three-course dinner.' A large formal meal is a banquet.

traps.why: A quick small snack is the opposite of a large formal meal.
A banquet may happen in a dining room, but it is the meal.
That is a bouquet, which only looks like banquet.

syn2.tip: Kings and award winners have banquets. Picture long tables, many guests, and course after course of food.

sc2.stem: Instead of the quick hot dogs they usually ate on Saturdays, the scouts sat down to a _____ with roast chicken, five side dishes, and three kinds of pie.

traps.why: A snack is small, but this meal had many dishes.
A nibble is a tiny bite, far too little for this meal.
Bouquet looks like banquet, but you cannot eat a bunch of flowers.

sc2.tip: 'Instead of the quick hot dogs' signals a contrast. A meal with roast chicken, five sides, and three pies is a feast.

example: She accepted the award with humility.
hook: Humility is the noun for humble: people with humility do great things without bragging about them.

traps.why: Pride is the opposite of humility.
Humidity looks like humility, but it means dampness in the air.
A shy person is quiet, but humility means not acting proud.

syn1.tip: Humility goes with the word 'humble.' A humble person does not brag or act more important than others.

sc1.stem: Despite winning first prize, Aiden showed _____, thanking his teammates instead of bragging about himself.

traps.why: Pride would lead to bragging, but Aiden did not brag.
Winners feel joy, but the clue is about not bragging.
Humidity looks similar but means damp air.

sc1.tip: 'Despite winning' and 'instead of bragging' are your clues. Aiden could have been proud, but he acted humble.

traps.why: Showing off is the opposite of humility.
