Arguing can be upsetting, but lament is about sadness, not fighting.
Joking is lighthearted, but lament is full of sorrow.

syn2.tip: When you lament something, you are sad it is gone. Look for the choice with a heavy, sorrowful feeling.

sc2.stem: When her best friend moved across the country, Lily would _____ the loss for weeks, wishing they could still walk to school together every morning.

traps.why: Lily wished her friend were still there, so she was not celebrating.
Notice is too weak; Lily felt deep sadness for weeks.
Accepting means being calm about it, but Lily kept wishing things were different.

sc2.tip: A best friend moving away causes sadness, and "wishing they could still walk to school together" shows Lily missed her.

meaning: to give off or send out
example: Fireflies emit a soft glow.
hook: E means out and mit means send, so to emit is to send out, like a phone emitting a beep.

traps.why: Absorb means to take in, the opposite of sending out.
Omit looks like emit, but it means to leave out.
Admit sounds like emit, but it means to let in or confess.

syn1.tip: Emit starts with e, meaning out, and mit, meaning send. Things that emit send something out, like light or sound.

sc1.stem: On summer nights, fireflies _____ a soft yellow glow that blinks on and off above the grass.

traps.why: The glow blinks above the grass, so fireflies send it out, not take it in.
Omit looks like emit but means to leave out.
Admit sounds like emit but means to confess or let in.

sc1.tip: The clue is "a soft yellow glow that blinks on and off." The fireflies are giving off light.

traps.why: Soaking up is taking in, the opposite of giving off.
That is what omit means, a word that looks like emit.
Mit means send, but emit is about giving off, not mailing.

syn2.tip: Think of a heater that emits warmth or a skunk that emits a smell. Something comes out of it.

sc2.stem: Because the old school bus would _____ thick clouds of black smoke from its tailpipe, the city replaced it with a cleaner electric bus last year.

traps.why: Smoke pouring from a tailpipe is going out, not being collected.
Omit looks like emit but means to leave out.
Buses don't measure smoke; the problem was the smoke coming out.

sc2.tip: "From its tailpipe" and "replaced it with a cleaner" bus show the old bus was sending out dirty smoke.

example: Luminous stars glowed on my ceiling.
hook: Luminous paint glows in the dark, like the stars stuck on a bedroom ceiling after the lights go out.

traps.why: Dim means not bright, the opposite of luminous.
Humorous looks a bit like luminous, but it means funny.
Colorful things can be bright, but luminous means giving off light.

syn1.tip: Lumin is in illuminate, which means to light up. Luminous things shine or glow.

sc1.stem: Deep in the dark ocean, the _____ jellyfish gave off its own soft light, glowing like a tiny lamp.

traps.why: The jellyfish gave off light, so it was not dark.
Humorous looks like luminous but means funny.
Jellyfish are slippery, but the clue is about giving off light.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "gave off its own soft light, glowing like a tiny lamp." Choose the word meaning glowing.

traps.why: Shadows come from darkness, the opposite of luminous.
Glass lets light through, but luminous things make their own light.
Some bright things are hot, but luminous is about light, not heat.

syn2.tip: The ending -ous means full of, so luminous means full of light, like a glowing moon.

sc2.stem: Most of the rocks in Dad's collection look dull and gray, but one _____ crystal shines so brightly at night that it lights up the whole shelf.

traps.why: The word "but" shows this crystal is different from the dull rocks.
Rocks can be heavy, but the clue is about shining brightly.
Crystals can be precious, but the clue is that it lights up the shelf.

sc2.tip: "But" sets up a contrast with "dull and gray," and "shines so brightly" tells you the crystal gives off light.

example: She kept meticulous notes in science.
hook: A meticulous baker measures every grain of sugar and lines up each sprinkle on a cupcake.

traps.why: Careless means not paying attention, the opposite of meticulous.
Ridiculous rhymes with meticulous, but it means silly.
Fussy sounds annoying, but meticulous is a compliment about careful work.

syn1.tip: Meticulous is a compliment for someone who checks every tiny detail. Painstaking means taking great pains, or effort, to get it right.

sc1.stem: Checking every tiny detail twice, the _____ model builder made sure each little piece was glued exactly in place.

traps.why: Someone checking every detail twice is not careless.
Ridiculous sounds like meticulous but means silly.
Checking everything twice takes time, so speed is not the point.

sc1.tip: The clue is "checking every tiny detail twice" and "exactly in place." That describes someone extremely careful.

traps.why: Sloppy and rushed is the opposite of careful about details.
Meticulous people may look neat, but the word is about careful work.
Careful work can be slow, but lazy is negative and meticulous is positive.

syn2.tip: You might hear "meticulous notes" or "meticulous work." It describes someone who gets every little detail right.

sc2.stem: Unlike his messy older brother, who tosses clothes everywhere, Marco is so _____ that he folds every shirt perfectly and lines up his pencils by color.

traps.why: "Unlike his messy older brother" tells you Marco is not sloppy.
Sorting by color sounds artsy, but the clue is about careful order.
Ridiculous sounds like meticulous but means silly.

sc2.tip: "Unlike his messy older brother" signals a contrast. Folding every shirt perfectly shows Marco pays close attention to details.

example: The hikers ascended the steep trail.
hook: Picture an astronaut's rocket ascending into the sky, rising higher and higher until it disappears into the clouds.

traps.why: Sink means to go down, the opposite of ascend.
Attend looks like ascend, but it means to be present at.
Hikers may wander, but ascend means to go up.

syn1.tip: Think of an elevator that ascends to the top floor. Ascend always means going up.

sc1.stem: The hikers began to _____ the steep mountain trail, climbing higher until the town below looked tiny.

traps.why: The hikers were climbing higher, so they were not going down.
Attend looks like ascend but means to be present at an event.
Hikers might admire a trail, but the clue says they were climbing.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "climbing higher until the town below looked tiny." The hikers were going up.

traps.why: Falling downward is the opposite of going up.
Moving sideways is a direction too, but ascend means up.
Standing still is not moving at all; ascend is moving up.

syn2.tip: Ascend begins with the same sound as "a stairway." Imagine climbing a stairway up.

sc2.stem: As the hot-air balloon began to _____, the people waving on the field below grew smaller and smaller until they looked like ants.

traps.why: If the balloon landed, the people would look bigger, not smaller.
Balloons can wobble, but that wouldn't make people look tiny.
A deflating balloon sinks, so the people would not shrink below.

sc2.tip: Cause and effect: people looking "smaller and smaller" and "below" shows the balloon was rising higher.

meaning: to keep away from on purpose
example: Cats shun water whenever they can.
hook: When the lunch table shuns someone, everyone turns away and nobody saves them a seat.

traps.why: Welcome means to greet warmly, the opposite of shun.
Shine looks like shun but means to give off light.
Teasing is unkind too, but shun means to stay away.

syn1.tip: When you shun something, you stay away on purpose. Cats shun water; picture a cat jumping away from the bath.

sc1.stem: After Ben cheated at tag, the other kids began to _____ him on purpose, refusing to let him join their games.

traps.why: The kids refused to let Ben join, so they did not welcome him.
Forgive is kind, but the kids were angry and left Ben out.
Tag is the game, but the kids kept Ben out of their games.

sc1.tip: The clue is "refusing to let him join their games" and "on purpose." The kids stayed away from Ben.

traps.why: Reaching out to someone is the opposite of keeping away.
Arguing is unfriendly, but you have to be near someone to argue.
Shine looks like shun, but shun has nothing to do with light.

syn2.tip: Shun has a cold, unfriendly feeling. People shun someone by turning away and leaving them out.

sc2.stem: Most dogs at the park love to splash in the pond, but our dog Max will _____ the water, walking far around it to keep his paws dry.

traps.why: "But" shows Max is unlike the dogs who love the water.
Dogs drink water, but Max walks far around it to stay dry.
Max walks far around the water, so he does not visit it.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Max with dogs who "love to splash." Walking "far around it to keep his paws dry" means he stays away.

example: The diligent student checked every answer.
hook: A diligent beaver works all day, carefully stacking stick after stick until the dam is finished.

traps.why: Lazy means avoiding work, the opposite of diligent.
Delicate looks a bit like diligent, but it means easily broken.
Intelligent rhymes with diligent, but it means smart, not hardworking.

syn1.tip: Teachers praise diligent students who keep working steadily. It is a positive word about effort, not about being smart.

sc1.stem: As a _____ student, Rosa worked hard every single night, carefully finishing her homework before even thinking about playing.

traps.why: Rosa worked hard every single night, so she was not lazy.
Delicate looks like diligent but means fragile.
Rosa finished homework before even thinking about playing.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "worked hard every single night, carefully finishing her homework." Pick the word meaning hardworking.

traps.why: Idle and careless is the opposite of working hard and carefully.
Diligent is about effort, not about how smart or fast you are.
Bossy is negative, but diligent is praise for hard work.

syn2.tip: Think of "diligent effort" or "diligent student." The word describes someone who keeps working carefully until the job is done.

sc2.stem: Because Theo practiced his piano scales every single afternoon without skipping a day, his teacher praised him as the most _____ student she had ever taught.

traps.why: A careless student would not practice every day without skipping.
Theo never skipped a day, so he was not lazy.
Piano practice is noisy, but the teacher praised his steady effort.

sc2.tip: Cause and effect: "Because" Theo practiced "every single afternoon without skipping a day," the teacher praised his hard work.

example: Squirrels hoard nuts for winter.
hook: Picture a dragon lying on a giant hoard of gold, hiding it away and never sharing a single coin.

traps.why: Share means to give some away, the opposite of hoard.
Board looks like hoard, but it means to get on a bus or plane.
Stealing takes from others, but hoarding means saving up what you have.

syn1.tip: Squirrels hoard nuts for winter by gathering lots and hiding them. Think of a big secret pile.

sc1.stem: My little brother likes to _____ his Halloween candy, collecting huge piles and stashing them under his bed instead of sharing.

traps.why: The sentence says "instead of sharing," so share is wrong.
Board looks like hoard but means to get on a vehicle.
He was stashing piles under his bed, not eating the candy.

sc1.tip: The clue is "collecting huge piles and stashing them under his bed instead of sharing." That means saving and hiding.

traps.why: Giving away freely is the opposite of keeping and hiding.
That means steal; hoarding is keeping a big supply of your own.
You might hoard food, but hoarding means saving it, not gobbling it.

syn2.tip: A hoard is a hidden stash, like a dragon's gold. To hoard is to collect lots and hide it away.

sc2.stem: Instead of spending her allowance right away like her friends, Nora likes to _____ every coin in a jar hidden on the top shelf of her closet.

traps.why: "Instead of spending" tells you Nora does the opposite of spend.
Coins can be polished, but the clue is about keeping them hidden.
Trading gives coins away, but Nora keeps every coin in a hidden jar.

sc2.tip: "Instead of spending" signals a contrast, and "in a jar hidden" shows Nora collects her coins and hides them away.

example: The soldier received a medal for valor.
hook: Soldiers can earn a Medal of Valor for great bravery, like charging into danger to save a friend.

traps.why: Cowardice means lack of courage, the opposite of valor.
Value looks like valor, but it means how much something is worth.
Brave people may win, but valor means courage, not winning.

syn1.tip: You often see valor with medals: "a medal for valor." Medals like that honor heroes who show great courage.

sc1.stem: The firefighter received a medal for _____ after bravely climbing a tall ladder to rescue a frightened kitten.

traps.why: Nobody gets a medal for cowardice, and the firefighter acted bravely.
Rescues can be fast, but the sentence says the firefighter acted bravely.
Value looks like valor but means worth.

sc1.tip: The clue is "medal for" plus "bravely climbing a tall ladder." Medals like this reward great courage.

traps.why: Fear is the feeling that valor overcomes, its opposite.
Heroes earn honor, but valor means the courage itself.
Valor looks like value, which means worth, but valor is courage.

syn2.tip: Valor is a hero word. Think of knights and firefighters who face danger without backing down.

sc2.stem: Even though she was terrified of the dark cave, Priya showed great _____ when she crawled inside to lead her lost little brother safely back out.

traps.why: "Even though" she was terrified, she went in anyway, which takes courage.
Rescues can take patience, but crawling into a scary cave takes courage.
Carelessness is negative, but Priya's rescue was a brave, good act.

sc2.tip: "Even though she was terrified" signals a contrast. Doing something scary anyway to save her brother shows great courage.

example: We spoke with reverence about our grandparents.
hook: Reverence is the hushed, deep respect you feel at a war memorial; it comes from the verb revere.

traps.why: Scorn means looking down on someone, the opposite of reverence.
Reference looks similar but means mentioning or looking something up.
People may stay silent out of reverence, but reverence is the feeling of respect.

syn1.tip: Think of the verb revere, which means to deeply respect. Reverence is that deep respect itself.

sc1.stem: The visitors walked through the ancient temple with _____, speaking softly to show their deep respect.

traps.why: Disrespect is the opposite of the deep respect the sentence describes.
Visitors may be curious, but the sentence says they showed deep respect.
Reference looks like reverence but means mentioning something.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank: 'speaking softly to show their deep respect.' Pick the word that means deep respect.

traps.why: Mockery means making fun of something, the opposite of reverence.
Approval is much weaker; reverence is deep, serious respect.
Relevance looks similar but means being connected to the topic.

syn2.tip: Reverence is a serious, hushed feeling, like standing in a grand old church. Look for the choice with that deep, wondering respect.

sc2.stem: Most kids rushed past the old war memorial chatting loudly, but Leo stopped, removed his cap, and stood in silent _____ for the soldiers who had served.

traps.why: Removing his cap shows respect, not mockery.
Boredom has the wrong feeling; Leo stopped on purpose to honor soldiers.
Nothing shows Leo was puzzled; removing a cap is a sign of honor.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' shows Leo acted differently from the loud kids. Stopping and removing his cap 'for the soldiers' shows deep respect.

example: The crafty raccoon opened the trash can.
hook: A crafty fox in a fable tricks the farmer; this crafty has nothing to do with glue and glitter crafts.

traps.why: Honest means truthful and open, the opposite of sneaky and crafty.
Artistic fits arts and crafts, but crafty means sneaky and clever.
Cranky looks similar but means grumpy.

syn1.tip: Picture the crafty fox in fables who tricks everyone. Crafty describes clever tricks, not art projects.

sc1.stem: The _____ raccoon pretended to be asleep until the campers left, then sneakily unzipped their cooler and stole the hot dogs.

traps.why: Pretending to sleep was a trick; the raccoon was busy stealing, not lazy.
An honest raccoon would not trick campers and steal hot dogs.
Artistic fits arts and crafts, not a raccoon tricking campers.

sc1.tip: Look at 'pretended to be asleep' and 'sneakily unzipped.' A raccoon that tricks people to steal food is clever in a sneaky way.

traps.why: A trusting person believes others easily; a crafty one tricks them.
Wise is a good kind of smart; crafty is clever in a sneaky way.
Handy means good at making things, like crafts, not sneaky.

syn2.tip: Crafty has a sneaky feeling. Pick the word for someone who quietly tricks others to get what they want.

sc2.stem: Grandpa thought the chess game would be easy to win, but his _____ opponent quietly set a trap and captured his queen with a surprise move.

traps.why: A trusting player would not quietly set a trap.
Chess players can be nervous, but setting a trap shows sneaky cleverness.
Handy means good with your hands, not good at sneaky tricks.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' shows Grandpa was wrong. An opponent who 'quietly set a trap' is clever in a sneaky way.

example: The eloquent speaker moved the crowd.
hook: Eloquent comes from Latin for 'speak out'; picture a speaker whose words flow so beautifully the crowd stands and cheers.

traps.why: Tongue-tied means unable to get words out, the opposite of eloquent.
Elegant looks similar but means graceful and stylish, often about looks.
Loud is about volume; eloquent is about speaking well.

syn1.tip: Eloquent always goes with speaking or writing. Think of a speech so smooth and beautiful it moves people.

sc1.stem: Ava was an _____ speaker whose clear and beautiful words made the whole audience nod, smile, and even cheer.

traps.why: An awkward speaker would not use clear and beautiful words.
Ordinary is too weak; this speaker made the whole audience cheer.
Angry has the wrong feeling for words that made people smile.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank: 'clear and beautiful words.' A speaker whose words are clear and beautiful is eloquent.

traps.why: Mumbling unclearly is the opposite of clear, beautiful speech.
Loud talking is about volume, not about speaking well.
Anyone speaking aloud does this; eloquent means speaking especially well.

syn2.tip: Eloquent describes more than just talking. It means the words are clear, well chosen, and moving.

sc2.stem: Jamal usually mumbled and stared at his shoes during class talks, but at the science fair he was so _____ that the judges praised how smoothly he explained his volcano.

traps.why: Shy fits if you miss 'but'; the judges praised his smooth explaining.
Being loud is not the same as explaining smoothly.
The judges praised how smoothly he explained, not his jokes.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' flips his usual mumbling. The judges praised 'how smoothly he explained,' so he spoke clearly and well.

example: The rowdy fans cheered all game.
hook: Picture rowdy fans in the bleachers: stomping, shouting, and spilling popcorn everywhere.

traps.why: Calm means quiet and peaceful, the opposite of rowdy.
Rowdy fans may be at games, but rowdy means noisy and rough.
Cheerful is a pleasant word; rowdy describes rough, out-of-control noise.

syn1.tip: Think of a rowdy crowd or rowdy kids at a sleepover. The word means loud, rough, and hard to control.

sc1.stem: The _____ campers stayed up yelling, wrestling, and banging pots until the counselor came to quiet the noisy, rough crowd.

traps.why: Sleepy campers would not stay up yelling and wrestling.
Banging pots might suggest hunger, but the clue says noisy and rough.
Shy campers would be quiet, not yelling and banging pots.

sc1.tip: The end of the sentence says it: 'the noisy, rough crowd.' Yelling, wrestling, and banging pots are rowdy behavior.

traps.why: Quiet and gentle is the opposite of rowdy.
A bit chatty is far too mild; rowdy is loud and rough.
Rowdy starts with row, but it has nothing to do with rows.

syn2.tip: Rowdy describes behavior that is loud and rough, like kids wrestling and yelling. Don't let the 'row' at the start fool you.

sc2.stem: The library was usually silent, so when a _____ group of teenagers burst in shouting and shoving, every reader looked up and frowned.

traps.why: A quiet group would not be shouting and shoving.
Studious fits a library, but these teens were shouting and shoving.
Friendly is too pleasant; the readers frowned at the group.

sc2.tip: 'Usually silent' sets up a contrast, and 'shouting and shoving' made readers frown. You need a word for noisy and rough.

example: The defiant toddler shouted, "No!"
hook: Defiant comes from defy: picture a toddler with crossed arms stamping a foot and shouting no at bedtime.

traps.why: Obedient means doing what you are told, the opposite of defiant.
Defensive looks similar but means protecting yourself from attack or blame.
A grumpy person is in a bad mood but may still obey.

syn1.tip: Defiant comes from defy, which means to boldly refuse. Picture someone crossing their arms and saying no.

sc1.stem: When told to go to bed, the _____ toddler crossed her arms, stamped her foot, and boldly shouted, "No!"

traps.why: It was bedtime, but a sleepy toddler wouldn't stamp and shout no.
An obedient toddler would go to bed, not shout no.
Cheerful has the wrong feeling; she crossed her arms and stamped.

sc1.tip: Look at what she did: 'crossed her arms, stamped her foot, and boldly shouted.' She was boldly refusing to obey.

traps.why: Eager to obey is the opposite of defiant.
Upset kids may cry, but defiant means boldly refusing orders.
Defiant looks like defend, but it means refusing to obey.

syn2.tip: Defiant goes with defy, as in 'defy the rules.' It means boldly saying no to an order.

sc2.stem: Most of the players followed the coach's new rule without complaint, but one _____ player kept wearing his lucky hat and announced he would never take it off.

traps.why: Cooperative fits the other players, not the one who refused.
He didn't forget; he announced he would never take the hat off.
Nothing about an injury; the clue is his refusal to follow the rule.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts him with players who obeyed 'without complaint.' Announcing he would 'never take it off' is boldly refusing.

example: The gallant firefighter rescued the kitten.
hook: Picture a gallant knight who bows politely to the queen, then charges bravely into danger to save someone.

traps.why: Cowardly means easily scared, the opposite of gallant.
Heroes may be strong, but gallant means brave and noble.
Reckless is bravery gone too far, without care or good sense.

syn1.tip: Gallant often describes knights and rescuers. Think of someone brave who also behaves nobly.

sc1.stem: The _____ knight bowed politely to the queen, then bravely rode off to rescue the lost lamb from the mountain.

traps.why: A rude knight would not bow politely to the queen.
A timid knight would not bravely ride off to rescue anything.
The lamb was lost, not the knight.

sc1.tip: He 'bowed politely' and 'bravely rode off to rescue' a lamb. Being polite and brave together is what gallant means.

traps.why: Timid and selfish is the opposite of brave and noble.
Gallant sounds a bit like gallop, but it's about courage, not riding.
Knights might be rich and famous, but gallant means brave and noble.

syn2.tip: Gallant describes how someone acts, not what they own. Think of a knight who is both courageous and honorable.

sc2.stem: Because Grandpa had run into the icy lake to pull out a stranger's dog, the town gave him a medal for his _____ act.

traps.why: Foolish has the wrong feeling; the town honored him with a medal.
The lake was icy, but the medal was for his bravery.
Saving a stranger's dog is the opposite of selfish.

sc2.tip: Look at cause and effect: he risked an 'icy lake' for a stranger's dog, so the town 'gave him a medal.'

example: The courteous boy held the door open.
hook: Courteous comes from court: picture someone with royal court manners, holding the door and saying please.

traps.why: Rude is the opposite of courteous.
Curious sounds similar but means wanting to know things.
Courteous comes from court manners, but it doesn't mean royal.

syn1.tip: Courteous comes from court, where people were expected to have good manners. Think 'please' and 'thank you.'

sc1.stem: The _____ boy held the door, said "please" and "thank you," and let the older woman go first.

traps.why: A rude boy would not say please or let others go first.
An impatient boy would not let the older woman go first.
Curious sounds like courteous but means wanting to know things.

sc1.tip: He 'held the door,' said 'please' and 'thank you,' and let someone 'go first.' Those are all polite, respectful acts.

traps.why: Insulting means hurting feelings, the opposite of courteous.
Shy people are quiet, but that doesn't make them polite.
Flattering goes too far, giving too much praise to please someone.

syn2.tip: A courteous person treats others with good manners and respect. Look for the choice about treating people well.

sc2.stem: Unlike the shoppers who pushed and grumbled in the long line, the cashier stayed _____, greeting each customer warmly and thanking them for their patience.

traps.why: Grumpy fits the shoppers, but 'unlike' shows the cashier was different.
The cashier was greeting and thanking people, so not silent.
Curious sounds similar but means wanting to know things.

sc2.tip: 'Unlike' sets the cashier against the pushing, grumbling shoppers. Greeting people 'warmly' and 'thanking them' shows good manners.

meaning: to calm someone by giving what they want
example: A cookie appeased the crying toddler.
hook: Appease comes from an old French phrase meaning 'to peace': you calm someone by handing over what they want.

traps.why: To anger someone is the opposite of calming them down.
Applaud looks similar but means to clap for someone.
Apologizing says sorry; appeasing means giving someone what they want.

syn1.tip: Listen for 'peace' inside appease. You appease someone to bring peace, often by giving in to them.

sc1.stem: To _____ her whining little brother, Ava finally gave in and handed him the last cookie he kept demanding.

traps.why: Teasing would make him whine more, not settle him.
Handing over the cookie is giving in, not punishing.
Applaud looks similar but means to clap for someone.

sc1.tip: Ava 'gave in' and handed over what he 'kept demanding.' Giving someone what they want to stop the whining is appeasing.

traps.why: To annoy someone makes them more upset, the opposite of appease.
Appear looks similar but means to come into view.
Forgiving means letting go of your own anger, not calming someone else.

syn2.tip: Think of a parent handing a crying toddler a cookie. You appease someone to quiet and settle them down.

sc2.stem: The zookeeper tried to _____ the hungry, roaring lion with a big bucket of meat, but the noisy animal only kept roaring louder.

traps.why: No one offers food to make a lion angry.
A roaring lion is already awake.
Applaud looks similar but means to clap for someone.

sc2.tip: 'But' shows the plan failed. Offering a hungry lion meat is an attempt to calm it by giving what it wants.

example: Dad told an anecdote about his first job.
hook: An anecdote is a short true story, like Grandpa's tale about the day a goat ate his lunch.

traps.why: Antidote looks similar but means a cure for poison.
A novel is a long made-up book; an anecdote is short and true.
A riddle is a puzzling question, not a story about something that happened.

syn1.tip: Anecdotes are what grownups tell at dinner: 'Did I ever tell you about the time...?' That's a short story.

sc1.stem: At dinner, Dad told an _____ about the time our dog stole a whole pizza, and everyone laughed.

traps.why: Antidote looks similar but means a cure for poison.
An excuse explains a mistake; Dad was telling a funny story.
An insult is mean, but everyone laughed at a story.

sc1.tip: Dad tells about 'the time our dog stole a whole pizza,' and 'everyone laughed.' A short, true, funny story is an anecdote.

traps.why: That's an antidote, which only looks like anecdote.
An anecdote is short and true, not long and made up.
Too general; an anecdote is specifically a short true story.

syn2.tip: An anecdote is usually told out loud and is about something that really happened. Think of a funny family story.

sc2.stem: Our teacher's speeches about grammar usually put us to sleep, but her _____ about getting locked in the school overnight kept every student wide awake.

traps.why: A lecture is a teaching talk, like the boring grammar speeches.
Antidote looks similar but means a cure for poison.
A quiz tests you; it isn't about something that happened to her.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts boring grammar speeches with her tale 'about getting locked in the school overnight.' A short true story is an anecdote.

example: The obedient dog sat on command.
hook: Obedient comes from obey: picture a puppy that sits the instant you say sit.

traps.why: Defiant means boldly refusing to obey, the opposite of obedient.
Obvious looks similar but means easy to see or understand.
Smart dogs learn tricks, but obedient means doing what you're told.

syn1.tip: Obedient comes from obey. An obedient pet or child follows instructions.

sc1.stem: The trained puppy was an _____ student, sitting, staying, and rolling over exactly when she was told.

traps.why: An unruly student would not sit and stay when told.
Obvious looks similar but means easy to see.
Nothing shows anger; the puppy did tricks exactly when told.

sc1.tip: She did tricks 'exactly when she was told.' Doing what you are told is the meaning of obedient.

traps.why: Breaking the rules is the opposite of being obedient.
That means obvious, which only looks like obedient.
Learning fast is about being smart, not about following orders.

syn2.tip: Look for obey at the start of obedient. Being obedient means following orders or instructions.

sc2.stem: Since Marco always finished his chores the moment his parents asked, they called him their most _____ child and let him stay up late.

traps.why: A stubborn child resists, but Marco did chores right away.
Staying up late is the reward, not a clue that he was sleepy.
Marco never forgot; he did chores the moment he was asked.

sc2.tip: Cause and effect: he did chores 'the moment his parents asked,' so they rewarded him. Doing what you're asked right away is obedient.

example: We devised a plan to surprise Mom.
hook: Devise and device come from the same old word: you devise a plan, and the result might be a clever device.

traps.why: Copying uses someone else's idea, the opposite of inventing your own.
Advise looks like devise but means to give advice.
You might discuss a plan, but devising means creating it.

syn1.tip: Devise is close to device, a thing someone invented. To devise is to think up something new.

sc1.stem: Stuck inside on a rainy day, the cousins worked together to _____ a clever plan for building the best blanket fort ever.

traps.why: They worked together on the plan, so they were not rejecting it.
Advise looks like devise, but you advise people, not plans.
Forts get taken apart later, but here a plan is being made.

sc1.tip: The cousins are making "a clever plan" from nothing on a rainy day, so the blank means to invent or come up with.

traps.why: Carrying out a plan happens after you devise it.
Copying something down repeats an idea instead of inventing one.
That is what advise means, a word that looks like devise.

syn2.tip: People devise plans, schemes, and tricks. Each one has to be thought up first, so devise means to invent.

sc2.stem: Since none of the store-bought games seemed fun anymore, Maya decided to _____ her own board game, with brand new rules, pieces, and a map she drew herself.

traps.why: Buying is one way to get a game, but hers is brand new.
Copying is the opposite of making brand new rules yourself.
Revise looks similar, but you can only revise something that already exists.

sc2.tip: "Her own," "brand new rules," and "a map she drew herself" show Maya is creating something, so the blank means to invent.

meaning: to make something seem bigger than it is
example: Don't exaggerate; it was a small fish.
hook: Exaggerate has a double g, as if the word itself got stretched bigger than it needed to be.

traps.why: Understating makes things seem smaller, the opposite of exaggerating.
People repeat stories, but exaggerating means making them sound bigger.
Exclaim also starts with ex, but it means to shout out.

syn1.tip: Think of a fish story where a tiny fish grows bigger each time it is told. That is exaggerating.

sc1.stem: Grandpa likes to _____ his fishing stories, claiming that the little trout he caught was as big as a canoe.

traps.why: Minimize means make smaller, but the trout became as big as a canoe.
Stories can be recorded, but the clue is about making things bigger.
Exchange starts like exaggerate but means to trade.

sc1.tip: A "little trout" claimed to be "as big as a canoe" is a small thing made to sound huge.

traps.why: Playing something down makes it seem smaller, the opposite.
Exaggerating can be funny, but it is not the same as joking.
Exaggerating only makes something seem bigger; it doesn't actually grow.

syn2.tip: When you exaggerate, you stretch the truth so something sounds larger, better, or worse than it really is.

sc2.stem: Jamal claimed the roller coaster line took five hours, but we really waited only twenty minutes, so I told him not to _____ so much.

traps.why: Jamal made the wait sound longer, not shorter.
The story is about time, but Jamal did not measure it correctly.
Explore starts with ex too, but it means to look around a place.

sc2.tip: "Five hours" set against "only twenty minutes" shows Jamal made the wait sound much bigger than it was.

example: Climbing the icy cliff was perilous.
hook: Perilous means full of peril, and peril means danger, like a rope bridge swinging over a river of crocodiles.

traps.why: Safe is the opposite of perilous.
Dangerous things can be hard, but perilous is about danger, not difficulty.
Precious looks a bit like perilous but means very valuable.

syn1.tip: Perilous is peril plus ous, which means full of. Peril means danger, as in "in grave peril."

sc1.stem: The explorers began a _____ climb up the icy cliff, full of danger at every slippery step.

traps.why: An icy cliff full of danger is not an easy climb.
Peaceful has a calm feeling, but every slippery step was dangerous.
Precious looks like perilous but means valuable.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank right after it: "full of danger at every slippery step." Look for the word that means dangerous.

traps.why: Free from harm means safe, the opposite of perilous.
A little tricky is much too weak; perilous means real danger.
Adventures can be fun, but perilous has a scary, dangerous feeling.

syn2.tip: The ending ous means full of, and peril means danger. Put them together and you get full of danger.

sc2.stem: Because the frozen pond had thin ice and deep water below, the park ranger warned that skating there would be _____ for anyone.

traps.why: Rangers don't warn about harmless things; thin ice means danger.
Thrilling sounds exciting and fun, but a warning signals danger.
Ponds can be busy, but thin ice is about danger, not crowds.

sc2.tip: "Thin ice and deep water" are the cause, and the ranger "warned" as the effect. So the blank means dangerous.

example: Soft music soothed the fussy baby.
hook: Soothe sounds like the soft "shhh" a parent whispers to soothe a crying baby.

traps.why: Irritate means to bother, the opposite of soothe.
Soothing eases pain, but it doesn't cure or heal it.
Shoot sounds a little like soothe but means something very different.

syn1.tip: Think of soothing music or a soothing voice. Both make you feel calm and comfortable.

sc1.stem: A warm bath helped _____ Lucy's sore, aching muscles after the long, rocky hike.

traps.why: Straining muscles hurts them more; a warm bath helps them.
Exercise builds muscles, but a bath makes sore ones feel better.
Warm water relaxes muscles; it doesn't tighten them.

sc1.tip: A "warm bath" after a "long, rocky hike" makes "sore, aching muscles" feel better, so the blank means to calm or ease.

traps.why: Annoy means to bother, the opposite of soothe.
Cure is too strong; soothing just makes you feel better for now.
Soothing can help someone fall asleep, but it means to calm.

syn2.tip: You soothe a scraped knee, a crying baby, or hurt feelings. Each time you are comforting someone.

sc2.stem: The puppy whimpered nervously during the thunderstorm, but Ben's gentle petting and quiet humming began to _____ her until she fell asleep.

traps.why: Frighten means to scare, but the puppy ended up asleep.
Scolding is harsh, but Ben's petting was gentle and quiet.
Waking is about sleep too, but the puppy fell asleep.

sc2.tip: The "but" turns from a nervous puppy to "gentle petting" and sleep, so the blank means to calm.

example: The beach was desolate in winter.
hook: Desolate holds sol, as in solo: a desolate place leaves you all alone, with nobody else around.

traps.why: Crowded means full of people, the opposite of desolate.
Desperate looks like desolate but means willing to try anything.
Peaceful is quiet in a pleasant way; desolate is quiet and lonely.

syn1.tip: Desolate starts like deserted and has sol inside, like solo. Both point to an empty, lonely place.

sc1.stem: The ghost town felt _____, its dusty streets empty and lonely, with no people, no shops, and no sound but the wind.

traps.why: Lively is the opposite of streets with no people and no sound.
Desperate looks like desolate but describes a feeling, not an empty place.
Cozy is warm and friendly, but this town feels empty and lonely.

sc1.tip: The words right after the blank, "empty and lonely," restate its meaning. "No people, no shops" confirms it.

traps.why: Busy and lively is the opposite of desolate.
Calm and quiet sounds pleasant, but desolate feels bleak and lonely.
Stormy nights can feel gloomy, but desolate means empty and bare.

syn2.tip: Picture a desolate desert or an empty winter beach: nobody there, nothing growing. That is desolate.

sc2.stem: In summer the campground is packed with tents and laughing families, but by January it is _____, with snow covering every empty picnic table.

traps.why: Crowded fits summer, but "but" switches to an empty January.
Cheerful describes the laughing summer, not the empty winter.
Popular places draw visitors, but this one has empty tables.

sc2.tip: The "but" sets January against "packed" summer days, and "every empty picnic table" tells you the place is deserted.

meaning: to prevent; or to turn away
example: Quick thinking averted a disaster.
hook: Avert holds vert, meaning turn, as in reverse: you turn your eyes away, or turn trouble away before it happens.

traps.why: Causing a problem is the opposite of averting it.
Alert looks like avert but means to warn someone.
Predicting trouble means seeing it coming, not stopping it.

syn1.tip: You often hear "avert a disaster." When a disaster is averted, it never happens because someone stopped it.

sc1.stem: The kids were told to _____ their eyes, or turn them away, while Dad wrapped their birthday presents.

traps.why: Focusing your eyes points them at something, not away.
Alert looks like avert but means to warn.
Eye tests are about eyes, but the clue says turn them away.

sc1.tip: The words "or turn them away" right after the blank explain it. To avert your eyes is to turn them away.

traps.why: Turning toward something is the opposite of turning away.
Vert does mean turn, but avert means turn away, not flip.
Eyes open wide in surprise; averted eyes turn away.

syn2.tip: People avert their eyes from something they shouldn't see. The vert in avert means turn.

sc2.stem: When the lifeguard spotted a swimmer struggling, she raced into the water and pulled him to shore, which helped _____ a terrible accident.

traps.why: Her rescue stopped the accident; it didn't cause it.
She did more than watch; she acted to stop the accident.
Alert looks like avert, but you alert people, not accidents.

sc2.tip: Her quick rescue is the cause, and the effect is that the accident never happened. So the blank means to prevent.

example: The lenient teacher gave us extra time.
hook: A lenient teacher goes easy: extra time on the test, no punishment for a small mistake.

traps.why: Strict is the opposite of lenient.
Lazy is an insult; lenient means kindly going easy on people.
Lean looks like the start of lenient but means thin.

syn1.tip: A lenient rule or a lenient parent lets things slide. Think of it as the opposite of strict.

sc1.stem: Unlike strict Mr. Park, our _____ coach forgives late arrivals and lets small mistakes slide without any punishment.

traps.why: Stern means strict, but the coach is unlike strict Mr. Park.
Punctual is about being on time, but the clue is about forgiving.
A grumpy coach wouldn't kindly forgive mistakes.

sc1.tip: "Unlike strict" tells you the coach is the opposite of strict, and "forgives late arrivals" proves it.

traps.why: Harsh means severe, the opposite of lenient.
Spoiled describes a kid who gets too much, not a forgiving adult.
Careless means not paying attention; lenient means kindly going easy.

syn2.tip: A lenient judge gives a light punishment. Being lenient means forgiving mistakes instead of being strict.

sc2.stem: Because the librarian was so _____, she let me return my overdue book without paying a fine, saying everyone forgets sometimes.

traps.why: A strict librarian would make you pay the fine.
Librarians are linked with quiet, but that doesn't explain skipping the fine.
Stingy means unwilling to give, the opposite feeling of letting the fine go.

sc2.tip: "Because" links the blank to what she did: skipping the fine and "saying everyone forgets." That points to forgiving.

example: The tiny cottage was a humble abode.
hook: Abode comes from abide, meaning to stay: your abode is the place where you stay and live.

traps.why: A neighborhood holds many homes; an abode is one home.
Furniture goes inside a home but isn't the home itself.
An address tells where a home is; an abode is the home.

syn1.tip: You may have heard "Welcome to my humble abode," a joking way to say "Welcome to my home."

sc1.stem: Grandpa jokingly welcomed us to his humble _____, which was really just a tiny cabin he called home.

traps.why: Grandpa called the cabin home, not a place to work.
A neighborhood is too big to be just one tiny cabin.
An attic is only part of a home, not the whole cabin.

sc1.tip: The blank is explained as "a tiny cabin he called home," so it means a home.

traps.why: An office is a building you work in, not where you live.
Building is too general; an abode is specifically where someone lives.
A guest visits a home; an abode is the home itself.

syn2.tip: Abode is tied to abide, meaning to stay. The place where you stay and live is your home.

sc2.stem: The castle was a royal _____ for hundreds of years, but now nobody lives there, and tourists simply walk through its empty halls.

traps.why: It may be like a museum now, but "but" points back to living there.
A kingdom is a whole country, much bigger than one castle.
A throne is a royal chair, not a place to live.

sc2.tip: "But now nobody lives there" contrasts with the past, so the castle was once where royals lived: a home.

example: A commotion broke out when the goat escaped.
hook: Commotion has motion inside: picture a whole fair moving and shouting at once when a goat gets loose.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of commotion.
A celebration is noisy but happy; commotion is noisy confusion.
Crowds can cause a commotion, but a crowd is just people.

syn1.tip: Look for motion inside commotion. Lots of noisy, confused motion all at once is a commotion.

sc1.stem: The runaway goat caused quite a _____ at the county fair, with people shouting and chasing it between the booths.

traps.why: Shouting and chasing are the opposite of silence.
Fair booths make profits, but the goat caused shouting and chasing.
Promotion looks like commotion but means a move up or an ad.

sc1.tip: "People shouting and chasing it between the booths" describes noisy confusion, so the blank means a disturbance.

traps.why: Peaceful quiet is the opposite of commotion.
Music can be loud, but commotion means messy confusion.
A soft murmur is far too gentle for a commotion.

syn2.tip: People say "What's all the commotion?" when they hear shouting and running. It means noisy confusion.

sc2.stem: The library was peaceful all morning until the fire alarm went off, and suddenly a _____ of shouting kids and scraping chairs filled the room.

traps.why: A hush is quiet, but the room filled with shouting.
A fire alarm brings confusion, not a happy party.
Emotion looks like commotion but means a feeling.

sc2.tip: "Peaceful" ends "until the fire alarm went off," then "shouting" and "scraping" describe noisy confusion.

example: The fickle cat loved me, then ignored me.
hook: Picture a fickle friend flipping like a coin: best buddies today, strangers tomorrow.

traps.why: Steady means staying the same, the opposite of fickle.
Picky people are fussy, but fickle means changing your mind often.
Prickly looks a bit like fickle but means spiky or grouchy.

syn1.tip: People talk about fickle weather, which keeps switching from sun to rain. Fickle means always changing.

sc1.stem: The _____ toddler wanted the red cup, then the blue one, then the red one again, changing her mind every minute.

traps.why: A stubborn toddler would stick with one cup.
Cups suggest drinking, but the clue is about changing her mind.
Tickled rhymes with fickle but means amused.

sc1.tip: The example shows it: "the red cup, then the blue one, then the red one again" and "changing her mind every minute."

traps.why: Firm and steady is the opposite of fickle.
Hard to please means picky, not constantly switching.
Open to ideas sounds good; fickle is a complaint about switching.

syn2.tip: Fickle has a negative feeling. A fickle fan or friend can't be counted on because they keep changing their mind.

sc2.stem: My brother has supported the same baseball team since he was four, but my sister is _____ and cheers for whichever team happens to be winning that week.

traps.why: Loyal describes the brother; "but" shows the sister is different.
Athletic is about sports, but the clue is about switching teams.
Sickly sounds like fickle but means often ill.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the sister with the brother who backs "the same team." Cheering for "whichever team" is winning means changeable.

example: Our frugal family reuses wrapping paper.
hook: A frugal shopper clips coupons, buys on sale, and saves every leftover dollar in a jar.

traps.why: Wasteful is the opposite of frugal.
Stingy is about money too, but it is unkind; frugal is sensible.
Fragile looks a bit like frugal but means easy to break.

syn1.tip: Frugal people are careful with money. Picture a frugal family that reuses wrapping paper to save.

sc1.stem: Grandpa is so _____ that he eats a simple lunch, reuses every paper bag, and never wastes a single penny.

traps.why: Grandpa never wastes a penny, so wasteful is the opposite.
Wealthy is about having money, not about saving it carefully.
Greedy means wanting more; reusing bags shows careful saving, not greed.

sc1.tip: Look at the examples: "reuses every paper bag" and "never wastes a single penny." Those describe someone careful with money.

traps.why: Spending quickly is the opposite of being frugal.
This is about money, but frugal means not wasting it, not having lots.
That sounds selfish; frugal is a sensible, not mean, way with money.

syn2.tip: Frugal is about not wasting. If you picture someone saving every penny, careful with money fits best.

sc2.stem: Although Mia's brother spends his allowance on candy the day he gets it, Mia is _____ and saves most of hers for a new bike.

traps.why: "Although" signals Mia is unlike her spending brother, so wasteful is backward.
Generous people give money away; Mia saves hers.
Greedy sounds harsh; saving for a bike is sensible, not greedy.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets Mia against her brother, who spends right away. Since she "saves most of hers," the blank means careful with money.

example: I loathe the taste of olives.
hook: Say loathe with a scrunched-up face, like when you taste something you truly cannot stand.

traps.why: Adore means to love, the opposite of loathe.
Dislike is too weak; loathe means hating very strongly.
Fear means being afraid, which is a different feeling from hating.

syn1.tip: Loathe is a stronger hate than dislike. If you would push a food away in disgust, you loathe it. Detest is just as strong.

sc1.stem: Ari is not afraid of mushrooms; he simply happens to _____ their slimy taste more than any other food.

traps.why: The sentence says Ari is "not afraid," so fear is ruled out.
Slimy is a bad word for taste, so enjoy goes the wrong way.
Crave means want badly; a slimy taste suggests he hates it.

sc1.tip: "Not afraid... he simply" tells you it is a different feeling than fear. "Slimy taste" and "more than any other food" point to strong hatred.

traps.why: Liking very much is the opposite of loathing.
Minding a little is far too weak for loathe.
Loath without the e means unwilling; loathe with an e means hate.

syn2.tip: Loathe is a strong word for a strong feeling. Look for the choice that matches hating, not just minding.

sc2.stem: My cat seems to _____ bath time, because she hisses, scratches, and hides under the bed whenever she hears the tub filling up.

traps.why: Hissing and hiding show the cat does not enjoy baths.
Tolerate is too weak; hissing and scratching show strong hatred.
Needing a bath is not why a cat hisses and hides.

sc2.tip: "Because she hisses, scratches, and hides" gives the reason. Those actions show a very strong hatred of bath time.

example: The gullible boy believed the moon was cheese.
hook: To gull someone is an old way to say trick them, so gullible means easily tricked.

traps.why: Suspicious people doubt things, the opposite of gullible.
Honest people tell the truth; gullible people believe whatever they hear.
Tricky describes the prankster, not the person who gets fooled.

syn1.tip: Gullible people believe whatever they hear. Think of the boy who believed the moon was cheese. He was far too trusting.

sc1.stem: Max is so _____ that he believed his sister when she said spaghetti grows on trees, and he falls for every prank.

traps.why: Suspicious people doubt things; Max believes everything, so it is backward.
Mischievous describes his prank-playing sister, not Max who falls for pranks.
Spaghetti is food, but the sentence is about believing a silly story.

sc1.tip: Look at "believed his sister" and "falls for every prank." Both show someone who is easily tricked.

traps.why: Hard to trick is the opposite of gullible.
Liars do the tricking; gullible people are the ones tricked.
Gullible has gull in it, but it is not about birds.

syn2.tip: Gullible ends in -ible, which means able to be. A gullible person is able to be fooled very easily.

sc2.stem: Lena is careful and checks every fact, but her cousin is so _____ that he believed a TV ad promising a pill that makes you fly.

traps.why: "But" means the cousin is unlike careful Lena, so careful is backward.
Wanting to fly is adventurous, but the clue is believing a silly ad.
A wise person would not believe a pill makes you fly.

sc2.tip: "But" sets the cousin against careful Lena. Since he "believed a TV ad" about flying pills, he must be easily fooled.

example: We got a cordial welcome at the inn.
hook: Cordial comes from the Latin word for heart, so a cordial greeting is a warm, from-the-heart hello.

traps.why: Hostile means unfriendly, the opposite of cordial.
Cordless looks like cordial but means without a wire.
Stiff manners are about greetings too, but they feel cold, not warm.

syn1.tip: Cordial is used for a welcome or greeting. A cordial welcome is warm, like an innkeeper with hot cocoa. Pick the warm, kind word.

sc1.stem: The innkeeper gave us a _____ welcome, greeting us warmly with hot cocoa and a friendly smile.

traps.why: Chilly means unfriendly, but the innkeeper greeted us "warmly."
Brief is about length; the clue tells how friendly the welcome felt.
A formal welcome is stiff, not warm with cocoa and smiles.

sc1.tip: The words after the blank explain it: "greeting us warmly" and "a friendly smile." The blank means warm and friendly.

traps.why: Cold and rude is the opposite of cordial.
Cord means rope, but cordial has nothing to do with rope.
Polite but distant lacks the warmth that cordial has.

syn2.tip: Cordial has cor, the Latin for heart, inside it, like courage. Think of a heartfelt, warm welcome.

sc2.stem: The new neighbors seemed cold at first, but after we brought them cookies, they became quite _____ and invited us over for lemonade every Saturday.

traps.why: "But" shows they changed from cold, so distant is backward.
Cookies are food, but the clue is about how they treated us.
Nosy neighbors are interested in you, but nosy is a negative word.

sc2.tip: "Cold at first, but" tells you they changed to the opposite of cold. Inviting you over every Saturday shows they became warm and friendly.

example: The coach rebuked him for being late.
hook: When the coach blows the whistle and sharply tells a late player off in front of everyone, that is a rebuke.

traps.why: Praise means to say good things, the opposite of rebuke.
Rebuild looks like rebuke but means to build again.
Remind is too gentle; rebuke means criticize sharply.

syn1.tip: Rebuke shows up when someone in charge is angry: "The coach rebuked him for being late." It means a sharp telling-off.

sc1.stem: The coach had to _____ the players sharply for goofing off during practice, telling them firmly it must stop.

traps.why: Praise is for good work, not for goofing off.
Teasing is playful, but "firmly" shows the coach was serious.
Training is a coach's job, but the clue is about criticizing bad behavior.

sc1.tip: Look at "sharply," "goofing off," and "telling them firmly it must stop." The coach is harshly criticizing the players.

traps.why: Praising warmly is the opposite of rebuking.
Re often means again, but rebuke does not mean repeating yourself.
Gentle suggestions are far too soft for a rebuke.

syn2.tip: Think of rebuke as a sharp scolding. The right choice should sound stern and critical, not gentle or kind.

sc2.stem: Instead of choosing to _____ Leo for spilling paint on the floor, the art teacher calmly handed him a towel and said accidents happen to everyone.

traps.why: Nobody praises a paint spill; "instead of" points to something harsh.
The teacher did help, so "instead of" can't introduce helping.
Comfort is kind, like what she did, so it can't follow "instead of."

sc2.tip: "Instead of" means the teacher did the opposite of the blank. She stayed calm and kind, so the blank is something harsh, like scolding.

meaning: to twist out of its true shape
example: The funhouse mirror distorted my face.
hook: Picture a funhouse mirror that stretches your nose long and squashes your legs short; it distorts you.

traps.why: Straighten is the opposite of distort, which bends things out of shape.
Distract looks like distort but means to pull attention away.
Destroy is too strong; a distorted thing is bent, not ruined.

syn1.tip: Think of a contortionist, who twists their body into strange shapes. Distort shares that twisting idea.

sc1.stem: The funhouse mirror would _____ Kai's reflection, stretching his face long and making his legs look tiny.

traps.why: Mirrors get cleaned, but cleaning would not stretch Kai's face.
Kai can still see his reflection, so it isn't hidden.
Shatter means break into pieces; the mirror only stretches his reflection.

sc1.tip: The clue follows the comma: "stretching his face long and making his legs look tiny." That is twisting the reflection out of shape.

traps.why: Distorting moves things away from normal, so this is the opposite.
Dis can mean not, but in distort it means apart.
Cutting into pieces breaks something; distorting only changes its shape.

syn2.tip: Distort is used for mirrors, pictures, and sounds that come out warped. The answer should describe changing a shape, not destroying it.

sc2.stem: When the old speaker began to _____ the music, the singer's sweet voice came out crackly and strange, so Dad finally unplugged it.

traps.why: Crackly and strange is worse, not better, so improve is backward.
The voice still came out, so the music was not silenced.
Recording music wouldn't make the singer's voice come out crackly.

sc2.tip: Look at the effect: the sweet voice "came out crackly and strange." The speaker must have twisted the sound out of its true shape.

example: She used tact when telling him the truth.
hook: Tact is telling Grandma her lumpy sweater is cozy instead of saying it looks itchy.

traps.why: Rudeness is the opposite of tact, which avoids hurting feelings.
A tack is a small pin; it only looks like tact.
Tact often goes with telling the truth, but honesty can still be blunt.

syn1.tip: Tact is the skill of saying hard things kindly. Diplomats use it when talking to other countries, which is why diplomacy fits.

sc1.stem: Telling a friend her drawing needs work takes _____, so Leah found a kind way to say it without hurting her.

traps.why: Bluntness hurts feelings, but Leah wanted to avoid hurting her friend.
Drawing takes talent, but the clue is about speaking kindly.
Leah didn't get lucky; she carefully found a kind way to say it.

sc1.tip: The second half explains the blank: Leah "found a kind way to say it without hurting her." That skill is the missing word.

traps.why: Being blunt means not caring about feelings, the opposite of tact.
Tact comes from an old word for touch, but now it means people skills.
Shy people may stay quiet, but tact is skill, not fear.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "handle it with tact." Tact means knowing how to speak to people without upsetting them.

sc2.stem: Jamal blurted out that the cake tasted awful, but his sister showed more _____ by thanking the baker and saying she was too full for seconds.

traps.why: "But" contrasts her with rude Jamal, so rudeness is backward.
She said she was too full, so she showed no appetite.
Jamal was the blunt, honest one; his sister was being kind.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the sister with Jamal, who "blurted out" a hurtful truth. She found a polite way out, showing skill at not upsetting people.

example: The destitute family needed help.
hook: A destitute family has empty pockets, an empty pantry, and nowhere to sleep tonight.

traps.why: Wealthy means rich, the opposite of destitute.
Destined looks like destitute but means meant to happen.
Thrifty people save money; destitute people have none to save.

syn1.tip: Destitute describes people who need help because they have nothing. Penniless, without even a penny, matches that.

sc1.stem: After the flood washed away their farm, the family was _____, left with no money and nothing at all.

traps.why: Wealthy means rich, but the family had "no money."
A flood soaks things, but the clue is about having nothing left.
Thrifty people save money; this family had no money to save.

sc1.tip: After the comma, the sentence restates the blank: "left with no money and nothing at all." That means extremely poor.

traps.why: Very rich is the opposite of destitute.
Destitute is much stronger; it means having almost nothing.
That describes saving money, not having none at all.

syn2.tip: Destitute is a strong word. It doesn't mean a bit short on money; it means having almost nothing at all.

sc2.stem: The man had once owned three mansions and a yacht, yet after his business failed he was _____ and slept in a shelter each night.

traps.why: "Yet" signals a change from rich, so wealthy is backward.
He slept in a shelter because he had no home, not from sleepiness.
Owning mansions might make him famous, but the clue is about losing money.

sc2.tip: "Yet" shows a big change from owning mansions. Sleeping "in a shelter each night" tells you he had lost everything.

example: Don't omit your name on the test.
hook: If you omit the cheese from a cheeseburger, you just have a plain burger.

traps.why: Include means to put in, the opposite of omit.
Emit looks like omit but means to give off, like smoke.
Admit sounds like omit but means to let in or confess.

syn1.tip: Omit means leave out. You might omit onions from a sandwich. Exclude also means keep something out.

sc1.stem: Please do not _____ anyone's name from the class list, or that student will feel left out.

traps.why: Copying a name wouldn't make that student feel left out.
Emit looks like omit but means to give off, like light.
Learning a name from the list would make a student feel welcome.

sc1.tip: The clue is at the end: "or that student will feel left out." Leaving a name off a list makes someone feel left out.

traps.why: Put in is the opposite of leave out.
Mit can mean send, but omit means to leave something out.
Omit is often about lists, but it means leaving out, not writing down.

syn2.tip: Think of a test direction: "Don't omit your name." It means don't leave your name off.

sc2.stem: Because my little brother hates the taste of onions, Mom decided to _____ them from the recipe, so the soup had none at all.

traps.why: Copying onions from a recipe would still put them in the soup.
Measuring onions means using them, but the soup "had none at all."
Admit sounds like omit but means to let in, the reverse.

sc2.tip: Her brother "hates the taste of onions," and the soup "had none at all." So Mom left the onions out.

example: The mouse found a meager crumb of cheese.
hook: A meager meal is one lonely pea on a big white plate.

traps.why: Plentiful means a lot, the opposite of meager.
Eager hides inside meager, but it means excited to do something.
A meager meal might leave you hungry, but meager describes the amount.

syn1.tip: Meager is used for amounts that are too small, like a meager crumb or a meager allowance. Skimpy means not enough.

sc1.stem: The baby bird's dinner was a _____ portion, just one tiny worm, hardly enough to fill its belly.

traps.why: Generous means a lot, but one tiny worm is "hardly enough."
Worms may be healthy, but the clue is about how little there was.
Eager looks like meager, but a portion can't be eager.

sc1.tip: The clue restates the blank: "just one tiny worm, hardly enough to fill its belly." The blank means very small in amount.

traps.why: More than enough is the opposite of meager.
That means eager, a different word hiding inside meager.
Meager is stronger; it means so little it hardly counts.

syn2.tip: Think of a meager portion: so small you are still hungry. The answer should mean too little, not just a bit less.

sc2.stem: Last year the garden gave us baskets of tomatoes, but this summer, with so little rain, the harvest was _____ and filled only one small bowl.

traps.why: "But" signals a change from baskets, so plentiful is backward.
Ripe tells if tomatoes are ready, not how many there were.
There was "so little rain," so the tomatoes would not be soggy.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts this summer with last year's baskets. "Filled only one small bowl" tells you the harvest was very small.

example: The room grew somber when the news came.
hook: Picture a funeral: dark clothes, hushed voices, a gray sky. That heavy, serious mood is somber.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of somber; it means happy and bright.
Furious is a strong feeling too, but it means very angry, not sad.
Summery sounds a bit like somber but means warm and sunny.

syn1.tip: Somber describes a heavy, sad, serious mood, like at a funeral. Pick the choice with that dark feeling.

sc1.stem: The usually noisy auditorium grew _____ and serious as everyone quietly said goodbye to the beloved retiring principal.

traps.why: Rowdy means wild and loud, but everyone was quiet.
An auditorium can be crowded, but the clue is about the sad mood.
Festive is a happy party feeling, but this goodbye was serious and sad.

sc1.tip: The words "and serious" and "quietly said goodbye" tell you the mood was heavy and sad.

traps.why: Bright and lively is the opposite of a somber mood.
This is a bad mood too, but somber is quiet and sad, not loud.
Calm and peaceful is quiet like somber, but it feels pleasant, not sad.

syn2.tip: Think of a somber ceremony, like a memorial. Everyone is quiet, serious, and sad.

sc2.stem: Usually our team bus is loud and joking after games, but after losing the championship, the ride home was _____, with everyone staring silently out the windows.

traps.why: Lively fits only if you miss "but"; the team was silent after losing.
A bus ride can be bumpy, but the clue is about the team's sad mood.
Proud is a good feeling, but the team had just lost.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a change from "loud and joking." Losing and "staring silently" point to a sad, serious mood.

example: We admired the splendor of the palace.
hook: Imagine a palace with golden ceilings and sparkling chandeliers: its splendor makes you stop and stare.

traps.why: Ugliness is the opposite of splendor's great beauty.
Splinter looks like splendor but is a tiny sharp piece of wood.
Grand places often cost a lot, but splendor is about beauty, not money.

syn1.tip: Splendor sounds like "splendid," which means wonderful and grand. Look for the word about grand beauty.

sc1.stem: The _____ of the palace, with golden ceilings and sparkling chandeliers, amazed every tourist who stepped inside.

traps.why: Dullness is the opposite; golden ceilings and chandeliers are dazzling.
Palaces have guards, but golden ceilings describe the palace's beauty.
Gloom is dark and sad, but the tourists were amazed by beauty.

sc1.tip: "Golden ceilings and sparkling chandeliers" are examples of something grand and beautiful. The blank names that grandness.

traps.why: A plain look is the opposite of splendor.
Grand things can be big, but splendor is about beauty, not size.
Slight prettiness is far too weak; splendor is breathtaking.

syn2.tip: Splendor describes fireworks, a castle, or a sunset that takes your breath away. It means grand, dazzling beauty.

sc2.stem: Our campsite looked ordinary in daylight, but at night the _____ of the starry sky, with the Milky Way stretching overhead, left us speechless.

traps.why: Plainness fits only if you miss "but"; the night sky was amazing.
Cloudiness is about the sky, but this sky was starry and clear.
Loneliness is a sad feeling, but the sky left them amazed.

sc2.tip: "But" sets up a contrast with "ordinary." Something that leaves you "speechless" under the Milky Way must be grand and beautiful.

example: The radiance of the sunrise woke me.
hook: Radiance is related to "radiate," like rays of light spreading out from the sun in every direction.

traps.why: Darkness is the opposite of radiance, which is bright light.
The sun gives off heat too, but radiance is about light.
A flicker is a weak, unsteady light; radiance is bright and steady.

syn1.tip: Radiance sounds like "radiate" and "ray." Think of rays of light shining out.

sc1.stem: The glowing _____ of the full moon lit up the whole beach, making the sand shine silver.

traps.why: A shadow is dark and could not light up a beach.
The moon has a round shape, but a shape cannot light anything up.
Radius looks like radiance but is a math word for a circle's measure.

sc1.tip: The words "glowing," "lit up," and "shine silver" all point to light. The blank names the moon's bright light.

traps.why: A deep shadow is the opposite of shining light.
Bright things can be hot, but radiance means light, not heat.
A dim twinkle is too weak; radiance is a bright glow.

syn2.tip: The sun, a lamp, and a happy face can all have radiance. Each one gives off a bright, shining light.

sc2.stem: When Grandma opened the old jewelry box, the _____ of the diamond ring was so strong that we all had to squint at the sparkle.

traps.why: Dullness is the opposite; nobody squints at something dull.
A ring has weight, but weight would not make you squint.
Warmth is felt, not seen, so it would not make you squint.

sc2.tip: The effect "we all had to squint" tells you the cause was very bright light. Look for the word meaning a bright glow.

example: The incessant barking kept us awake.
hook: In- means not, and the rest comes from "cease": something that never ceases, like a car alarm all night.

traps.why: Occasional means only now and then, the opposite of never stopping.
Innocent looks like incessant but means not guilty.
Incessant noises are often loud, but the word means never stopping.

syn1.tip: Hear "cease," which means stop, inside incessant. Add in-, meaning not, and you get "not stopping."

sc1.stem: The parrot's _____ chatter never stopped, not even for a moment, from sunrise until long after bedtime.

traps.why: Rare means hardly ever, but this chatter never stopped.
Parrots are colorful, but the clue is about chatter that never stopped.
Innocent looks like incessant but means not guilty.

sc1.tip: The sentence says the chatter "never stopped, not even for a moment." The blank must mean nonstop.

traps.why: Now and then means with breaks, the opposite of incessant.
Incessant sounds can be harsh, but the word is about never stopping.
A little while is too weak; incessant means it goes on and on.

syn2.tip: Picture rain that falls all day without a pause. Incessant describes something that keeps going with no break.

sc2.stem: Most car alarms beep for a minute and then quiet down, but the one outside our window was _____, honking all night until the owner finally woke up.

traps.why: Brief fits only if you miss "but"; this alarm honked all night.
A car can be shiny, but the clue is about honking all night.
Occasional means now and then, but this alarm kept honking all night.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with alarms that "quiet down," and "honking all night" shows this one kept going without stopping.

example: The stingy king kept all the gold.
hook: Picture Scrooge counting coins and refusing to give his worker even a lump of extra coal: that is stingy.

traps.why: Generous means happy to give, the opposite of stingy.
Poor means having little money; stingy people may have plenty but won't share.
Stinky looks like stingy but means smelling bad.

syn1.tip: A miser is someone who hoards money. Stingy has that same tight, unfriendly feeling of refusing to give.

sc1.stem: The _____ pirate refused to share even one gold coin with his loyal crew, hiding the whole treasure for himself.

traps.why: A giving pirate would share, but this one refused.
Pirates can be fearsome, but the clue is about refusing to share.
Stringy looks like stingy but means thin and long like string.

sc1.tip: "Refused to share even one gold coin" and "hiding the whole treasure for himself" describe someone who will not give anything away.

traps.why: Eager to share is the opposite of stingy.
Stingy looks like sting plus -y, but it is not about stinging.
Careful with money sounds sensible and good; stingy is a selfish, negative word.

syn2.tip: Say it with a soft g, like "stin-jee." It describes people who keep everything for themselves and will not share.

sc2.stem: Grandpa always gave us extra candy on Halloween, but his neighbor was so _____ that she handed out one tiny raisin per kid and kept the big chocolate bars.

traps.why: Generous fits only if you miss "but"; she kept the chocolate.
Spooky goes with Halloween, but the clue is about not sharing.
Cheerful is a pleasant word, but keeping the treats is selfish.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the neighbor with generous Grandpa. Giving "one tiny raisin" and keeping the chocolate shows she did not want to share.

example: We enjoyed the tranquility of the lake.
hook: Picture a still lake at dawn, no wind, no voices, just one bird singing: that calm is tranquility.

traps.why: Chaos means wild confusion, the opposite of tranquility.
Sleep is restful, but tranquility is a calm, quiet feeling or place.
Loneliness is quiet too, but it feels sad; tranquility feels pleasant.

syn1.tip: The word "tranquil," meaning calm, is inside tranquility. The Sea of Tranquility on the moon was named for calm.

sc1.stem: After the noisy city, the _____ of the still mountain lake, where only birds were singing, felt wonderful.

traps.why: Commotion means noisy activity, like the city, not the still lake.
Mountain lakes can be cold, but the clue contrasts noise with calm.
Emptiness feels lonely and sad, but this place felt wonderful.

sc1.tip: "After the noisy city" sets up a contrast, and "still" and "only birds were singing" describe a calm, quiet place.

traps.why: Noisy confusion is the opposite of quiet calm.
Boredom is quiet but unpleasant; tranquility is a peaceful, good feeling.
Total silence goes too far; a tranquil place can still have birdsong.

syn2.tip: Tranquil means calm. Add -ity and the word names the state of being calm and peaceful.

sc2.stem: Because the baby had finally fallen asleep and the dog was napping by the fire, a sweet _____ filled the house for the first time all day.

traps.why: An uproar is loud, but everyone was sleeping.
The dog is mentioned, but it was napping, not barking.
Sadness is the wrong feeling for a sweet, restful moment.

sc2.tip: The cause is "the baby had finally fallen asleep" and "the dog was napping." That leads to a calm, quiet house.

example: The drab room needed some bright paint.
hook: Drab is the color of a gray, rainy Monday: no sparkle, no brightness, just plain and dull.

traps.why: Colorful is the opposite of drab.
Dirty things can look dull, but drab means plain and colorless, not unclean.
Hideous means terribly ugly; drab is only plain and boring.

syn1.tip: Think of a drab gray sweater next to a rainbow one. Drab things lack color and brightness.

sc1.stem: Unlike her bright, sparkly sneakers, the school uniform was _____, a plain brownish gray without a speck of color.

traps.why: Dazzling is the opposite; the uniform had no color at all.
Clothes can be comfortable, but the clue is about having no color.
Uniforms have a price, but the clue describes plain brownish gray.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her bright, sparkly sneakers" signals a contrast, and "plain brownish gray without a speck of color" tells you the meaning.

traps.why: Bright and cheerful is the opposite of drab.
Old things can look drab, but drab is about color, not damage.
Drab is boring, not frightening; scary is the wrong feeling.

syn2.tip: Drab often describes clothes, walls, or weather. It means plain, colorless, and boring to look at.

sc2.stem: The old classroom walls were so _____ that the students voted to cover them with bright murals of rainbows, jungles, and planets.

traps.why: Vivid walls would already be bright, so nobody would need murals.
Walls can be sturdy, but that would not make students add bright murals.
Cheerful walls would not need fixing; the walls were dull.

sc2.tip: The result, covering the walls with "bright murals," tells you the walls were plain and lacked color.

example: A spilled drink was the only mishap.
hook: Mis- means badly, and hap means luck, as in "happen" and "perhaps": a mishap is a bit of bad luck.

traps.why: A success goes well; a mishap goes wrong.
A disaster is huge; a mishap is a small accident.
Mishmash looks like mishap but means a jumbled mix.

syn1.tip: Mis- means badly or wrong, as in misspell. A mishap is something that happens badly, a small accident.

sc1.stem: Spilling a little juice on the rug was only a small _____, so Mom just laughed and grabbed a towel.

traps.why: Spilling juice is not a triumph; it is a little accident.
A catastrophe is huge, but this was "only a small" spill.
Juice can be a snack, but spilling it is an accident.

sc1.tip: "Only a small" and "Mom just laughed" tell you it was a minor bit of bad luck, nothing serious.

traps.why: Good luck is the opposite of a mishap.
A tragedy is far too serious; a mishap is minor.
Hap is not "happy" here; it means luck, and a mishap is an event.

syn2.tip: Think of tripping and dropping your lunch tray. That small, unlucky moment is a mishap, not a big tragedy.

sc2.stem: The class trip went perfectly except for one _____, when Jamal's hat blew into the duck pond and he had to fish it out with a stick.

traps.why: A highlight is a best moment, but "except for" points to something going wrong.
A tragedy is too serious for a hat in a pond.
Class trips can have picnics, but the clue is the hat accident.

sc2.tip: "Except for" signals something went wrong on a perfect trip. A hat blowing into a pond is a small, unlucky accident.

example: The new girl seemed aloof at first.
hook: Picture a cat on a high shelf, watching the party below and ignoring everyone who calls its name: that cat is aloof.

traps.why: Friendly is the opposite of aloof.
Hostile means openly unfriendly and ready to fight; aloof is just cool and distant.
Lonely people are apart but wish for friends; aloof people choose distance.

syn1.tip: People say someone "kept aloof," meaning they stood apart from others. An aloof person feels cool and far away, even in the same room.

sc1.stem: Priya was not shy; she simply chose to stay _____ at the party, standing coolly apart and barely nodding when anyone said hello.

traps.why: Timid fits only if you miss "not shy"; Priya chose to stay apart.
Sociable means friendly and chatty, but she barely nodded hello.
Aloft looks like aloof but means up in the air.

sc1.tip: "Not shy" rules out fear, and "coolly apart" and "barely nodding" show she chose to keep her distance from others.

traps.why: Warm and welcoming is the opposite of aloof.
Shy people stay apart from fear; aloof people stay apart by choice.
That is aloft, which looks like aloof but means up high.

syn2.tip: Aloof people keep their distance on purpose. They are not scared, just cool and uninterested in being friendly.

sc2.stem: Because the famous skater stayed _____ after the show, ignoring fans' waves and refusing to sign autographs, many kids left feeling disappointed.

traps.why: A chatty skater would talk to fans, not ignore them.
Skaters are graceful, but the clue is about ignoring fans.
Humble is a pleasant quality, but this skater disappointed the kids.

sc2.tip: "Ignoring fans' waves" and "refusing to sign autographs" show someone cool and distant, and that is why the kids felt "disappointed."

example: The zealous fans painted their faces.
hook: Zealous is zeal plus -ous, full of zeal, like a fan who paints their face and cheers until they lose their voice.

traps.why: Uninterested is the opposite of zealous.
Curious is too mild; zealous means extremely eager.
Zealous fans can be noisy, but the word means eager, not loud.

syn1.tip: Zeal means strong eagerness, and -ous means full of. Zealous people are full of eagerness for a cause, team, or hobby.
