All at once is too sudden; dwindling happens gradually.

syn2.tip: Dwindle is about getting smaller slowly, like a pile of snacks shrinking through the week.

sc2.stem: At first, hundreds of fans waited outside the stadium for autographs, but as the cold night went on, the crowd began to _____ until only a few were left.

traps.why: Grow is the opposite; the crowd ends with only a few.
Fans cheer, but cheering doesn't leave only a few people.
The night was cold, but shivering doesn't make a crowd smaller.

sc2.tip: Notice the contrast: 'hundreds' at first, 'but' later 'only a few were left.' The crowd got smaller over time.

example: She gave a tactful answer about the ugly hat.
hook: Tactful means full of tact, the skill of saying hard things gently, like politely thanking someone for a gift you dislike.

traps.why: Rude is the opposite of tactful.
Tasteful looks similar but means having good style.
Tact is about how you tell the truth, not whether you do.

syn1.tip: Tactful ends in -ful, so it means full of tact. Tact is the skill of being careful with other people's feelings.

sc1.stem: Not wanting to hurt Grandma's feelings, Lily gave a _____ answer about the itchy sweater Grandma had knitted for her.

traps.why: A blunt answer might hurt Grandma's feelings.
Answers can be quick, but quick has nothing to do with feelings.
The sweater is scratchy, but an answer can't be.

sc1.tip: The sentence begins with the reason: 'Not wanting to hurt Grandma's feelings.' So Lily's answer was careful and kind.

traps.why: Blunt and hurtful is the opposite of tactful.
Tactful sounds like tack plus -ful, but tacks have nothing to do with it.
That describes tactical, which looks similar but means clever planning.

syn2.tip: Someone tactful chooses gentle words so nobody gets hurt. Think of the opposite, tactless, which means hurting feelings without meaning to.

sc2.stem: Instead of laughing at Ben's terrible haircut like the others did, Ana was _____ and said only that it would grow back soon.

traps.why: Rude fits the laughing kids, but 'instead of' shows Ana was different.
Stylish is about hair, but the clue is about Ana's kind words.
Mocking is what the others did, not Ana.

sc2.tip: The words 'Instead of laughing' contrast Ana with the others. Saying 'it would grow back soon' is a gentle, kind response.

example: The twins bicker over the front seat.
hook: Picture two kids in the backseat: 'My side.' 'No, my side.' That endless small arguing is bickering.

traps.why: Agree is the opposite of bicker.
Flicker looks similar but means to flash on and off.
Battle is far too strong; bickering is small, petty arguing.

syn1.tip: Think of brothers and sisters arguing over who gets the front seat. Bicker means arguing about small, silly things.

sc1.stem: The twins always _____ over silly things, like who gets the window seat or the bigger slice of pizza.

traps.why: Agreeing doesn't fit fights over who gets the window seat.
The things are silly, but fighting over seats isn't laughing.
Worry is a feeling inside; the twins are clashing with each other.

sc1.tip: Look at the examples: 'who gets the window seat or the bigger slice.' Those are small things kids argue about.

traps.why: Getting along well is the opposite of bickering.
Bicker starts with bi like bicycle, but has nothing to do with bikes.
Fighting with fists is too strong; bickering is only words.

syn2.tip: Bickering is petty arguing, the kind of back-and-forth over tiny things that siblings do on long car rides.

sc2.stem: At school, Leo and Sam are best friends who share everything, but at home the brothers _____ about whose turn it is to feed the dog.

traps.why: Agree fits best friends, but 'but at home' signals the opposite.
Friends joke, but 'but' shows home is less friendly.
Forgetting is not something that contrasts with being best friends.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' contrasts 'best friends who share everything' with home. Arguing about a small chore like feeding the dog is bickering.

example: My brother's handwriting is illegible.
hook: Legible means readable, so il-legible means not readable, like a doctor's scribbled note.

traps.why: Neat writing is easy to read, the opposite of illegible.
Illegal looks similar but means against the law.
Misspelled words are a writing problem, but you can still read them.

syn1.tip: Legible means clear enough to read. The il- at the start means not, so illegible means not readable.

sc1.stem: Dr. Patel's handwriting was so _____ that the pharmacist could not read a single word on the note.

traps.why: Legible means readable, but the pharmacist could not read it.
Eligible looks similar but means allowed to take part.
A doctor's note is important, but importance doesn't stop someone reading it.

sc1.tip: The clue is "could not read a single word." Handwriting that nobody can read is illegible.

traps.why: Easy to read is the opposite of illegible.
Against the law means illegal, a word that only looks like illegible.
Pencil writing can be perfectly clear; illegible is about being unreadable.

syn2.tip: Find the word legible inside, which means readable. Adding il- flips it to not readable.

sc2.stem: Unlike her neat, careful printing in third grade, Maya's rushed notes this year were so _____ that even she couldn't figure out what she had written.

traps.why: Tidy matches her old printing, but "unlike" signals the notes changed.
Illegal looks similar but means against the law, not messy.
Colorful notes can still be read; she couldn't read hers.

sc2.tip: "Unlike her neat, careful printing" signals a contrast. If even she "couldn't figure out" her notes, they were illegible.

example: The puppy cowered during the thunderstorm.
hook: Picture a scared puppy shrinking low under the table during a thunderstorm; that is cowering.

traps.why: To strut is to walk proudly, the opposite of shrinking in fear.
Cover looks like cower but means to put something over.
A growl shows anger at a threat, not shrinking away in fear.

syn1.tip: Picture a frightened animal making itself small. Cower is a fear word, so look for shrinking back.

sc1.stem: During thunderstorms, our puppy would _____ under the kitchen table, crouching low with its tail tucked between its legs.

traps.why: Strutting is proud walking, but the puppy crouched with its tail tucked.
A napping puppy is relaxed, not crouching low with a tucked tail.
Barking is a puppy sound, but the clue describes a scared posture.

sc1.tip: Look at "crouching low with its tail tucked between its legs" during "thunderstorms." That is a scared puppy cowering.

traps.why: Standing proudly is the opposite of crouching in fear.
That is what cover means, a word that only looks like cower.
Bowing is bending down with respect, not with fear.

syn2.tip: Cower always has fear in it. Think of someone hunched and trembling, trying to hide from danger.

sc2.stem: My little brother acts brave all day, but when the lights go out, he will _____ under his blanket until Dad checks the closet for monsters.

traps.why: Relaxing is calm, but "but" shows he stops acting brave.
Giggling is happy, but he is afraid of monsters.
Snoring happens under blankets, but he's awake and scared, waiting for Dad.

sc2.tip: "Acts brave all day, but" signals a change. Waiting for Dad to check for "monsters" shows fear, so he cowers.

example: The gleeful kids splashed in puddles.
hook: Glee is great delight, and -ful means full of, so gleeful means full of happy delight.

traps.why: Gloomy means sad, the opposite of gleeful.
Gleaming looks similar but means shining brightly.
Gleeful kids may be loud, but gleeful is about a happy feeling.

syn1.tip: Glee means great delight, and -ful means full of. A gleeful person is full of happy delight.

sc1.stem: With a _____ giggle, Toby watched his snowball sail over the fence and land right on his big brother's hat.

traps.why: A gloomy giggle makes no sense; Toby is delighted by his shot.
Nervous has the wrong feeling; Toby is enjoying his perfect throw.
Grateful looks similar but means thankful, which doesn't fit this moment.

sc1.tip: The snowball landed "right on his big brother's hat," and Toby let out a "giggle." That shows playful delight, so gleeful fits.

traps.why: Sorrow is sadness, the opposite of glee.
Slightly pleased is too weak; gleeful means bursting with delight.
Gleeful people may be energetic, but the word means delighted.

syn2.tip: You may know the word glee from "shouting with glee." Add -ful, meaning full of, and you get full of delight.

sc2.stem: When the principal announced that summer vacation would start a day early, the _____ students cheered, hugged, and danced right out the classroom door.

traps.why: Disappointed students wouldn't cheer and dance about extra vacation.
Anxious means worried, the wrong feeling for cheering and dancing.
Tardy is a school word meaning late, not a feeling of joy.

sc2.tip: The cause is vacation starting "a day early"; the effect is students who "cheered, hugged, and danced." That joy means gleeful.

example: We trudged home through the deep snow.
hook: Imagine dragging heavy boots through deep snow, step after tired step; that slow, heavy walk is a trudge.

traps.why: Skipping is light and bouncy, the opposite of trudging.
Nudge rhymes with trudge but means to push gently.
Travel is too general; trudge means walking slowly and heavily.

syn1.tip: Picture tired hikers dragging their feet through mud. Trudge has a heavy, worn-out feeling, so look for slow, heavy walking.

sc1.stem: Tired after school, the kids had to _____ home through the deep, wet snow, their heavy boots dragging with each step.

traps.why: Skipping is bouncy, but their boots were dragging with each step.
Zooming is fast, but the kids were tired and slow.
Skating is a snow and ice activity, but they were walking in boots.

sc1.tip: Look at "tired," "deep, wet snow," and "heavy boots dragging." Those all describe slow, heavy walking, which is trudging.

traps.why: Running lightly is the opposite of walking slowly and heavily.
Push gently is what nudge means; nudge only sounds like trudge.
Go somewhere is too general; trudging is a slow, heavy walk.

syn2.tip: Say trudge slowly; it even sounds heavy. It describes tired feet dragging, like walking home through deep snow.

sc2.stem: In the morning we raced to the beach, but after a long afternoon in the hot sun, we had to _____ back to the car with our heavy bags.

traps.why: Race fits the morning, but "but" shows the trip back was different.
Swimming is a beach activity, but you can't swim to a parked car.
Skipping is cheerful and light, but they were tired and carrying heavy bags.

sc2.tip: "We raced to the beach, but" signals a contrast. After "a long afternoon" with "heavy bags," they walked slowly and heavily.

example: After soccer, I was famished.
hook: Famished and famine both come from an old Latin word for hunger, so famished means extremely hungry.

traps.why: Full means you've had enough to eat, the opposite of famished.
Famous looks similar but means well known.
Thirsty is needing a drink; famished is needing food.

syn1.tip: Famine means a time when there is no food, and famished comes from the same idea. Think of being so hungry you could eat anything.

sc1.stem: Having skipped lunch to finish his art project, Diego felt _____ by dinner and wolfed down three plates of pasta.

traps.why: Someone stuffed wouldn't wolf down three plates of pasta.
He may be proud of his art project, but the clue is about eating.
Finished looks a bit like famished but means done.

sc1.tip: The cause is "skipped lunch"; the effect is he "wolfed down three plates of pasta." Skipping a meal and eating lots shows extreme hunger.

traps.why: Very full is the opposite of very hungry.
That means famous, a word that only looks like famished.
You might be tired after skipping meals, but famished is about hunger.

syn2.tip: Think of famine, a time without food. Famished is how your stomach feels after a long day with nothing to eat.

sc2.stem: Although Mia had eaten a huge breakfast, by the end of the long hike she was so _____ that she ate two sandwiches and a whole bag of apples.

traps.why: Satisfied fits the big breakfast, but "although" shows she got hungry again.
Hikers can get sunburned, but that wouldn't make her eat so much.
Famous looks like famished but means well known.

sc2.tip: "Although" means the breakfast didn't last. Eating "two sandwiches and a whole bag of apples" shows she was extremely hungry.

example: The teacher beckoned me to her desk.
hook: When a friend curls a finger toward you to mean come here, they beckon you.

traps.why: To dismiss is to send someone away, the opposite of beckon.
Reckon rhymes with beckon but means to think or guess.
Whispering uses your voice; beckoning is a gesture saying come here.

syn1.tip: Picture someone waving you over with their hand. That silent come-here gesture is a beckon, a kind of signal.

sc1.stem: From across the playground, Grandpa gave a little wave of his hand to _____ us over for lunch.

traps.why: To shoo is to wave someone away, not call them over.
Chasing is rough, but Grandpa gave a gentle little wave for lunch.
Grandpa can't carry kids across a playground with a wave.

sc1.tip: The clue is "a little wave of his hand" to get you "over for lunch." A hand gesture asking you to come is a beckon.

traps.why: Send away is the opposite of calling someone closer.
Waving goodbye is a hand gesture, but it means leave, not come.
That is what reckon means; reckon only looks like beckon.

syn2.tip: Beckon is always about getting someone to come closer. Think of a hand gesture that says come over here.

sc2.stem: When the lifeguard spotted us swimming too far out, she began to _____ us back toward shore, waving her arms until we swam closer.

traps.why: Dismiss means send away, but she wanted them to swim closer.
Splashing happens in water, but waving arms called them back.
Towing means pulling with a rope or boat, but they swam back themselves.

sc2.tip: The effect tells you: she waved her arms "until we swam closer." Her gesture made them come, so she beckoned them.

example: The chipmunk scampered up the tree.
hook: Picture a squirrel scampering up a tree trunk on quick, light little feet.

traps.why: Crawling is slow, the opposite of quick, light scampering.
Scatter looks similar but means to spread out in all directions.
Move is too general; scamper means running quickly and lightly.

syn1.tip: Picture a mouse dashing off on tiny feet. Scamper is quick, light running, so look for the fast, small-step word.

sc1.stem: Quick and light on their tiny feet, the chipmunks would _____ across the path before disappearing under a log.

traps.why: Plodding is slow and heavy, not quick and light.
Stomping is heavy, but the chipmunks were light on their feet.
Animals swim, but chipmunks cross a path on their feet.

sc1.tip: The clue is "quick and light on their tiny feet." Running that way is scampering.

traps.why: Walking heavily is the opposite of running lightly.
Animals that scamper may climb, but scamper means running quickly.
Small animals often hide, but scampering is quick running.

syn2.tip: Scamper is how small, playful animals move, like chipmunks or kittens. It is quick, light, and a little bouncy.

sc2.stem: The old dog lumbered slowly across the yard, but the new kitten would _____ past him in a quick blur of tiny paws.

traps.why: Trudge matches the slow old dog, but "but" shows the kitten is different.
Crawling is slow, but the kitten moved in a quick blur.
Kittens stare, but a stare can't move past him in a blur.

sc2.tip: "Lumbered slowly... but" sets up a contrast. The kitten moves in "a quick blur of tiny paws," which means it scampers.

example: Dew glistened on the grass.
hook: Picture dew on morning grass glistening in the sun, shining because it is wet.

traps.why: Fading means growing dim, the opposite of shining.
Listen is hiding inside glisten, but it means to hear.
Wet things drip, but glisten is about shining, not falling drops.

syn1.tip: Glisten looks like listen with a g, but it is about light. Think of wet streets or dewy grass shining in the sun.

sc1.stem: After the morning rain, the wet leaves seemed to _____ in the sunlight like tiny jewels.

traps.why: Darkening is the opposite of shining like jewels.
Leaves rustle, but that's a sound, and jewels are about shine.
Listen looks like glisten but means to hear.

sc1.tip: Look for "wet leaves," "in the sunlight," and "like tiny jewels." Wet things shining in the sun glisten.

traps.why: Growing dim is the opposite of shining.
Hear carefully means listen, a word that only looks like glisten.
Glistening things are often wet, but glisten means shine.

syn2.tip: Glisten is a light word. Picture raindrops on a car or sweat on a runner catching the sunlight.

sc2.stem: The old copper penny looked dull in my pocket, but after I washed it and set it on the wet sink, it began to _____ under the bathroom light.

traps.why: Fade matches "dull," but "but" shows the penny changed after washing.
Wet metal can rust, but that makes it duller, not brighter.
Coins jingle, but the clue is about how it looked under the light.

sc2.tip: "Looked dull... but" signals a contrast. After washing, the wet penny caught the light, so it began to glisten.

example: It is unkind to jeer at the other team.
hook: Jeer rhymes with cheer but means nearly the opposite: rude shouting that makes fun of someone.

traps.why: Praising someone is saying nice things, the opposite of jeering.
Peer looks like jeer but means to look closely.
Complaining is grumbling about something, not making fun of someone.

syn1.tip: Picture a rude crowd booing and shouting insults. Jeer is a mean word, so pick the choice about making fun of someone.

sc1.stem: Good sports never _____ at the other team, even when a player misses an easy shot.

traps.why: Good sports do cheer, so "never cheer" makes no sense here.
Smiling is friendly, and good sports often smile at opponents.
Peer looks like jeer but means look closely.

sc1.tip: "Good sports never" do something rude when a player "misses an easy shot." Making fun of a mistake is jeering.

traps.why: Cheering someone on is supportive, the opposite of jeering.
Look closely at means peer, a word that only looks like jeer.
Laughing along is friendly; jeering is rude laughing at someone.

syn2.tip: Jeer has a nasty feeling. You jeer at someone when you shout rude things to make them feel bad.

sc2.stem: Because some fans began to _____ at our goalie whenever she missed, the referee warned them that poor sportsmanship would get them sent home.

traps.why: Cheering is good sportsmanship, so no referee would warn them for it.
Waving is friendly, not poor sportsmanship.
Glancing at a goalie is harmless; it wouldn't get fans sent home.

sc2.tip: Look at the effect: the referee warned them about "poor sportsmanship." Rude behavior "whenever she missed" means they jeered.

meaning: to be slow; to waste time
example: Don't dawdle on the way to school.
hook: A kid who dawdles pokes along, stopping at every bug and puddle on the way.

traps.why: Hurrying is moving fast, the opposite of dawdling.
Doodle sounds like dawdle but means to draw little pictures.
Slow kids may complain, but dawdle is about taking too long.

syn1.tip: Picture a kid poking at every bug on the way to school. Dawdle has a slow, time-wasting feeling.

sc1.stem: Mom warned Theo not to _____ on the walk to school, moving at a snail's pace and poking at every bug.

traps.why: Theo was moving at a snail's pace, not hurrying.
Doodle sounds like dawdle but means drawing, not moving slowly.
Shouting is noisy, but the clue is about moving slowly.

sc1.tip: The clue is "moving at a snail's pace and poking at every bug." Going that slowly is dawdling.

traps.why: Rushing ahead is the opposite of being slow.
That means doodle, which only sounds like dawdle.
Dawdling can make you late, but it means being slow, not arriving.

syn2.tip: Parents often say "Don't dawdle" when you are taking forever. It means being slow and wasting time.

sc2.stem: Kayla usually rushes through breakfast, but on lazy Saturday mornings she likes to _____ over her pancakes for nearly an hour.

traps.why: Hurry matches "usually rushes," but "but" shows Saturdays are different.
People argue over things, but nothing in the sentence suggests a fight.
Panic is a worried feeling, wrong for a lazy, relaxed morning.

sc2.tip: "Usually rushes... but" signals a contrast. On "lazy" mornings she takes "nearly an hour," so she dawdles.
